Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.
McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.
"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."
For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"
McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.
Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."
Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.
"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.
Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.
Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.
The high price of cutting benefits
About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.
To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.
Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.
The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.
One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.
"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.
Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."
Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.
Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."
Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."
"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."
Confusion and longer wait times
The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.
As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."
State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.
Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.
"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.
"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.
Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.
McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.
His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.
"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."
When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.
Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.
McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."
"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."
Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.
The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.
Nebraska's health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.
He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.
"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.
The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.
"We definitely had fun"
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.
"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.
Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.
"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.
Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."
"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.
CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.
In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.
"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.
Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.
"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.
Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and "process guides" — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.
"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.
Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.
Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system, according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.
In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.
Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.
"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."
Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."
Dropping Medicaid enrollment
As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.
Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.
As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.
Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.
McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.
"The cancer has grown so much," he said.
He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.
KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

The sound of firecrackers filling the air is not far away as Deepavali draws closer. But the excitement of bursting firecrackers comes with a word of caution from ophthalmologists as they warn that a moment of carelessness can cause eye injuries ranging from minor abrasions to severe ocular trauma.
M. Elangovan, director, Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital (RIO-GOH), Chennai, said that there are different types of crackers. “Bursting types (explosive crackers) will produce irregular, small and forcible particles in all directions and are the most dangerous. These particles can travel at such a velocity that they could hit or penetrate any soft surface. Then, there is direct heat injury caused by crackers such as sparklers that can cause scar formations in the cornea or conjunctiva due to the heat generated. Sudden and close exposure to bright light-emitting crackers can also cause bleaching or temporary blackout due to the impact on the rod and cone cells in the retina,” he explained.

Social media users are spreading seven rules that U.S. President Donald Trump has allegedly proposed to limit privileges for lawmakers in Congress.
The alleged rules, according to many Facebook posts, included proposals like removing pensions for Congress members and requiring lawmakers to participate in the same government-run social services many Americans use, like Medicare for health care insurance and Social Security for retirement paychecks. Here's how the claim usually went, per the aforementioned posts:
I'm in agreement From Fox News. I wonder how loud it'll get if Trump could pull this off. It will be interesting.
President Trump is asking everyone to share this, in three days, most people in the United States will have seen the message. This is an idea that should be passed around, regardless of political party.
The TRUMP Rules:
1. Tenure / No Pension. A Congressman/woman collects a salary while in office and receives no pay when they're out of office. And no more perks go with them.
2. Congress (past, present, & future) participates in Social Security. All funds in the Congressional retirement fund move to the Social Security system immediately. All future funds flow into the Social Security system, and Congress participates with the American people. It may not be used for any other purpose.
3. Congress must purchase their own retirement plan, just as ALL Americans do.
4. Congress will no longer vote themselves a pay raise. Congressional pay will rise at the ok same rate as the COLA for monthly Social Security recipients minus 1% if having a budget balance deficit.
5. Congress loses their current care system and participates in the same health care system (Medicare) as the American people.
6. Congress must equally abide by all laws they impose on the American people (i.e. NO MORE INSIDER TRADING!!!).
7. All contracts with past and present Congressmen/women are void. The American people did not make this contract with Congressmen/women. Congress made all these contracts by and for themselves.
Serving in Congress is an honor and privilege, NOT a career.
The Founding Fathers envisioned citizen legislators should serve their term(s), then go home and go back to work … not get all kinds of freebies. Term limits of 2 terms and treat them like a regular citizen!
You will need to copy and paste.
I AGREE SO I'M SHARING!
Meanwhile, Snopes readers asked about similar posts and searched the website using the keywords "Trump rules."
The above text is a copypasta — a copy-and-pasted internet hoax common on Facebook. As Snopes has previously reported, variants of this particular copypasta have spread online since at least 2009, when a version of the rules listed above were labeled "The 28th Amendment" and attributed to business magnate Warren Buffet.
Internet users circulated it as the "Congressional Reform Act of 2017" during Trump's first term and the "Congressional Reform Act of 2025" in 2025, during his second term.
Fox News, which the copypasta cited as its source, has not reported on "The TRUMP Rules" as of this writing, per a search of the news outlet's website. As of this writing, Trump has also not posted about this particular copypasta online, according to two databases that track his social media output. The White House web page for news releases did not reference these supposed rules. Finally, a search for "The TRUMP Rules" on Google returned no credible and relevant results treating the list as a legitimate proposal.
Thus, we have rated this claim false.
The so-called reforms listed in the act also include a mixture of rules that already exist and proposals that would actually change existing policy. Here's a breakdown of what these supposed reforms would and would not change:
Do Congress members receive pensions?
Congress members, like most federal employees, are eligible for a pension. Here's the pension eligibility requirements, per the Congressional Research Service:
Members of Congress are eligible for a pension at the age of 62 if they have completed at least 5 years of service. Members are eligible for a pension at age 50 if they have completed 20 years of service, or at any age after completing 25 years of service. The amount of the pension depends on length of service (as measured in months) and the average of the highest three years of salary. By law, the starting amount of a Member's retirement annuity may not exceed 80% of his or her final salary.
Do Congress members pay into Social Security? Do they pay into their own retirement plans?
Per our previous reporting, Congress members have paid into Social Security since 1984, when they first became eligible for Social Security benefits.
Congress members first elected in 1984 or later are covered automatically under the Federal Employees' Retirement System, which other government workers use, and can decline coverage.
Aside from Social Security, lawmakers elected before 1984 can be covered under the Civil Service Retirement System, a separate pension plan, CSRS Offset, which is a mix of CSRS and Social Security, or Social Security alone. Lawmakers also pay into these plans — how much they pay and which plans they pay into differs based on when they were elected.
Can Congress members approve a pay raise for themselves?
Congress members can vote for a pay raise as dictated by the Constitution, but the raise doesn't take effect until the next election due to the 27th Amendment. Technically, a law passed in 1989 grants Congress an automatic cost-of-living pay raise, but lawmakers have blocked those pay increases from taking effect for years. Rank-and-file members of Congress, who receive $174,000 annually as of this writing, have not increased their pay since 2009.
Do Congress members have their own health care system? Do they participate in Medicare?
Under the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly known as Obamacare, lawmakers must give up the insurance coverage previously provided to them via the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and buy health insurance through a plan or exchange created under the act. The Office of Personnel Management has also dictated that members of Congress must purchase through DC Health Link, a program offered under the ACA.
Members of Congress also pay into Medicare and are eligible for it, just like any American.
Are Congress members allowed to participate in insider trading?
Congress members are allowed to trade stock, but legally, they're not supposed to conduct insider trading. The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 — known as the STOCK Act — prohibits members of Congress from using "any nonpublic information derived from the individual's position ... or gained from performance of the individual's duties, for personal benefit."
Critics argue the STOCK Act failed to stop insider trading, however, and no member of Congress has been prosecuted for insider trading under the STOCK Act as of this writing — although policy experts have said there's been "persistent credible allegations" of insider trading since the act passed.

Breast cancer begins long before the lump: why diet and lifestyle matter
While genetic predisposition is one factor, a majority of breast cancers develop in women with no family history: metabolic health and physical inactivity play a role too, and it is important for women to know about these factors
Students seen taking part in a ‘Pink Umbrella’ walk to create awareness on breast cancer. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
Last month, celebrated as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reminded us, as it does every year, about the importance of mammograms, early diagnosis, and advances in treatment. These messages save lives and deserve continued attention. However, there is another conversation that often receives far less attention: the role of food, physical activity, obesity, diabetes, physical activity, and metabolic health in breast cancer.
In my oncology clinic, patients are often surprised when I bring up these topics. They say, “Doctor, I knew breast cancer was related to family history. I didn’t know that lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and obesity had anything to do with it.”

While the Friday after Thanksgiving has traditionally been the busiest shopping day of the year, Black Friday deals have gradually spread well beyond the day. First came Cyber Monday, then Cyber Week. Now, early Black Friday deals kick off before November has even started. The tricky part for early birds is knowing what’s a genuine deal and what’s likely to go even lower when Black Friday arrives.
The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we only highlight deals on devices we've tested and would recommend to our own friends and family. Some of these picks may be cheaper for Black Friday, but these are the discounts that have caught our eye so far.
Updated November 7: We've added new deals on Google Pixel 11 phones, Google Pixel earbuds, a Rocco minifridge, a Dreo space heater, and a Petkit automatic litter box. We've also checked for accuracy throughout. Louryn Strampe contributed to this story.
The best trackers for anyone with an iPhone; you can use them to keep tabs on your keys, luggage, bike, or whatever else you worry might go missing. Each AirTag location is marked clearly in the Find My app. The battery should last you a year, and we have a guide on how to replace your AirTag battery. Just please don’t use them to track people. This is the lowest price we have seen on the single tag, but it drops this low pretty frequently.
For Apple fans with an iPhone or MacBook, the Apple AirPods Max 2 are the best over-ear headphones. They offer great sound quality, effective noise cancellation, and good transparency modes. They are usually a little too pricey for our tastes compared to Sony and Bose options, but at $100 off, they look more tempting. Before you pull the trigger, they will likely drop by at least another $30 for Black Friday.
If you want to pair wireless earbuds with your iPhone and enjoy a seamless, feature-rich experience, you should snag the AirPods Pro 3. They are comfy, boast top-notch active noise cancellation, and can even translate some languages in real time. That said, they are at this price often enough that I hesitate to call it a great deal, and they will likely drop by another $20 for Black Friday.
At $10 below their all-time lowest price, this is a great deal if you're in the market for our top Android earbuds. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are comfortable, have a long-lasting battery, and have clear sound with seamless noise cancellation. We think they're especially good for listeners with small ears. They might get cheaper for Black Friday or Cyber Monday, but likely not by much.
Google's full Pixel 11 lineup is on sale for less than we've seen all year long. Like some of these other tech deals, it's possible that we see prices drop a bit more later this month, but we don't anticipate it being by much. Each of these phones features incredible cameras and snappy performance, and they're available in a wide array of eye-catching colors. Whether you go with the base Google Pixel 11 or opt for the 11 Pro or 11 Pro XL, you'll be getting one of our favorite Android phones.
With a great camera, solid performance, and super-slick software features, the Pixel 10 Pro is an excellent Android phone. It also has proper Qi2 support for fast wireless charging, but more importantly, the magnets inside make it easy to attach to docks and chargers. Its bigger sibling, the Pro XL, has been my daily driver for most of the last year, and it has served me well. It has frequently dropped to this price before, but I still think it’s a good deal. Note that Amazon prices may vary based on the seller, so double check before adding to cart.
This is one of our favorite 3-in-1 chargers for keeping your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch charged up from a single outlet. The unique feature is its height adjustability, enabling it to pull double duty as a tripod for shooting video or FaceTime calls with family or friends. It has been on sale (close to half price) for a while now but has never been lower than $60 at Best Buy. Snap it up while you still can.
Gadgets are too boring. I want more anthropomorphized devices in my life. Ugreen simply added a wee robot face to this wireless charger that changes its expression based on the charging status. I immediately like it more than all my old faceless chargers. The charging pad supports Qi2/MagSafe and tilts up to 70 degrees to reveal a second pad to charge AirPods or other wireless earbuds. It even has a USB-C port for a third gadget. At 40 percent off, this is the lowest price I’ve seen.
My pick for the best budget Wi-Fi router dips down to this price fairly often, but it’s a great deal for a Wi-Fi 7 router with four antennas, a 2.5-Gbps WAN, a 2.5-Gbps LAN, and three gigabit LAN ports. It’s only dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), so there’s no 6-GHz option, and performance is limited, but for a small home with modest demands, this is a tough price to beat.
I always associate Black Friday with footage of excited shoppers struggling to carry huge TVs out of big box stores. The reality is that most Black Friday TV deals are on terrible models you should never buy. But this deal on LG’s 55-inch C6 OLED TV caught my eye. At $400 off the regular price, it is the cheapest it's ever been. The sale price on the 65-incher also makes it a better option than the entry-level LG B6 we just reviewed. Just make sure you pair it with a streaming device and disable the tracking.
This security camera records video at up to 2K at 30 frames per second, offers a 150-degree field of view, and connects directly to your Wi-Fi network. The Tapo app can detect motion (person, pet, vehicle) and enables you to set activity zones and privacy zones. The two-way audio is okay, and there’s a built-in alarm function. You can also slip a microSD card in for local recording. It lacks HDR, but it still earns a spot in our best outdoor security cameras guide. It has bounced between $90 and $65 for the last year, but it’s now down to $60.
It may not be one of the best video doorbells you can buy, but at this sale price, Blink’s latest wired doorbell is the cheapest option worth considering. It delivers reasonably good 2K footage and passable two-way audio, though it’s definitely less responsive than some other options on the market. If you want person detection and cloud storage, you’ll also need to spring for the subscription (from $3 a month). The battery version is also on sale at $39 ($41 off).
Permanent outdoor lights are a great way to avoid having to get up the ladder every holiday season. They offer simple white lighting, different colors, and also holiday-themed lighting effects. Eufy’s lights aren’t the brightest, but they hold up well against the competition and support Matter, so you can tie them into any smart home ecosystem. All lengths are on sale, but the 200-foot string has the best discount and is at its lowest price ever.
If you like to run an organized household, the best digital wall calendars are sure to appeal. You can use them to sync your digital calendars, create lists of chores, and plan your family meals. The Everblog HomeCal is our pick for folks who can’t stomach another subscription. It also works like a digital photo frame if you upload your snaps, and you can log into apps like Netflix and Spotify on it. This is the lowest we’ve seen it drop so far.
A good laptop docking station lets you convert your laptop into a desktop for a comfier experience when you’re working from home, and this compact beauty from Belkin is one of our top picks. GaN technology (gallium nitride semiconductors, a faster, more compact alternative to silicon) lets Belkin pack more ports than you can shake a USB-C cable at, including 96-watt power delivery, three 4K display ports, a gigabit Ethernet port, and more. This deal equals the lowest price we’ve seen.
Learning about the wildlife in your garden can be a lot of fun, and the best smart bird feeders are an ideal way to see which feathered friends are in the area. The thoughtfully designed Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 has a removable 1.5-liter dual-hopper seed reservoir, is easy to clean, and boasts a solar roof to keep the camera charged up. It snaps 8-megapixel photos, captures 4K video, and includes a nifty AI bird-identification feature. We’ve seen it on sale before, but never this low.
This recently released designer minifridge from Rocco is being tested by WIRED editor Kat Merck, but so far, she likes it. It has a minimalist design, a dark glass door, and sliding drawers for smooth organization of all your must-have snacks and drinks. Some might use it for wine or beer, but I dream of this bedside for a crisp Diet Coke and some midnight charcuterie. Every color is discounted for Black Friday.
Our favorite space heater has only sold for less once before, and that price was a mere $5 cheaper than you'll get right now. Space heaters tend to get more expensive during the winter months. If you know you're in the market, this might be a great fit. It checks every box for safety, efficient heating, and aesthetics. It doesn't get too loud, and we like that the display can be dimmed and the control beeps can be muted.
Automatic litter boxes are sought after, but can be a hefty investment. This is a solid deal on our top pick. It should work well for most one- or two-cat households. It cleans efficiently and even has a deodorizing spray that it dispenses as needed. We wish the app were a little easier to use and more feature-rich, but if you won't miss bells and whistles like a camera inside or AI waste detection, this is a solid deal.

On Nov. 6, after Republicans lost the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, purported footage of U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., spread in which he was unresponsive when a reporter asked for his reaction to the GOP's losses and whether he thought "Republicans would get anything done in the lame-duck session."
In the clip, McConnell, seated in a wheelchair, stared ahead, blinking a few times while someone (possibly an aide) spoke to the reporter off-camera. McConnell briefly glanced at the reporter.
Posts on X (archived), Facebook and YouTube sharing the video questioned the state of McConnell's health. (The senator had been hospitalized for several months earlier in 2026.)
The footage, which appeared on Newsmax show "Frontline" on Nov. 6, is authentic and was taken by Newsmax reporter Kilmeny Duchardt on Capitol Hill. There is no visible manipulation with artificial intelligence or other digital editing tools. As such, we rate this claim as true.
Snopes reached out to McConnell's staff to learn more about his health and his reaction in the video. We will update this post if we learn more.
On Nov. 6, "Frontline" host Carl Higbie shared the clip of McConnell on his show. The footage is available on Newsmax as well as YouTube.
Off screen, someone interrupted Duchardt, who said, "OK, no problem," suggesting she was interacting with the senator's aide.
Higbie reacted to the video saying, "That can't be legal, he's a vegetable!" He asked Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general under President Donald Trump, for his reaction. Wold said:
This isn't just an ideological conflict for the soul of the Republican Party now, it is a generational one. We are tired of the geriatric gerontocracy ruling the conservative movement … the idea that [Republican Sen. Thom Tillis] and these folks now want to negotiate on things like amnesty with the Democrats. Look, you can't negotiate with a tiger when your face is inside of its mouth, OK? And what we need now are fighters who are not wheelchair-bound, but who can actually stand on their own two feet.
Over the years, Snopes readers have frequently asked us if the senator is dead or dying. Snopes has reported on many rumors about McConnell's health, including investigating a claim the U.S. government paid for his polio treatment.

Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children's and teenagers' use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.
The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans' exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.
Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.
However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on November 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared.
According to the civil society coalition Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organised crime.
“I don't think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”
The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.
Benigno Gomez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities' need to reduce students' time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren't allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.
During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico's Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”
Parents seek reassurance
Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of October 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town -- which relies on mango and shrimp production -- was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.
More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.
“Just hearing my daughter's voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community -- admitting that she didn't hesitate to interrupt her daughter's class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”
In defence of the regulation
For Israel Sanchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government's decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organisation, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sanchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.
Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialisation and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximise our attention.”
The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.

Lately a new kind of pitch has found its way into my inbox. “Not sure if you've heard,” writes someone named Nick, “but AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI are paying media companies such as Wired $350K to $1.8M as a one time fee for a copy of their old work records (documents, emails, slack messages, tickets, etc.) for training better models.”
Another email with a similar pitch (adding call transcripts to the list of desired information) raised the stakes to a possible $2 million. “Public data is exhausted, and the labs are spending over $45B on private data to build better models,” writes someone named Cora.
While I was aware that AI companies are buying expert data from various sources, there hasn’t been that much attention paid to it. But once I looked into it, I discovered that this business is way bigger than I suspected—and according to its practitioners, it could have as much impact on workers and society as the data centers that are dominating the news these days.
The companies that contacted me are part of an industry boom in data acquisition that’s been quietly buying the workflows of sizable companies and is still so hungry that it’s bleeding into our inboxes. A freelance writer recently wrote about her experience with a company called Handshake, which offered her $1,000 for her work on a single story. (She didn’t sell.) A representative from Handshake confirmed the offer to me: “We license professional documents across a lot of fields so the labs can test and train how models handle real knowledge work,” he said. “Journalism is one of those fields.” Handshake tells me that a big part of its business is buying graduate students’ papers and coursework.
An entrepreneur friend of mine tells me he’s been getting mail from multiple companies whose business is “helping startups wind down their companies," as one email from a company named Sunset explained it. “We handle the full process, scrubbing and anonymizing the data so the company people and any identifying details are stripped out, then brokering the deal with the labs.”
Those newer data acquisition startups are hoping to achieve the quick success of the dominant companies in the field, which themselves are only a few years old. Industry leaders Handshake, Micro1, and Mercor are snapping up databases as if it were a modern gold rush. The industry leader seems to be Mercor, founded in 2023; last year its three cofounders became billionaires at 22. Like all the companies, it claims to have partnerships with just about all the major AI labs. (The response from the companies themselves was more circumspect: Anthropic acknowledges that there’s a big market for data, but told me that it doesn’t buy workflow from live companies like WIRED. OpenAI didn’t come up with a response before publication.)
In an interview, Mercor CEO Brendan Foody told me that the market is poised to explode as the AI industry seeks dramatically more data. Mercor originally started as an AI recruiting company, but as the team got to know the players, it learned that the big labs were frustrated by the quality of the data. Generally, the industry had been hiring experts to simulate actual workflow, but that didn’t capture the messiness of an actual operating business. He urged me to consider that Big AI has two bottomless needs: compute and data. While the industry is very publicly making giant investments in the former, data gathering is just as important.
Foody is ready when I bring up privacy concerns. When a business streams the data to Mercor, the company strips out any personal identifying information, or PII. This de-identification can be verified, he says. Like all the people in data acquisition I spoke to, he felt that technology has solved the privacy issues of buying all that information.
Not surprisingly, Micro1 CEO Ali Ansari agrees that the data-buying market will soon approach that of AI’s compute infrastructure. He says that today, labs, enterprises, and robotics companies pay about $40 to $50 billion a year to get data. (I was unable to verify this.) “In the next two to four years, this is going to be over a trillion dollars a year,” says Ansari, who founded the company in 2022. Micro1 uses the information it buys largely to improve AI models it builds itself, but it also sells to big AI firms.
“Pretty much everybody’s trying to get into the data space now because there’s so much demand,” he says. “If you look at the YC startups, about half of them are data companies.” (Actually, it’s more—in the most recent YC batch, 40 of the 65 launched companies are classified as data startups.)
The Wild West aspect to this quest for fresh data got rare exposure when a bankrupt Spirit Airlines put its digital assets up for sale. The corpus included 80,000 email accounts, 500 million internal messages, 20.6 million Microsoft Sharepoint files, and a million time-card records. Google seemingly got the prize with a $10 million bid, but then Micro1 topped it by $2.5 million, setting off an argument over who the winner was. Presently the sale is on hold, for a reason that calls into question the entire practice of selling off human workflow: The flight attendants’ union has charged that the sale involved their private information.
The union’s objections cast a light on the dark side of this gold rush. Despite the claims of virtually all the data companies that no PII goes into AI models, critics feel that there is still danger of personal data leaking out. “It’s not clear that anonymizing can fully get rid of privacy issues,” says Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, general counsel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which has filed an amicus brief on behalf of the flight attendants. “Emails and Teams messages contain unstructured data, which is harder to root out. There may be messages where employees talk about doctor’s appointments or family issues.”
“We haven't set the norms and the standards for data acquisition, and it’s not being done appropriately ” says Gordon Ritter, a venture capitalist who has taken on the issue as a cause. “The AI industry is moving far faster than our ability to actually set the standards, and it's partially intentional.”
Probably the most troubling aspect of the data-gathering movement is that, in essence, it enlists workers, not always with explicit consent, to contribute to an effort where the ultimate goal is to replace or automate the human work that goes into all those documents, messages, and emails. When Mercor says that its motto is “Organizing human intelligence to power the AI economy,” the unspoken message is that the economy of flesh and blood workers will have less work to do. As the president of the flight attendant’s union told an interviewer: “This is really only data that became valuable in the age of AI in order to train models to replace jobs and commodify other portions of working in a work environment.”
When I ask Micro1’s Ansari whether one day the default for corporations will be selling their workflow data to big AI companies on an ongoing basis, he answers affirmatively. “I think it’s going to become more common than ads as a revenue line item for companies,” he says. I note that there is already considerable pushback to AI, and that people might not be happy with the idea that everything they do at work gets funneled into the maw of a big AI model.
“I think it’s a fair point,” says Ansari. But, in his view, such objections will be manageable. He suggests that workers will understand that the fruits of their labor will result in better AI models, which will make their lives easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in.” (I’ve found that the future abundance that AI will supposedly produce is a handy justification for all sorts of compromises.)
I did follow up on one of the cold pitches I got, from a woman whose email domain was gorexen.com. A “gorexen,” by the way, is a fusion of two Pokemon critters that “siphons the body fluids of prey through its thin, tubular mouth.” She set up a meeting with me with a two-year-old company called Tenkara (the name seems to be associated with a type of Japanese fly fishing). I found myself talking to “head of commercialization” Jonah Stillman, a young startup-looking dude sitting in an office in San Francisco.
I began peppering him with questions. Tenkara’s quest for data seems to be to boost the quality of its AI model to run office operations for manufacturing companies. (How WIRED’s archives would help is a mystery.) He confirmed that a big part of his job is doing calls like this to snap up data. I told him that the set of our meeting gave me a Glengarry Glen Ross vibe, but he wasn’t familiar with the reference.
I am, of course, not authorized to sell the documentation of WIRED’s editorial process to an AI company, and I did not risk my job by offering Jonah and his company the goods. I also wouldn’t be too pleased if my bosses made the sale.

The 16 Best Subscription Boxes for Kids
Featured in this article
Rather than give your kid a big, expensive present once or twice a year, why not surprise them with subscription boxes for kids once a month? I have an 8-year-old and a 10-year-old, and they are thrilled when a package arrives in the mail that isn’t bills, replacement chargers from Amazon, or Garnet Hill catalogs.
Subscription boxes for kids can be useful educational supplements for homeschool or remote learning. Most are consumable, so your kid can have a treat that won't be left to molder in a corner of a playroom until they're 25. They're also handy to have around the house if you can’t send your sniffly kid to school or a big indoor birthday party. As a bonus, they’re usually affordable. I tested some of the subscriptions on this list, like the Lovevery Reading Skill Set 3-box set ($160), and I bought others for my kids and their friends. These are our favorites. Be sure to check out our other buying guides for kids, including the Best Strollers, the Best Kids Bikes, and the Best STEM Toys.
Updated November 2025: We refreshed information on all the crates, added new pictures, and added the Lovevery reading skill set box, CrunchLabs Creative Kits, Bookroo, and Enlightened Generation. We also updated links and prices.
- Best Box for All Ages KiwiCo Kiwi Crate We subscribed to Kiwi Crate's monthly subscription for so long that the company sent us a cautious email asking whether it was OK that we were getting repeat boxes. I now check in every year to discover that yes, the company's boxes are still amazing. Each box comes with a single, delightful, themed activity that's appropriate for a kid aged anywhere from a few months old to 18 years. A recent Delivery Bot ($24) aimed for 9+ years entertained my 8-year-old son for an afternoon. I can't extoll the virtues of this crate enough. The instructions are clear enough for young kids to follow. The pieces are easy for little fingers to manipulate (he did need some adult help adjusting the wheels), and the final project is always delightful: a little remote-controlled delivery bot that you can put things in and drive your sister and mother (literally) crazy! Kiwi Crate offers various gift boxes for all ages, from toddlers under 2 to teenagers. You can also select one-off boxes for specific interests, such as music, mazes, holiday crafts, and robots, or different themes, like Atlas Crates for geography or Doodle Crates for drawing. Kiwi is noted for its careful curation—the projects are fun and age-appropriate, but it doesn't break my kids' hearts when they inevitably lose or destroy them. If you're looking for just one crate, get this one and no one in your house will be disappointed.
- Best Clothing Box Stitch Fix Kids Clothes Box As my kids have gotten older, shopping for their clothes has become more and more difficult. One child has sensory issues. He hates stiff or tight fabrics, clothes that are too fuzzy, certain colors, and all jackets. The other is a budding fashionista who is on a running team and dances and needs workout clothes, baggy jeans, or whatever else happens to not be in her closet at the moment. Whenever I find a sweatshirt they will wear, Target immediately discontinues it and my cycle of living hell continues. Stitch Fix will cure what ails you, and you can start or stop your subscription as needed. You enter your child's age and size; color preferences and patterns to avoid; themes that they like; features to avoid (no crop tops); activities they like; and most importantly, budgets for every category. Stitch Fix sends you a box and you and your child keep what you like and send back the rest. I recently re-tested the box with my now-10-year-old, and both of us liked the new picks. I was able to easily get an assortment of athletic clothing for her, as well as a cloud sweater she adores. This is an easy way to update wardrobes for kids who grow out of everything instantaneously and are really hard to shop for. ★ Alternative: I also tried a box from Kidpik (starts at $100) for my now-8-year-old. Kidpik's selection is so appealing and stylish that my husband asked if the clothes came in his size. The clothes are much sturdier than the Stitch Fix selections. However, the selection is much smaller, and my son rejected half the clothes that Kidpik sent. Stitch Fix's extensive style quiz ensures that there's at least a fighting chance that your child will like any given garment.
- Best Puzzles Highlights Puzzlemania Book Club Subscription My kids are 8 and 10, and they are obsessed with puzzles of all kinds. This is great because they are at the age when they need to practice reading, and there are only so many times you can force them to reenact The Lord of the Rings trilogy. The classic children's publisher Highlights also offers a few different reading and activity boxes, in addition to the iconic magazine. My kids and I tried the I Can Read book club ($14/month) and the Puzzlemania subscription ($4/month). Puzzlemania was delightful. Each puzzle book is 32 pages and has a wide variety of puzzles, including sticker puzzles, word searches, Mad Libs–style storytelling, and riddles. We spent several afternoons filling in sticker puzzle pieces and playing the Highlights version of Sudoku. They both loved this puzzle pack so much that I bought the Highlights Great Big Book of Really Hard Puzzles ($13), which I'm anticipating will keep them occupied for at least one weekend trip or two.
- Best Science Box CrunchLabs Hack Pack This is coming with a big disclaimer: CrunchLabs, the company founded by former NASA engineer and YouTuber Mark Rober, says that its Hack Pack is for people over 14 years old. However, my 8-year-old put it together with minimal help in an afternoon, although it did take him much longer than the 60-minute estimated time for a teenager. ("Why are you so worried, Mama?" he admonished me when I showed skepticism. "The drawings show you exactly what to do.") Each box has a robot to assemble that illustrates a STEM principle, complete with a battery and an Arduino microcontroller. You can also unlock a video, but the drawings in the included manual were clear and big enough that we could put it together without the help of the internet. Our box had the infrared turret to illustrate the principle of infrared communication. My 8-year-old was thrilled, hiding it and using the infrared remote to ambush his sister with a barrage of foam darts. You can also unlock a web-based coding console to hack the robot by locking out other users. It's expensive, but the price-per-payoff valuation is worth it—the STEM principle it illustrated was interesting, the build process was engaging without being frustrating, and the project itself was very fun. ★ Alternatives: I love Mark Rober, so this is obviously the best box, but there are a ton of different science boxes. Kiwi Crate has a dedicated science crate. For much younger kids, Little Passports has an Early Explorers box ($25/month) aimed at children as young as 3. Science Expeditions is aimed at children over the age of 8; the projects are a little bizarre, like extracting the DNA from a strawberry. Neither my child nor I knew what we were supposed to do with this. Finally, a lot of people like Steve Spangler's Science Club STEM kits ($35), which are huge and come with multiple projects. These are fairly simple, like a marshmallow masher that you could Google yourself and make with stuff you probably have at home. However, I thought it was worth it to have the lesson and objects bundled so I didn't have to drink and empty a plastic soda bottle myself.
- Best Craft Kit CrunchLabs Creative Kit CrunchLabs is great, but it is aimed at older kids—my son needed a bit of help. The newly launched Creative Kit is aimed at 6- to 10-year-olds, so it's for a slightly younger demographic. I'm shocked at how well-thought-out these kits are. CrunchLabs sent the Ice Cream Stand and the Architect's Treehouse. The morning after both of the crates were assembled, both begged to get more. Even after my 8-year-old son had put together the tiny ice cream stand, he continued to play with it all afternoon. It comes with delightful little accessories, like moldable ice cream in different “flavors” (colors), little toppings, and tiny cones and cups. (I was just offered a tiny scoop of “Super Strawberry Smash.”) Unlike most tie-dye or pinwheel kits, the Creative Kit encourages play long after the craft has been completed. My 10-year-old likes these better than the Kiwi Crates because “it's like building a tiny town!”
- Best Reading Support Box Lovevery Reading Skills Support Box Now, my third-grader is a voracious reader. But it took him a few years and some hurdles to get to this point. In that time, the Reading Skill Set ($155) by Lovevery was invaluable. These books and games are a complete homeschool reading curriculum aimed at kindergarten through the second grade, but we used them as supplementary materials. Each set comes with three separate components: lovely, sturdy games; a few books; and parent course materials to explain both. The set was particularly crucial for my son during the second grade years. I particularly liked that the skill set addressed common errors and advanced vowel rules. It is really hard to remember what the letter “e” does in a word! My son found the board game to be very fun, like Chutes & Ladders but for word play. It was almost a disappointment when we realized, at the end of the summer, that he could actually read perfectly.
- Best Book Club Literati Book Club If you and your family are struggling to find reading material for your required 20 minutes of reading per day for school (that's not Wings of Fire over and over again), I highly recommend a book subscription. We paid for a Literati subscription until its curation system worked against them. Literati offers book clubs that take newborn children up to their teens. Literati will send your child five books each month. Return any books you don't like and pay Amazon's list price for the rest. Every book was a hit, and each kid had to have every book in every box. For the sake of my wallet and our already-groaning bookshelves, I had to stop the subscription. You can gift a subscription or a one-time, age-appropriate theme box with a card, personalized stickers, and artwork. It's a great way to expose your children (and yourself!) to wonderful new works of art or literature without dragging them to a bookstore. ★ Alternatives: Having to send back books your kid loves is a trap. If you want to just get and keep a book subscription, Bookroo ($20) is what you want; my son's first box just arrived with The Map Trap, of Andrew “Frindle” Clements fame, and he loves it. Also, if you or your child is bilingual, you might want to consider Curio ($58/quarterly), which currently offers themed books and audio reading guides in different age ranges for Spanish, Chinese, and French.
- Best Snack Box Universal Yums Snack Box This is the best box. And kids need to snack every day anyway, so you might as well read and learn while you're at it. My kids tear into the Universal Yums snack box like a very small pack of very tiny wolves. My colleague Louryn Strampe recommends it in her Best Snack Boxes guide and Best Subscriptions guide. You can choose a small, medium, or large box, and it includes an informative booklet, games, and trivia. Food is a great way to learn about geography and different cultures. Every month, my kids and I open the box, look at a globe, and do a lot of Googling. We have liked several foreign candies enough to start ordering them separately on Amazon. Even when the snacks aren't a hit—I got the salted truffle French fries all to myself—my kids always try them and ask a lot of questions about why a country is called the Kingdom of Butterflies and when we can visit.
- Best Coding Box Lingo Subscription Box Lingo was founded by Aisha Bowe, a former NASA scientist, and is intended to bring STEM skills to children who may have been underexposed. That description does not precisely apply to my 7-year-old, but he nevertheless enjoyed this kit. We tried In the Driver's Seat ($75), which teaches you how to build a backup sensor for a car. Mileage will vary, and the kit is technically aged for sixth to 12th graders. However, my son and I found it easy to follow along once we figured out how to log in to the Lingo portal and access all the videos on his iPad. We followed the video instructions in the portal to learn how to build circuits on a breadboard using lights and resistors, and program to turn the lights on and off. I particularly like that it doesn't purport to teach children coding via puzzle pieces or blocks but uses an actual circuit board and a real programming environment. Lingo also offers teacher support if you get stuck. However, I should note that while the kit contains all the hardware components you need to build the sensor, you will need your own iPad or laptop to access the videos and instructions.
- Best for Preschoolers Lovevery Play Kit We first received a Lovevery kit when my son was 2 years old. Now he’s 8, and I still find the company’s sturdy, Montessori-inspired toys in use around our house. Lovevery (pronounced “love-every”) promotes what it calls stage-based learning. At each stage of development, babies need different (beautiful, colorful, durable) toys to help them develop different parts of their brain. It’s pretty cute to term every stage with a different focus, like The Inspector or The Explorer, although I have to admit that I’m not so sure my son enjoyed experimenting with gravity that much more at 10 months than at a year old (he still dropped things on the floor is what I’m saying). My much older daughter also enjoyed arranging giant, gorgeous felt flowers just as much as my son did. If you’re a special person in a little one’s life and want to send them attractive and sturdy toys to pass down to others, this is the best toy subscription to get. ★ Alternative: Is your toddler going through a specific (very annoying) phase, and you need some help? Lovevery also offers parent course packs (starting at $50) to address needs like potty training or getting a new sibling. The course pack offers access to the Lovevery app, video content, toys, and books.
- Best for Babies Lalo’s Play Boxes are made for the littlest people in our lives. There are 10 different boxes of toys that are designed for different months within the first two years of a kiddo’s life, starting at the zero-to-12-month infant stage. It’s available both as a subscription or a one-off purchase of a specific developmental window, such as three to four months or 16 to 18 months, and you can add it to a registry on Babylist. The toys are beautifully made with nontoxic materials. Most of the toys I tested with my son were made of wood, like the wooden blocks he likes to knock over from the 19 to 21 month box and the drum he plays from the 13 to 15 month set. Each box comes with a little Play Guide to describe how the toy is meant to be used and to stimulate their age group. I also liked when the booklet gave tips on how to use the toys when my son got older, too. I tried out two different Lalo Play Boxes and was happy to see that my son was usually interested in at least three of the items consistently, which is pretty great for a toddler! I’m honestly jealous of how pretty some of the toys are, and regularly resist the temptation to steal the cute Stacking Rocket for my bedside table. —Nena Farrell
- Best for Artists SketchBox Art supplies—drawing, painting, pastels—are the delight of my family's life. SketchBox is a monthly box, and each month has a theme that's put together by an artist. My daughter's charcoal box was assembled by mixed media artist Nikoli Shaver and included a graphite starter kit, a small pack of media-appropriate paper, an eraser, charcoal pencils, and more. This box has an amazing value—the Nitram starter kit alone costs $16, and my 10-year-old spent several days sketching, tapping, and blending. If you're unsure of where to start with watercolor or oil pastels and find wandering Blick's aisles to be intimidating, these boxes are a great place to start. You can get a basic box for $25 or a premium one for $35, which has a higher-quality selection plus a piece of art to inspire you. ★ Alternatives: Art subscriptions are a great way to buy an assortment of materials so that you don't find yourself with 400 extra pipe cleaners on your hands. The Kids Art Box ($38) is aimed at children 3 to 7 years old. It's expensive, but five activities are quite a lot, even though I did have to hunt through my house for supplementary materials like extra paintbrushes and jars. Finally, one of my favorite boxes is the Zollie (starting at $40) craft kits. These boxes are not subscription-based, but you can order up to five kits at once. Each kit has everything you need to complete several small fiber-art projects, like embroidering flowers or knitting washcloths. My 10-year-old spent several happy afternoons looking up the QR code, watching the videos, and teaching herself how to do slip stitches and French knots.
- Best Baking Kit Bake Eat Love Baking Kit Cooking and baking subscription boxes are some of the best subscription boxes I've tried. Feeding kids every day is a chore, and I welcome any way to get some variety. Bake Eat Love is the first kit I was just as excited to try as my kids. That said, the Bake Eat Love boxes are probably best suited for an older age group, with slightly more sophisticated palates. We tried the sampler box with tiramisu cupcakes. While I love the light, fluffy texture of tiramisu and the innovative recipe, my son was perturbed to find that a cupcake he assumed was chocolate tasted more like Mommy's coffee. The kit does include a few prepackaged ingredients, but as with most cooking and baking sets, you do have to have a basic set of cooking utensils and a few ingredients that might require an extra shopping trip, like mascarpone. ★ Alternatives: I have gifted several Raddish Kids cooking club subscriptions ($24) to several nieces and nephews. The recipes are extremely easy for little kids to follow (my children particularly loved making pretzels), and the included tiny utensils are adorable and perfect for tiny hands (and for moms who just like using tiny things). We also tried Eat2Explore ($30), which was founded by a graduate of the French Culinary Institute. Each box features fun tools, nonperishable seasonings, recipe cards, and educational booklets from different countries. The salmon teriyaki was not the right pick for a child who has described fish as smelling like “stinky garbage,” but he did love using the included chopsticks. This is a fun, relatively affordable way to try to expand a kid's picky palate.
- Best Sticker Club Stickii Club My kids' appetite for stickers is endless. I find them constantly, on the mirrors in our house, on their school planners and water bottles, and occasionally stuck to the back of my chair or in the car. Stickers are also an accessible way of supporting independent artists. Maybe you can't buy a painting or a T-shirt, but a sticker only costs a few dollars and you can display it everywhere. For $12 a month, Stickii Club offers three different sticker styles—Cute, Vintage, or Pop—along with a storage sleeve and three stationery items, like a notepad, card, or stamp. The club works with independent artists and illustrators (no AI-generated art yet) to produce sheets of original designs. We tried the Pop subscription. These stickers are marvelous. There's a huge variety in the sheets sent. Some are vinyl, some are transparent, but all are high quality and intricately detailed. The artist is also noted on each corner so we can look them up ourselves. My kids were delighted and traded them with each other like currency. I am now investing in Stickii folios (from $18) in the hopes that I can keep these just a little bit more organized (and sticking a few on my laptop while I'm at it). ★ Alternative: You can't pick the style of box with a Pipsticks Kids Club sticker pack ($20), but with such a big selection, there are bound to be stickers that your child or children will love. It includes 15 sheets of Pipstickers, collectible stickers, a postcard, an activity book, and more. I have two kids who love stickers, and even we found the classic pack to be a bit much; Pipsticks also has a petite pack option for $14.

The story so far: The Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report of 2021, released by the Office of the Registrar General of India recently, showed that India has maintained its Total Fertility Rate (TFR) at 2.0 — the same as reported in 2020. While the national average for TFR has remained the same, there is a wide regional variation in TFR data for States and Union Territories (UTs) reported independently.
The highest TFR was recorded in Bihar at 3.0 and the lowest was reported for West Bengal and Delhi at 1.4. The data went on to reveal that in the decade between 2009-11 and 2019-21, TFR has been on an overall decline, in States, and nationally, albeit at different rates.

ED attaches Rs 10-crore properties in J&K in central employment scheme fraud case
The loans were secured using dummy beneficiaries and fake invoices in collusion with J&K Bank officials, with 540 loan accounts turning NPA and outstanding dues touching around Rs 32 crore.
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has attached 11 properties worth Rs 10.63 crore in Jammu and Kashmir in connection with an alleged fraud involving loans sanctioned under the Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP).
The properties, comprising land and buildings, are located in Srinagar and Bandipora districts. According to the ED, they are held or controlled by suppliers-cum-brokers and a bank official involved in the misuse of the government employment scheme.
The ED's Srinagar Zonal Office issued a provisional attachment order to prevent the properties from being sold or transferred during the investigation. The action follows allegations that PMEGP loans were fraudulently obtained using fake documents and dummy beneficiaries, with the involvement of officials from two branches of Jammu and Kashmir Bank.
The agency began its investigation based on two cases registered by the CBI Anti-Corruption Bureau in Srinagar. The cases alleged that borrowers, bank officials and private individuals conspired to cheat J&K Bank and misappropriate loan funds. The CBI's ACB registered another case in the matter in June 2026.
During the investigation, the ED examined the Sumbal and Gamud Gadkhud branches of J&K Bank and found that 270 term loan accounts and 270 working capital accounts linked to the PMEGP scheme had turned into non-performing assets (NPAs). The total outstanding amount in these accounts was around Rs 32 crore.
The ED's investigation revealed that loans were sanctioned in the names of dummy beneficiaries using their identity documents and other details. Fake invoices from firms and companies that did not exist were submitted to secure the loans.
The central agency alleged that private individuals acting as suppliers-cum-brokers arranged these documents and worked in collusion with bank officials to facilitate the loan approvals.
The ED identified Hilal Ahmad Wani and others as key players in the fraud. They persuaded beneficiaries to apply for PMEGP loans and used their KYC documents and other papers to secure the funds.
According to the agency, fake invoices were generated in the names of firms registered under the suppliers-cum-brokers or their family members, even though the firms did not exist.
The money obtained through the fraud was subsequently moved through multiple bank accounts. The ED said part of the funds was used to construct or renovate properties held in the names of the accused or their family members, while the remaining amount was diverted for personal use.
The investigation has so far traced proceeds of crime worth Rs 11.37 crore, the agency said. It added that a substantial portion of the money had been siphoned off and that the accused were involved in diverting and concealing the funds.
The 11 properties worth Rs 10.63 crore have now been provisionally attached as part of the investigation.

‘Growing a beard doesn’t make you Revanth Reddy’: Telangana CM takes swipe at KT Rama Rao
Reddy also said political posturing without substance is like a fox trying to look like a tiger.
Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy on Saturday took a swipe at Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS) working president KT Rama Rao for allegedly copying his looks, saying “simply growing a beard does not make you look like Revanth Reddy”.
Reddy also said political posturing without substance is like a fox trying to look like a tiger, and that mere imitation would not earn KT Rama Rao, popularly known as KTR, the trust of the voters.
"Just as a fox cannot become a tiger by trying to mimic its stripes, you cannot become a tiger by imitating one. Simply growing a beard does not make you Revanth Reddy. It took him 50 years to grow a beard. Who knows how many more years it will take for him to gain some wisdom?" Reddy said, while addressing a gathering in Vikarabad.
"Until the leader changes the mindset, the people of Telangana will never trust (him),” he added.
He continued: "Even if you take 10 births or hang yourself from a toddy tree, you remain Taraka Rama Rao but cannot become Revanth Reddy in your life. You need the courage to take care of activists, keeping them close to your heart.”
There was no immediate comment from Rao or the BRS at the time of filing this report. The jibe is the latest in an ongoing war of words between the Congress and the BRS, with leaders from both parties trading barbs over governance, leadership and development in the state.
Reddy alleged that despite serving as chief minister for 10 years and the state budget touching ₹20 lakh crore, BRS president K Chandrasekhar Rao has not completed any pending irrigation projects.
Though the Congress government in undivided Andhra Pradesh planned the Pranahita Chevella project to provide irrigation to over 16 lakh acres, KCR transformed it into the Kaleshwaram project by changing its location and escalating the cost, the chief minister alleged. The project was constructed by KCR and it "collapsed" during his regime, he added.
He also alleged the BRS leaders are spreading disinformation that Godavari water is going to neighbouring Andhra Pradesh due to the negligence of the Congress government.
