It’s fast, scoring mid- to high-table results in my tests, and it proved reliable. It also has DSL or fiber-optic modems, an integrated DECT base station for cordless phones, built-in storage (NAS), and support for Zigbee to connect smart home devices. You don’t need an account to set it up or configure it. There’s a firewall and guest network option in the straightforward web interface (you can use the mobile app if you prefer). AVM’s routers are developed and manufactured in Europe, making them an interesting, privacy-focused alternative to routers from China or the US. The company also has a strong track record of supporting its products for years after release. Folks in the UK and Europe looking to upgrade to Wi-Fi 7 should consider this router. My fingers are crossed that AVM expands into the US next.
Asus RT-BE92U for $265: After a simple setup and a trouble-free week of speedy, stable internet across the 2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz bands, I can recommend this router. It has Wi-Fi 7 benefits like MLO and 320-MHz channels, support for a guest network, VPN services, free security software, and parental controls. It also boasts a 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, three 2.5-Gbps LANs, and a USB 3.2 port. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 device came perilously close to claiming the midrange spot above, but was a smidge slower on the 5-GHz and 6-GHz bands and had a considerably shorter range. However, if your home is around 1,500 square feet and you’d rather avoid a subscription, the RT-BE92U is an excellent alternative. Customer reviews suggest some folks have had trouble with this router, but the latest firmware was rock solid for me.
Asus RT-BE88U for $339: This dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router is an odd prospect because it does not offer the 6-GHz band at all, just 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. But you can still combine those bands with MLO and enjoy features like 4K QAM, and this router will be fast enough for the average home. It has ports galore (two 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, four Gigabit, and one USB 3.0). It outperformed several more expensive routers on the 5-GHz band, and that’s likely what most of your devices are using most of the time right now. Asus also offers free security software and parental controls with its routers, so there’s no need for subscriptions. But when I consider that you can snag the Netgear Nighthawk RS300 listed above for less, I find it tough to recommend this router to folks in the US. If the 6-GHz band is unavailable or nerfed in your country, the RT-BE88U is for you.
Netgear Nighthawk RS700 for $540: Although I had setup issues that required a factory reset, there’s no hiding the top-notch performance of this router. It’s a Wi-Fi 7 tri-band router with two 10-Gbps Ethernet ports, four gigabit ports, and a USB 3.2. The tower design is new for the Nighthawk line, and it looks great. This router will blend in far better than our bulky Wi-Fi 7 pick above from Asus, and it was slightly faster on the 6-GHz band, though not the 5-GHz or 2.4-GHz bands. It mainly misses out on a recommendation because it is more expensive. We’re already seeing discounts on the RT-BE96U, and Asus offers free security software and parental controls. If you get the Nighthawk RS700S, the “S” at the end denotes a free year of Netgear Armor, which costs $100 a year thereafter. If you need parental controls, that’s another $70 a year.
TP-Link Archer BE800 for $400: With a fresh design that’s more desktop PC than router, the BE800 tri-band beast came out high up in my tests on the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands, proving impressively swift for file transfers and downloads. It also boasts speedy ports galore, a cool but kind of pointless customizable dot-matrix LED screen, and the Tether app offers a guest network, IoT network, VPN server or client, EasyMesh, QoS for device prioritization, and remote management.
Netgear M3 for £450: I was very impressed by this mobile 5G router. Slip a SIM in there, and it connects to 4G or 5G networks to deliver Wi-Fi to your devices. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model that’s speedy on the 5-GHz band. The M3 had no trouble handling multiple connected devices (up to 32) and served a stable internet connection for around 10 hours. You can charge via the USB-C port, and there’s a 2.4-inch LCD color screen for configuration. It’s a solid hot spot for business or personal travel. Sadly, the M3 doesn’t seem to be available in the US, but folks in the UK can save some money and snag this instead of the M7 above (it’s frequently discounted).
Firewalla Gold SE for $549: This quirky portable device is perfect for people who worry about security and privacy. It offers comprehensive tools for monitoring all traffic in and out of your house, robust and detailed parental controls, ad-blocking, and enhanced security with a built-in firewall and VPN option. It serves as a router, but you will want to pair another router in access point mode for Wi-Fi in your home. It’s expensive and may prove intimidating for inexperienced folks, but it offers deep insight into your network and an impressive depth of security features without an additional subscription. The Gold SE has two 2.5-Gbps ports and two gigabit ports and is suitable for folks with up to 2-gigabit connections. If your internet is only one gigabit, try the more affordable but slightly less capable Firewalla Purple ($399).
What About Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 Routers?
While I recommend buying a Wi-Fi 7 router if you’re upgrading, there are loads of Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 routers that will serve the average family well. With Wi-Fi 6E you still get the faster 6-GHz band. The bulk of household traffic still likely uses 5 GHz, and you can save a lot of money by sticking with Wi-Fi 6 for a bit longer.
Netgear Nighthawk RAXE300 for $300: The curvy spaceship design in matte black is a little more stealthy than your average gaming gear, but those wings contain antennas for a strong signal throughout your home. The Nighthawk RAXE300 is a tri-band router with Wi-Fi 6E support, covering the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. It served seamless, speedy Wi-Fi during two weeks of testing, with zero issues while handling a revolving mix of four simultaneous gaming and video streams. A single 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN port, five gigabit LAN ports, and a USB-C 3.0 port will be enough for most folks.
The Nighthawk app is excellent and offers band splitting, guest network options, and a host of analytical tools. The Premium Smart Parental Controls ($8/month or $70/year) and Netgear Armor ($100/year) are slick, but the extra expense is hard to swallow when many competitors offer cheaper or free alternatives with similar features. This is discontinued, but a few places still have stock, and it’s still a great router.
TP-Link Archer AX55 for $90: This affordable Wi-Fi 6 router is still a decent pick for the average home. The slick black finish is attractive, and there are four antennas to direct Wi-Fi to every corner (it is worth tweaking and testing different positions). Performance was solid throughout my two-floor, 1,600-square-foot home but dropped off slightly in the back garden. Stability was excellent over a couple of weeks of testing, and this router ticks many feature boxes (MU-MIMO, beamforming, WPA3). It has four Gigabit Ethernet LAN ports, a single Gigabit WAN port, and a USB 3.0 port on the back, which is enough for most people.
I’m a fan of TP-Link’s Tether app, where you can review traffic, split bands, create a guest network, schedule reboots, set automatic updates, and even tell the LED to turn off at night. TP-Link’s basic free HomeShield tier offers network scanning, QoS (Quality of Service) for device prioritization, and basic parental controls so you can filter and blacklist websites and set the same bedtime every day. If you want a variable schedule, time limits, downtime, and real-time security protection, you must upgrade to HomeShield Pro (30-day free trial, then $6 per month or $55 for the year). If money is tight, you may even consider the next system down, the TP-Link Archer AX21 ($90). Performance is slightly weaker, but the experience is broadly similar.
Routers I Don’t Recommend
These are the internet routers we had issues with or can’t recommend for one reason or another.
Acer Connect X6E 5G: This is an interesting Wi-Fi 6E model with a 5G SIM card slot capable of keeping you online using a mobile network should your main broadband connection fail. It has two Gigabit Ethernet ports, a WAN/LAN, LAN, and an RJ-11 port for a phone line. It’s easy to set up and offers an NFC connection option, so you can just wave your phone over it to connect. This unusual blend of features could be good for business travelers. Performance was solid when it worked, and you can get a very fast connection at close range on both the 6-GHz and 5-GHz bands. Sadly, the range was limited, and the Connect X6E 5G was intermittently unstable during my testing, dropping devices randomly and cutting out repeatedly.
D-Link AX3000 DBR-330: This lightweight, rectangular travel router from D-Link is aimed at business professionals who travel for work. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router that can also serve as a hot spot, with a connection via USB. There’s even a potentially handy microSD/TF card slot for up to 2 TB of storage for file sharing or backup. Setup via the browser is easy, and there’s built-in VPN support. It proved nice and fast at close range, but it dropped off quickly, and I couldn’t get a signal two rooms away. It will work fine for a hotel room, though. You can get our TP-Link travel router pick above or the Asus RT-AX57 Go for similar money, and I prefer both of them.
Netgear Nighthawk RS200: The RS200 is Netgear’s dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router and the cheapest in its Wi-Fi 7 lineup. After the tri-band RS300 won a recommendation, I expected this router to perform decently, but I encountered several issues, including random drops and poor range. After turning the router off and on again, many devices, including my Pixel and iPhone, struggled to reconnect. Perhaps I have too many devices in my home for it, though Netgear suggests it can handle up to 80. It has two 2.5 Gbps ports, three gigabit Ethernet ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Test results were OK, but significantly slower than the RT-BE86U.
TP-Link Archer AX5400 Pro: This dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model is almost identical to the Archer AX73, except for the 2.5-Gbps WAN port. It delivers relatively fast speeds on the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands and boasts a 160-MHz channel width on 5 GHz. The range is good, easily covering my home and garden, but the performance was inconsistent. It was also relatively slow at moving files locally. There’s support for TP-Link OneMesh, VPN, and QoS, but you only get basic parental controls and network security unless you subscribe.
What Features Should I Look for in a Router?
My How to Buy a Router guide answers a lot of questions on the terminology you’ll come across when shopping for a new router. Still, here are a few other considerations.
Wi-Fi Standards: The Wi-Fi 8 standard is still a while away from final certification, though we are starting to see Wi-Fi 8 routers based on the latest spec. That's why most of my main picks are still Wi-Fi 7. That doesn’t mean Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 6E routers aren’t worth having, necessarily. But with cheaper dual-band Wi-Fi 7 routers available, there’s not much reason to buy anything older. Only Wi-Fi 6E, 7, and 8 routers offer extra bandwidth and faster speeds on the 6-GHz band, but devices like phones and laptops must also support the same standard for you to take advantage. The 6-GHz band is also short-range compared to the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, though Wi-Fi 8 extends it a bit.
Internet Speeds: Your maximum internet speed is set by your ISP and depends on your internet plan. It will likely fluctuate, depending on the time of day. Some ISPs guarantee a minimum download and upload speed. While your router can’t provide an internet connection that exceeds that speed, it can potentially go faster when you stream from a server in your home or move files from one device on your local network to another.
Coverage: It’s worth checking a prospective router’s coverage and speed, but understand that your home Wi-Fi mileage may vary. Construction materials in your house, your neighbors’ activity and Wi-Fi networks, your devices, and the position of your router are just a few of the factors that will impact your wireless performance.
Ports: Ethernet ports offer stable connections and are essential for some smart home setups that require a hub for lights or security cameras. Some network-attached storage (NAS) for backups or media will plug into your main router via USB. Ensure that the model you are considering has all the ports you need.
What Is the Difference Between a Modem and a Router?
A modem (modulator-demodulator) connects your home to your internet service provider (ISP) and the external internet. A router connects the devices within your home to that internet connection wirelessly via Wi-Fi or with Ethernet cables. Check out my Router vs. Modem guide to learn more.
Can a Single Wireless Router Cover Your Entire Home?
Manufacturers usually suggest a coverage range for a router in square feet, but every home is different, and the real-world range is likely to be shorter. Walls and other obstructions will weaken and block wireless signals. Ideal placement would be in the center of the home near the ceiling of the ground floor without any obstructions. A well-placed single router is generally enough to cover a typical two-floor home up to 2,000 square feet. For larger homes, it's worth considering mesh systems to create a reliable home network.
Where Should You Put Your Router?
Physically moving your router can make a real difference to Wi-Fi speeds. It should be central, out in the open, and high up. Walls, cupboards, and even bookshelves can interfere with your Wi-Fi signal, as can fish tanks, TVs, or microwaves. Even changing the angle or moving the antennas can impact the strength of the Wi-Fi around your home, so don't be afraid to experiment with different positions.
Can I Add Routers or Extenders to Make a Mesh?
Many manufacturers allow you to create a mesh network by adding more routers or devices like Wi-Fi extenders, but check what is supported before you buy. For example, Asus AiMesh enables you to link multiple routers, while TP-Link’s OneMesh only allows you to add power-line adapters or range extenders. EasyMesh is a standard certification by the Wi-Fi Alliance that hopes to allow the mixing and matching of devices from different manufacturers to form a mesh, but few devices support it so far. You can also buy single mesh routers, like an Amazon Eero, and then add more later if you find that you need them. Based on my testing, a mesh is always better than an extender.
How Do Ethernet Cables Compare?
Running an Ethernet cable to create a wired connection between your home router and device will provide a faster and more secure link than Wi-Fi. But running Ethernet cables everywhere can be tricky. Read my Ethernet guide to learn more. Wireless connectivity makes life easy and is often fast enough for most tasks, such as browsing the web or streaming video.
What About the US Ban on Foreign-Made Routers?
The Federal Communications Commission has banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US because of national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market must be approved.
The way the ban is described, it applies to every new Wi-Fi router, because there are no companies manufacturing routers or the components they are assembled from in the US. But companies can apply for exemptions.
All new models of foreign-produced routers will require Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security before the FCC can clear them for sale in the US. Read “Everything You Need to Know About the Foreign-Made Router Ban in the US” to learn more.
What About Firmware and Security Updates?
While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.”
What happens after that date is not clear, but if the FCC were to block further updates for the routers folks already own, it would exacerbate the very issue it is trying to address. The majority of routers that are compromised and used in cyberattacks are usually older devices that no longer receive security updates.
Should You Buy a Router Now?
If you live in the US and need a router or a mesh, you should buy one. Asus, Netgear, Eero, and a few others have been granted Conditional Approval already. All the major manufacturers I asked who responded or have released a statement, including TP-Link and Synology, are confident about getting exemptions, but whether they will is impossible to say for sure. An FCC spokesperson told me, “We expect approvals to be granted in a timely manner.”
The problem with waiting is that prices are likely to go up. I’ve already seen some price creep on systems from TP-Link, Netgear, and Eero, though this could also be due to the AI-driven RAM shortage.
How I Test Routers
To find the top Wi-Fi routers, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the router works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare.
I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test. I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers.
How Did I Select Products to be Reviewed
I try to test as many routers as I can. It’s not possible to test every device, so while I will typically test flagship releases, I also call in more affordable routers and try to find models to suit the average family home in terms of budget and performance. We are brand agnostic, so we will test routers from any manufacturer, provided we can get ahold of them. But we do lean toward testing more systems from the most popular brands. All the routers we test are provided by the manufacturers or their PR companies.
Most are loaned for a month or so and then returned. A handful of our recommended picks are kept for longer term testing. The remainder are donated to charities. I recently dropped off a batch to Reusing IT and have donated several devices to Oxfam and Shelter.

Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
- Published
A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.
Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

Pope meets with survivors of clergy abuse in Argentina as it reckons with legacy and ongoing cases
Pope Leo XIV have met with survivors of clergy abuse during his visit to Argentina
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV met with survivors of clergy abuse on Monday during his visit to Argentina, a country that has been reckoning with the Catholic Church’s legacy of sex abuse and cover-up, including in cases in which the Argentine Pope Francis intervened.
The Vatican said Leo spent about an hour meeting individually, and then as a group, with five victims of abuse by clergy and “church institutions” who were chosen by the local church. The meeting took place at the Catholic University of Argentina.
Leo listened to their “painful stories and proposals to consolidate paths of healing in the church,” said a statement from Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni.
Acknowledging that there were other groups of victims who had wanted to meet with Leo, “the pope expressed his closeness and desire to reinforce paths of protection, of welcome and accompaniment in the church,” it said.
Victims groups had said they wanted to meet with Leo and were denied, including a group of 43 women who allege they were subjected to human trafficking and forced labor at centers of the conservative group Opus Dei in Argentina.
Their allegations implicate senior members of Opus, some of whom have been formally accused in a criminal investigation into the women's claims. Prosecutors have requested that the members be summoned for questioning, but the judge has not ordered it. Opus has denied wrongdoing.
Given the ongoing criminal investigation, it is perhaps unlikely that Leo would have intervened by meeting with them in this case. However, in general, the American pope has followed in the footsteps of Francis and to a lesser extent Pope Benedict XVI by meeting with abuse survivors on his foreign trips, and another meeting is expected when he arrives later this week in Peru.
Ahead of the Argentine visit, survivors had also demanded stronger action from the Vatican against those accused or convicted in criminal courts but whose fates within the church’s internal legal processes haven’t been made public.
Survivors’ groups have cited several high-profile priests convicted of serious crimes, including Julio Grassi and former Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta. Francis intervened in both cases in favor of the priests who were subsequently convicted by criminal courts.
Grassi, once a prominent figure who ran homes for orphaned children, is serving a 15-year sentence for sexually abusing a minor. Francis, who at the time was still Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio and the archbishop of Buenos Aires, in 2010 commissioned a four-volume, 2,000-plus-page forensic study of Grassi’s case that concluded he was innocent, that his victims were lying and that the case never should have gone to trial.
Zanchetta, a former bishop close to Francis, was sentenced in 2022 to 4 1/2 years in prison for sexually abusing two seminarians. He was granted parole in 2025, prompting renewed demands that he be defrocked. Francis had initially rejected the accusations against Zanchetta and created a job for him at the Vatican that got him out of Argentina. The late pope eventually authorized a canonical criminal proceeding against Zanchetta in 2019, but the Vatican has not publicly announced a ruling.
The Vatican tends to not initiate canonical trials until all criminal appeals are exhausted, to not prejudge the outcomes, though it does recommend that bishops take precautionary measures during investigations such as removing priests from active ministry.

It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.
Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.
Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.
"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.
"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.
Blue wins, red losses
In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)
In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.
A big recruiting effort
Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action, a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.
The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton, says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.
"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.
Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.
Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.
"People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."
A key vote, a damaging investigation
Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.
During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."
Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.
In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.
All the way back to 1776
Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress.
"In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."
In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."
The new count
To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.
In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.
In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.
Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."
He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says
A health policy shake up?
Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.
Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys.
"I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."
Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.
"I do think that they really lead with what they essentially are, which is problem solvers," she says. "We can fix this problem — we can make health care accessible and affordable — and not make it a choice between life or debt."
Lexie Schapitl contributed reporting to this story.

Next-door neighbour to Valluvar Kottam, the Mathi Experience Store situated in the Anna Teresa Women’s Complex on Valluvarkottam High Road in Nungambakkam, carries swank. It is something of a “fishbowl shop”, its glass walls literally showcasing the products stacked on the shelves to someone lingering outside and yet to step into the outlet. And it is also a showcase for things unseen: women whose work is creating livelihoods and whose skills are finding markets, otherwise elusive. The store brings to the fore the creative skills of women from all the districts of Tamil Nadu, women who lack a privileged background but have the will to rise above that situation. It is a marketplace with a cause, bringing visibility to the products made by women self-help groups (SHGs) from the districts.
Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (a state-owned organisation established to promote self-reliance among women through “employment generation and economic independence") started Mathi Experience Store under what is called the Mahalir Thittam. This outlet offers an assortment of products, and when the calendar moves closer to Deepavali, one can shop for festival-related sweets and savoury packs made by SHGs.
Inside, the shelves “replicate” the map of Tamil Nadu. Traditional printed table runners from Udhagamandalam sit beside mudpots and tea cups from Viluppuram. Traditional music instruments from Thiruvallur, bamboo combs and toothbrushes from Kancheepuram, paintings from Thanjavur and exquisite showpieces from Nagapattinam: the “seats” are all taken.
The variety of products is staggering. Handloom textiles, handicrafts, spices, soaps, body care products, millet-based foods and a range of other food items, sanitary napkins and eco-friendly products complete the assortment. Buying the products here would help SHGs stay in business.
Five women currently manage the store in shifts, most of them from SHGs themselves. There is an endearing manifestation of inclusivity: a woman with hearing and speech disabilities is on the store’s rolls. Established in 2023, the store has kept a record of its progress from the very beginning. M. Mahalakshmi, an employee, smiles as she opens the register to show the very first entry, made by Member of Legislative Assembly for the Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni constituency, Udhayanidhi Stalin on the day he inaugurated the outlet.
“Everything in the store is organic and comes after quality checks,” she says.
The process of onboarding for SHGs begins with these groups approaching district officials for registering under Mahalir Thittam. According to the employees in the store, officials visit production sites to assess the products and their quality before they are selected for display. Products are reordered on the basis of demand. But Mathi is not just a place to shop. For those who would rather slow down and savour a cup of tea or coffee or perhaps a cappuccino, an adjoining cafe attached to the store offers that much-needed pause.
The menu also includes varieties of milkshakes and snacks to enjoy in the calm of its outdoor seating area, where one can sit back and enjoy the passing bustle of the city. The store overlooks the busy Valluvarkottam High Road, which during rush hour can pass off as a synonym for “bustle”
As Deepavali approaches, the shelves make room for traditional festive delicacies prepared by SHGs. “These delicacies are generally on demand,” Mahalakshmi notes. “The festival specials usually arrive a few days before Deepavali.”
Ponder over this, on Deepavali Eve: every purchase one makes at this store can do more than bring something home. It can help an underprivileged woman somewhere in Tamil Nadu progress towards building one of her own.
A success story called Thangam
Thangam Chellam, from a village, a little beyond Marthandam, in Kanniyakumari district, is well into her seventies but has retained the spirit of a 17-year-old, probably the reason why members of her self-help group would not allow her to relinquish the SHG’s headship. The Self-Help Group (SHG) was established in 2001 (and this is its silver jubilee year) with 20 women on board. Thangam points out that she started working after her husband’s demise. She joined the SHG which she has been heading since the beginning.
The SHG now consists of 14 members, and the group makes food items, juices, snacks, sweets, honey and pickles. Thangam is known for making a variety of juices, some of them unusual, such as hibiscus juice, gooseberry juice and nannari juice. Each member has a designated role, and the group has received formal training to strengthen its work. Out of the 14, five are adept at kitchen work.
Thangam’s voice carries the weariness of years spent earning a livelihood, but her spirit masks the age, as she continues to lead the enterprise. Her group participates in government organised exhibitions, which she says are its primary platform for reaching customers. The products have found demand among buyers, giving the group opportunities to showcase its work beyond its home district.
For women like Thangam and her group, every exhibition opens a door to new customers and possibilities. Thangam notes that her SHG was earlier making sweets for Deepavali but not any more. But there are those other food products that make her SHG’s presence felt at government-initiated food festivals and also at Mathi from time to time.

Bhumi Satish Pednekkar has raised concerns over the deteriorating air quality following Diwali celebrations, drawing attention to the health risks associated with firecracker pollution. With several cities witnessing a rise in pollution levels after the festival, the actor highlighted how poor air quality, noise pollution and firecracker waste affect not just people but also animals. She particularly emphasised the vulnerability of children, senior citizens and those with respiratory conditions.
Bhumi Satish Pednekkar raises concern over post-Diwali air pollution: “The AQI is hazardous”
Delhi has been among the worst-affected cities, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) entering the 'severe' category in several areas. Several people have expressed concern over the situation, and Bhumi also took to social media to highlight the consequences of firecracker use.
On Monday morning, the actor shared a detailed note on Instagram, reminding people that Diwali is meant to be a celebration of light, love and togetherness. However, she pointed out that the festivities are often followed by worsening air quality and other environmental concerns.
Her post read, "Diwali is a festival of light, love, family and new beginnings. But every year, along with the celebrations, comes a familiar aftermath: polluted air, firecracker waste, noise and frightened animals. Firecrackers release fine particulate matter and other pollutants that add to an already challenging air-quality situation. And the impact isn’t experienced equally. Children, older people, those with respiratory conditions and animals are particularly vulnerable. This year, let’s make a choice that allows everyone including the ones who cannot speak for themselves to enjoy the festival.”
View this post on Instagram
The actor also expressed her disappointment over the continued bursting of firecrackers during the early hours of Monday. Around 3 am, she shared another Instagram story, describing the situation as heartbreaking and pointing out the impact of celebrations on public spaces and the environment.
“Houses have caught fire, The AQI is hazardous, Roads are full of waste, Its 3 am and all I can hear are loud crackers. Our roads were full of people bursting crackers on them, Out in the open, even when it's not allowed. This is heartbreaking. @my bmc ®mumbaipolice,” Bhumi posted.
Meanwhile, monitoring data indicated elevated pollution levels across several parts of Mumbai. Kherwadi-Bandra East recorded an AQI of 264, followed by Sewri at 226, Ghatkopar at 221 and Chembur at 216. Byculla registered 193, while Mindspace-Malad West recorded 191, Kandivali West 187 and Worli 148. Kurla reported a comparatively lower AQI of 96.
In Uttar Pradesh, Lucknow also witnessed a layer of smog, with several areas waking up to hazy conditions following the celebrations. According to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), an AQI between 0 and 50 is classified as 'good', 51-100 as 'satisfactory', 101-200 as 'moderate', 201-300 as 'poor', 301-400 as 'very poor' and 401-500 as 'severe'.
Amid the deteriorating conditions, Stage III measures under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) remain in force following the Commission for Air Quality Management's (CAQM) decision. The restrictions include additional pollution-control measures, stricter enforcement and directions to concerned agencies to prevent further deterioration.
The emergency action plan covers Delhi and adjoining districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. It is implemented as a precautionary measure based on weather and pollution forecasts issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), allowing authorities to take preventive action before the overall AQI reaches the 'severe' category.

Record-setting 17-time Oscar nominee Diane Warren received a rock-star welcome as she hit Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film to accompany and discuss her original song “One Right Here” for Maserati: The Brothers, about the rise of the Italian racing car dynasty.
The songwriter, who was nursing a bout of laryngitis, was greeted with a cheer and shouts of ‘Diane, we love you’ from the crowd at UCLA’s Royce Hall.
The swooping crossover duet “One Right Here” is performed by iconic Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli and Grammy-winning singer Jennifer Hudson.
Working with Bocelli, who has previously collaborated with the likes of Luciano Pavarotti, Céline Dion, Stevie Wonder and Jennifer Lopez, was a dream come true, Warren said.
“I’ve been trying to get Andrea Bocelli to do a song of mine for 10 years,” she said. “He gets really close, and then he doesn’t.”
Warren recounted how she had written the song with Bocelli’s voice in her head after the film’s producer Andrea Iervolino told her the tenor had signed up to sing the track.
“I kind of didn’t believe him,” she said. “But I wrote the song for [Bocelli], for his voice, with those high notes. All that stuff he’s singing, I heard in my head… when I first heard him… when it was first sent to me, I was sobbing, hearing him, that’s a dream. And then the idea was the idea to put Jennifer on that with him, like two different worlds together.”
Produced by Iervolino under his Andrea Iervolino Company banner, Maserati: The Brothers is directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Bobby Moresco. The film tells the story of the Bologna-based Maserati brothers, whose passion for engineering and racing still defines Italian craftsmanship a century later. Al Pacino, Anthony Hopkins, Jessica Alba, Andy García, Michele Morrone and Salvatore Esposito feature in the ensemble cast.
Warren said she had wanted the song to encompass several aspects of the film.
“It’s about different things, the Maserati brothers who created the car, of course, but they loved each other and all the tragedy and triumph of that family. But then there’s also a couple love stories in there. I wanted the song to fit all that, and then the idea that there’s one right here who’s here for you,” she said. “Then I just had the idea of let’s make it a duet… as soon as I heard it because I wasn’t there when Andrea sang it, but I was there when Jennifer did… I was in the studio… . I was like, ‘Oh my God, this is better than I thought’.”

Sam Altman’s recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a “parody project” launched in response to Altman’s viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC.
As reported by The Verge, on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time.”
Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to “RAM Altman” on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, “objectively excellent and where the project gets its name.”
In an email to Ars, Kay said, “Ram-Altman is a bash script that takes MemTotal minus MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo, so the figure includes page cache and reclaimable slab but leaves out tmpfs and shared memory.”
If the script only showed what Linux reports as “free” RAM, it would paint an incomplete picture. Linux often reports a surprisingly small amount of “free” RAM, as it doesn’t count memory that is currently claimable for use. Linux will fill available RAM caches with file data for quick access, but the kernel can reclaim that usage at a moment’s notice when needed. The MemAvailable figure is the kernel’s own estimate of how much memory it could hand over without swapping.
used = MemTotal - MemAvailable
Users can schedule the script to ask the kernel for a status update every five minutes, and if more than 10 percent of RAM is available, it triggers a joke email from one of several joke templates. The script limits outgoing emails to one per day.

Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
- Published
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

A 22-second-long clip shared by X user Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) showing a massive crowd in a large open area went viral on November 1.
Thottathil posted the video with the caption, “Early in the morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed #ChaloDilli,” thus claiming that the crowd had gathered for the INDIA’s bloc’s rally on November 1 to protest against electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Early morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed ✊🏼 🔥
#ChaloDilli https://t.co/oM5kSpCNoH
— Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) November 1, 2026
The post by Thottathil, who was till recently a social media manager of Kerala Congress, amassed over 243,000 views and was reshared over 1,400 times. (Archive)
Congress leader Harish Rawat, too, shared the video on Instagram, claiming that the visuals were from the November 1 protest rally.
View this post on Instagram
Various other X handles posted the same 22-second clip, claiming that they are visuals from the ‘Chalo Dilli’ rally held on November 1. A few of them are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
In the comments of the video posted by Vijay, X users were quick to point out that the video was not from the November 1 ‘Chalo Dilli’ protest, and instead was from another rally held at an earlier date.
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on December 14, 2025.
This video, captioned “‘वोट चोरी’ के खिलाफ जनसैलाब 🔥🔥” (A public outpouring against “vote theft”), was uploaded during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests of December 2025.
View this post on Instagram
The comparison of certain keyframes of both videos reveals stark similarities, including the backdrop, the size of the crowd, a flag being waved in the front, and even a blue tent visible in the clip. See below:
A deeper dive revealed that Congress leader Harish Rawat had himself shared the video during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests on December 14, 2025. He has now shared the same clip again as scenes from the INDIA bloc rally of November 1, 2026.
To sum up, the viral clip with the massive crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan shared by Thottathil is an old clip from the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhoro” protests that was organised by Congress in December last year. Several users have falsely presented it as visuals from the recent ‘Chalo Dilli’ march on November 1.
Rajanyo Ghosh is an intern at Alt News.

In 2015, Donald Trump descended a golden escalator and launched a presidential campaign that reshaped American politics. More than a decade later, with his record-low approval ratings and the US embroiled in a war with Iran, he asked voters to treat the 2026 midterms as a referendum on him.
Did the midterms kill MAGA?
A former MAGA acolyte sorts through the wreckage.
“Please pretend I’m on the ballot. Because in a way, I am on the ballot,” Trump told a crowd in North Carolina last month.
As it turns out, voters did as Trump asked: Democrats won in a landslide, taking control of both chambers of Congress with victories in Republican strongholds like South Carolina and Kansas. Now, Republicans have to decide what those losses mean for the future of the movement Trump built.
As Vox’s Andrew Prokop reported, there are already competing explanations for the losses that are taking shape on the right. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance posted on social media. The conservative commentator Erick Erickson offered a longer list of reasons for the GOP’s failure: “It was also the corruption. The incompetence. The tariffs. The playing nice with Russia. The impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations.” Others emphasized affordability. “Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson wrote. “Especially for young people.”
Whoever defines what went wrong will likely help determine which parts of Trump’s politics survive, and who gets to lead the presidential ticket in 2028.
The conservative writer Rod Dreher has a stake in that debate. He supported Trump in 2024. He’s friends with Vance, and he shares the vice president’s interest in combining social conservatism with economic policies that support families. His critiques come from someone who wanted this administration to succeed.
Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Dreher about whether the midterms mean the end of MAGA, what might replace it, and whether Republicans can move past a president who still has two years left in office.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Before the midterm results even came in, you wrote that Republicans were likely to be shellacked and that they had nobody to blame but Donald Trump and themselves. What do you think it is your fellow conservatives need to admit today?
That MAGA is over. It’s done. It’s been a failure. It brought Trump to power twice. I think there were some good ideas in MAGA and certainly the old Republican establishment, the pre-Trump establishment, needed to go.
But MAGA couldn’t deliver on good government. And if you can’t deliver on good government, it doesn’t matter how charismatic the leader is. It’s not going to work. And I think that there can be no doubt after this week’s election that it was a complete referendum on Donald Trump and he failed. And we have to build from there.
You supported Trump in 2024. At the time you wrote that you were aware of some of his failings. I think many people who voted for Trump were aware of some of his failings, but he had a mandate.
He had the popular vote, he had the House, he had the Senate. Why couldn’t MAGA, his movement, deliver on good government?
“But MAGA couldn’t deliver on good government. And if you can’t deliver on good government, it doesn’t matter how charismatic the leader is.”
I think that it all comes down to the fact that Trump made decisions based not on rational calculation, by listening to expert advice, but on gut instinct.
I think that the wheels began to fall off of the Trump train on April 2, 2025. That was the so-called Liberation Day when Trump announced these wide tariffs. They weren’t thought out at all. They just came out of his gut. And that set a pattern for the way that Trump made decisions. Plus. he promoted people not based on competence, but based on loyalty to him, personal loyalty.
I think this administration has gone from one crisis to another because of that, because Trump doesn’t have a theory or practice of governance. When he came into office, he signed a bunch of executive orders. Some of them did things that I thought were really good, but he didn’t turn them into legislation. This is a guy whose party held both houses of Congress and the White House, yet he just sailed right along as if he was going to be president forever.
And then of course, this gets us to the Iran war, which was another gut instinct thing by Trump, which became the symbol for all of the disasters of Trumpism.
Can MAGA be divorced from Donald Trump? Can it exist without Donald Trump?
No, MAGA is Donald Trump. Donald Trump himself said so. The challenge is going to be, how does the Republican Party rebuild and regroup for 2028 with Trump still in the White House?
I mean, think about it. They’re fighting a two-front battle now. You’re going to have to fight the Democrats, who are energized, who are going to come in and make the next two years — justifiably, I would say — about investigating Trump administration corruption.
But they’re also going to have to fight Donald Trump himself. Sitting in the White House, he’s not going to shut up. He’s not going to do what is best for his party. He’s going to try to salvage his legacy.
What is the next conservative movement? Where do conservatives go from here?
The next few months are going to be really interesting in this respect. Until now, everybody on the right has thought that JD Vance, the vice president, is Trump’s natural successor, even though he hasn’t announced whether or not he’s going to run. I think that has now been called severely into question.
I say this as someone who’s a personal friend of the vice president and would like to see him be president one day. Nevertheless, even though he strongly opposed the Iran war from behind the scenes, he and Marco Rubio and everyone else in this administration are tied to it and all the other failures of Trumpism.
So who does that leave on the outside? I was very surprised, in the past 24 hours, to see and hear Gov. Ron DeSantis, the outgoing governor of Florida, who as we all remember, ran against Trump for the Republican nomination and never stood a chance. He’s not charismatic. He’s super competent, but not charismatic. And so Trump won the 2024 nomination.
Well, now DeSantis is coming out making strong, clear, rational critiques of MAGA and Trumpism. And I think that DeSantis could be the outside candidate who has the best [chance] because he’s the only national Republican politician not tainted by Trumpism.
JD Vance is a friend of yours. He’s credited you with getting him involved in politics. You say you’d like to see him be president. I think a legitimate question following what we’ve seen over the past two years and then last night is why?
Why do you want JD Vance to be president?
JD Vance has been associated with the national conservatism movement, as have I — the movement started by Yoram Hazony, which has been about prioritizing national sovereignty, national interest, a cultural conservatism that is also in favor of economic reforms to make it easier to raise families.
JD Vance has been the avatar for that sort of conservatism. I see the bones of this kind of conservatism within Trump and MAGA, but it got completely crushed by Trump’s own obsessions. If JD can go back to the man I think he is deep down and start to champion this sort of thing — more of a pro-family economic liberalism with social conservatism and no new wars — if it’s possible for any Republican to claim that now, then I think that he could have a chance.
I think he is a good man. I have criticized him publicly, in print, as a friend for not separating himself from the bigots on the dissident right — the antisemites and the white nationalists. This extremist crowd is going to make a bid for power in the rubble of MAGA. And I think whether it’s JD or whoever becomes a Republican standard bearer is going to have to face them down.
We’ve talked about JD Vance. We have talked about Ron DeSantis. They represent different things within conservatism. Tucker Carlson represents something else within conservatism. I think it’s something you don’t like very much. And, um, and then there’s Marco Rubio, who represents something that we were all familiar with from the early aughts.
What do you think of these two other boldface names as we head into 2028?
Tucker Carlson has beclowned himself, and it’s really sad. As someone who used to be friends with him, I thought he was a sensible, interesting commentator who often said a lot of common-sense things. But sometime in the last couple of years, he lost his mind and became antisemitic and just a crazy conspiracy theorist.
A lot of people are worried about his influence on the vice president because they’ve been close for years. Tucker was key in getting Donald Trump to choose JD Vance as vice president. I have no inside knowledge of that at all, but it worries me as well. I think JD is his own man, but it’s going to be very hard for JD going forward to maintain viability as a potential Republican Party leader until and unless he addresses the Tucker Carlson problem.
I don’t think Tucker’s going to run for president. If he did that, he could only be a spoiler, and I don’t think he actually wants it.
In Marco Rubio’s case, he’s been a real chameleon. He was against MAGA. He was the neocon’s neocon for a while, but he has been a faithful servant and executor of Trump’s foreign policy. And for some reason, it doesn’t seem to have stuck to him the way it has stuck to JD Vance. I’m not sure why that is, but with all of these guys who have been part of the Trump administration, it’s gonna be very, very hard to cut that albatross from around their neck.
One of the dynamics that we’ve seen in the Trump era over the last decade is that Republicans in Congress don’t want to stand up to Donald Trump. They don’t want to cross him.
What should Republicans in Congress do? Should they finally grow a spine and say, “Look, we don’t have to obey every single thing that President Trump says”?
Absolutely. I mean, what do they have to lose now?
Trump has never been loyal to anybody who’s pledged loyalty to him. Greg Abbott, the three-term governor of Texas who lost his bid for reelection — no sooner had the election been called and Trump put out a statement calling him a RINO.
Trump is not loyal. And so there is nothing in it left for Republicans to stick with him. He’s not going to be a factor in 2028. Maybe they want his endorsement in the 2028 primaries. Really? After this? That would be the kiss of death.
Republicans are now, and Congress is now, going to have to find a spine and stand up and establish some independence. If they had done that earlier, we might not be in the situation today.

In March this year, on the sidelines of Razorpay’s annual flagship event FTX, CEO Harshil Mathur told Inc42 that what mattered most to him was how Razorpay stands in the public markets, and not the fact that it went public. Eight months on, that test now has a rough date as the company sets off on the last leg of its IPO journey. Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed IPO. The fintech major is looking to raise ₹5,000-6,000 Cr through a mix of fresh issue and offer for sale at a valuation of around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027. Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi are the reported bankers. The headline number when it comes to Razorpay’s listing, or for that matter any listing within fintech circles, has been that of valuation.Sources suggest that Razorpay may be looking to list at a $5 Bn valuation, a markdown from the $7.5 Bn valuation that the company commanded in December 2021. But back in 2021, fintech valuations were sky high amidst a pandemic led funding boom that witnessed sharp corrections years down the line. Another fintech major, PhonePe, paused its mega listing in March 2026, with reports suggesting that volatile geopolitical tensions and valuation concerns led the payments company to put its IPO plans on hold. It has since revived them on the back of MDR. Sources told Inc42 in September that PhonePe is targeting a listing between February and March 2027 at a valuation of about $10 Bn. But Razorpay has a different story to tell the public investors as it seeks ₹5,000-6,000 Cr from them. The first part of that story is profit. “When you take out that one-time cost of the reverse flip, Razorpay was profitable — that profitability streak is maintained throughout. We hope the financials will continue to improve from here as a company that’s continuously growing,” Mathur had told Inc42 earlier. In FY25, Razorpay slipped into the red, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs from moving its domicile to India. It did not disclose the size of the loss. The reverse flip tax bill has been reported at about ₹1,245 Cr, or about $150 Mn. A year earlier, in FY24, its payments business had reported a ₹34 Cr profit against a total revenue of ₹2,068 Cr or a net margin of 1.6%. The company claims to lead India’s digital payments processing market in terms of total payments volume and is expanding across Southeast Asia and other geographies, but monetising this scale has always been a problem when it comes to payments companies. The 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on large UPI payments, due after Diwali, would be the first fee on a bulk of these payments, and it would arrive just ahead of the listing window. How much reaches Razorpay’s bottom line depends on two things: how it negotiates with the banks that receive the fee and the large merchants that pay the MDR. Sources we spoke to suggest that much of the revenue bump that companies like Razorpay will get out of MDR would not boost their topline significantly, but could feed profits strongly because it is a fee on rails that companies have already built. For Razorpay, it’s a boost to its search for the right valuation just in time. MDR on UPI would likely narrow the gap between the company’s sought valuation and its bottomline. It also gives Razorpay a growth story to take to public investors as it heads into the IPO. A Profitable Core Unlike many of its contemporaries eyeing a listing at the scale of Razorpay, the fintech has no major debt overhang and nearly half of the IPO proceeds are expected to be allocated for OFS. Company sources told us that the core online payments business is EBITDA profitable and generating strong cash flows, which is why the company is making bold investments in allied businesses and AI. Sources pointed towards capital allocations “between mature, cash-generating units and high-potential growth bets”, with AI-first products, financial infrastructure and new verticals taking the investment. The company has also given a timeline on profitability. “By the end of FY26, our India business should be solidly profitable. At the consolidated level, we’ll reach profitability about two to three quarters after that,” the company’s CFO, Arpit Chug, told Inc42 in October 2025. But FY26 has since closed, and Razorpay is yet to make those numbers public. The biggest factor in Razorpay’s IPO will be the profitability and the margins earned by its core business. In lieu of actual profit figures, Razorpay’s pitch to public investors rests on scale. It described itself in 2024 as India’s market leader in digital payments processing, with a majority share, and said in 2025 that it served 105 of India’s 119 unicorns. It claims to be processing a total payments volume (TPV) of over $180 Bn (as of 2024 end). When compared against its primary competitors Cashfree and PayU, Razorpay stands out for its scale and its focus on small and medium businesses. Razorpay claims to lead on overall volumes, enterprise accounts drive the bulk of volumes at Cashfree, Inc42 reported earlier. Razorpay, on the other hand, claims that 80% of its client base comprises SMBs and startups. Among the three, PayU India leads in terms of the topline. Its payments business alone earned $523 Mn (about ₹4,420 Cr) in FY25. It pulled ahead of Razorpay which reported ₹3,783 Cr in FY25, while Cashfree stood at ₹640.1 Cr. PayU owner Prosus claims the company has a 25% share of the Indian online payments, while processing $90 Bn in TPV in FY26. In a bid to race past the competition, Razorpay has been eyeing overseas markets by strategic tie-ups and acquisitions. Mathur earlier said that international was its fastest-growing business, with payments growing about 40% and newer segments at 70-90%. Outside India, Razorpay currently operates in Malaysia and Singapore and is eyeing expansion into the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam as its next Southeast Asian targets. The company, according to sources, is expanding majorly within Southeast Asia and expects the revenue from these countries to contribute 15% of its overall topline by 2030. Razorpay entered Malaysia by buying a majority stake in Curlec in 2022, launched its gateway there in 2023 and entered Singapore in March 2025. Closer to home, the biggest expected lever is UPI and the introduction of MDR soon after the festive season. About half of the payments flowing through Razorpay are on UPI, and that rail is about to start earning the fee that can feed the company’s bottomline. The Two Negotiations Behind Razorpay’s MDR Upside The first critical negotiation for Razorpay will be with banks. Payment aggregators such as Razorpay get no fixed share under NPCI’s stated framework, because they are not direct members of the UPI network and are part of it only through sponsor banks. So the aggregator’s cut has to come out of the acquirer bank’s share in the MDR, under a private contract between the two. Reports suggest that the talks have centred on aggregators keeping 50-80% of the acquiring bank’s MDR share. But there is also a flip side to it. Payment aggregators and gateways already earn technology, checkout and reconciliation fees from merchants, and with MDR coming into effect, the merchants can move to the aggregators and gateways that offer more reasonable take rates. Pine Labs CEO Amrish Rau has already flagged that talks with merchants have yielded this view among the primary customer base for payments aggregators. “From a commercial standpoint, I absolutely do believe when it comes to the largest of large merchants that we have with us, there will be a commercial conversation to be had, for sure,” Rau said in October 2026 after the Q2 results. Notwithstanding the restructured commercial agreements that the payment aggregators and gateways will sign with banks and merchants for the MDR regime, sources say that the fee could support higher valuations for IPO-bound companies such as Razorpay and PhonePe. “The headline MDR pool is not the same as revenue accruing to an individual participant. It depends on eligible transaction volumes, merchant mix and the prescribed distribution across the ecosystem,” PhiCommerce CEO Rajesh Londhe told Inc42. Listed peer Paytm has already put a number on what MDR will bring to the table. With its Q2 results, Paytm said it expects an uplift of about 2.5 bps in its overall payments processing margin, and that the actual outcome may stabilise in 2-3 quarters after implementation. As per sources, MDR could bring Razorpay ₹192-461 Cr of revenue a year once implemented, which would be about 5-12% of its FY25 revenue and 15-36% of its FY25 gross profit. As a result, analysts believe that Razorpay could see a valuation bump of $300 Mn-$1 Bn from the existing ask. That’s what the MDR effect can actually unlock, though much would also depend on the commercial agreements with banks and merchant talks. Razorpay’s technology prowess and merchant scale could be a huge lever in any talks with banks and merchants. However, what matters more than the scale will be the value of transactions and the scale of the clients themselves, which would directly boost revenue and improve margins. Nearly 80% of Razorpay’s customers are small businesses, digital-first brands and startups, and it has not disclosed how many of their tickets cross the ₹2,000 threshold required for the MDR boost. There is also no certainty as yet on the timeline by which fintech companies can expect the MDR outcome to start showing up on their P&L. Analysts tracking the industry, however, say that the companies would need a few quarters of data to give investors a credible outlook. For Paytm, that could be 2-3 quarters, and with Razorpay coming to the IPO table, investors would want to hear a number for the company. Will a listing between January and March of 2027 be enough to give investors a clear answer? The AI Story Needs Numbers Then there’s the AI story, which we had written about extensively earlier this year. According to Mathur, Razorpay is building a long-term business bet on AI and this is not related to the IPO and its outcome. The fintech sector has been one of the earliest adopters and partners of frontier AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude, experimenting with AI use cases for the millions of merchants on its platform. Razorpay’s Agent Studio, built on Anthropic’s Claude, offers small businesses task-specific agents for abandoned carts, disputes, subscription recovery and cash flow forecasting. Mathur wants Razorpay to be known as “an operating system for businesses” which is run on AI. That story gives investors a reason to look past the thin margins in the payments business, but the AI theme is not strong enough in the case of Razorpay yet. It has to make a bigger splash in terms of the outcomes it is seeing. . Rivals Cashfree, PayU and Pine Labs are also accelerating their AI led partnerships to offer new products to their existing merchant base. All these AI offerings have been particularly concentrated towards agentic workflows and ecommerce enablement. However, there is still little public evidence of what these agents earn. Mathur earlier told us that it will take a few years to assess the real term monetisation value that these AI capabilities can unlock for any fintech. Hence for an IPO-bound Razorpay, its core payments business is the only true and measurable metric for the public investors. The future bets may fructify but for now, they are unlikely to be a factor for investors. Even at a reported $5 Bn valuation, Razorpay goes to market with some real strengths such as 65% YoY revenue growth in FY25, about $180 Bn in annualised TPV, and a profitable core. While it is banking on the MDR regime to solve a lot of headaches, investors will want to see a lot more to justify the valuation ask. Whether the price holds depends on disclosures still to come, including its FY26 and subsequent financial performance and the results of its MDR negotiations with banks. And only then will Razorpay find out how much of its story the public market is willing to pay for.

Lionel Messi returned to the FIFPRO Men’s World 11 for a record-extending 18th selection on Monday, but Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane was a surprise omission from the team chosen by professional players from 73 countries.
Messi, who announced his international retirement in August after helping Argentina reach the World Cup final and continues to play club football for Inter Miami, was named in the World 11 for the first time since 2023.
The 39-year-old was selected in a forward line alongside Manchester City’s Erling Haaland, Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal.
Lamine, 19, became the first player to earn two World 11 selections before turning 20 after also making last year’s team. He was joined by fellow Spain World Cup winners Rodri, Pau Cubarsi and David Raya.
Kane’s absence was notable after a prolific 2025-26 season in which he helped Bayern Munich win the Bundesliga and captained England to the World Cup semifinals.
