If you have holiday travel plans coming up, having a reliable power bank is a must. Sling a decent power bank in your pocket or bag and you can keep your phone and other gadgets topped up. But what if you want something a little more powerful? The best laptop power banks boast larger capacities and faster charging speeds, and the EcoFlow Rapid Pro is my top pick.
Both EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro models are on sale right now. The larger 27650 mAh-capacity Rapid Pro X is $170 ($80 off), and the 20,000 mAh Rapid Pro is $70 ($56 off). While both have steadily dropped in price since its release in late 2025 and often go on sale, I have never seen them available for cheaper than this.
EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro X can deliver a total of 300 watts to power up a laptop, smartphone, and headphones simultaneously. It comes in just under the maximum capacity allowed on flights. This power bank has three USB-C ports, rated at 140 watts, 65 watts, and 65 watts, and a retractable 2-foot USB-C cable rated at 140 watts. The 3.9-inch LCD display shows remaining power as a percentage and the charging rate for every connected device. You can also cycle through the stats to see the temperature and battery health or change the brightness and screen timeout. You can even connect your phone to this power bank via the Ecoflow app if you want to.
This power bank supports almost every fast-charging protocol going (PD3.1, PPS, QC3.0, AFC, Apple2.4A, BC1.2, SCP, FCP, UFCS), but its greatest feature could be its super speedy recharge rate. Charge from a single USB-C input at 140 watts, and it takes an hour or so to fill, but you can plug in both at once to hit 80 percent from dead in under half an hour. If you don’t mind an extra purchase, Ecoflow’s dock can charge via the pogo pins on the bottom at 320 watts, enabling you to go from zero to 80 percent in just 20 minutes.
The smaller Rapid Pro matches its bigger sibling on most fronts, but has a lesser 20,000 mAh capacity, a maximum combined output of 230 watts with a 100-watt built-in 2-foot USB-C cable, a 100-watt USB-C port, and two 65-watt USB-C ports. It can also charge in under 20 minutes with the EcoFlow Rapid Pro Desktop Charger at $140 ($50 off). The charger has four USB-C ports and a USB-A port in front, so it can charge multiple gadgets while you juice up the power banks on top.

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker.
But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary.
The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024.
Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman.
In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust.
"I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote.
Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible.
"In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen."
'The king of tech'
Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years.
An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon, Meta, Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems.
Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives.
- Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair
- Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky
From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year.
"He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research.
Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away.
Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly.
The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang.
Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing.
No clear successor
With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor.
"There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said.
If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth.
But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job.
"You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said.
While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier.
O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that.
Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang, O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him.
Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time.
"It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."

After knife-edge vote, New Zealand parties put off coalitions talks
- Published
Who will form New Zealand's next government remains uncertain after the country's national election on Saturday, with final results not due for another couple of weeks.
It's the tightest vote that the country has seen in years, with the incumbent National Party and opposition Labour Party neck-and-neck in terms of party vote share.
In terms of seats, a National-led conservative coalition, which includes the Act Party and NZ First, are projected to win a combined 67 seats - giving them a narrow one-seat majority.
As questions about other coalitions swirl, party leaders are remaining tight-lipped, saying they would wait for the final results before formal discussions.
Major parties on both sides of the political aisle were "likely dissatisfied with their campaigns", Max Rashbrooke, adjunct senior research fellow at the Victoria University of Wellington, told the BBC.
The opposition Labour Party, led by Chris Hipkins, ran an election campaign that "seems to have inspired few voters", despite going up against Christopher Luxon, a "historically unpopular prime minister", Rashbrooke said.
On the other hand, he added, the incumbent National Party also "failed to spark enthusiasm" even though it "should have been safe" given the country hasn't seen a one-term government in more than 50 years.
The election dealt a huge blow to National with the loss of some of its most senior lawmakers, including Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, Transport Minister Chris Bishop and House Speaker Gerry Brownlee.
Act Party leader David Seymour has expressed interest in the finance minister portfolio, telling news outlet Stuff that National must recognise the voters' message and let its coalition partners play a bigger role.
"The government barely survived, it must now put its best foot forward in every step," he said.
The big winners of election night were "the more radical minor parties", Rashbrooke said.
The left-leaning Greens and the right-wing libertarian Act Party both saw new highs this election, while the Opportunity Party, a fledgling centrist party, scored a breakout victory. Having previously failed three times at getting into Parliament, it's now projected to get seven seats.
Opportunity's incoming lawmakers, including leader Qiulae Wong, arrived at New Zealand's parliament on Monday morning, for the start of what Wong said would be a week of "induction stuff".
Opportunity, which has rejected traditional political divisions, has said it's open to forming a coalition with either major party.
Whichever coalition they join, though, they would "really need to be comfortable with the overall direction the government is going in", Wong told reporters on Monday.
Wong said that although she has received calls of congratulations from Labour's Hipkins and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, they have not had any discussions about coalitions.
Luxon, who had previously ruled out working with Opportunity, told public broadcaster RNZ on Monday that he wanted to talk to Wong "shortly".
Counting is still underway for nearly 400,000 "special votes", which includes those from overseas voters and people outside of their electorate.
These make up 14% of total votes, and are likely to be important in the final count.
"They tend to lean left, as voters casting special votes tend to be younger and more likely to be renters - and therefore more likely to be living outside their electorate," senior politics lecturer Claire Timperley told the BBC on election night.
"The overseas vote might be more likely than usual to be disaffected by the current coalition, given we've seen increasing numbers of New Zealanders moving overseas as a result of cost-of-living challenges."
Faced with a stagnating economy and challenging job market, a record number of Kiwis are moving overseas in search of better career opportunities. More than 114,000 people migrated out of the country in the year leading up to August.
Young people the BBC spoke to ahead of the election said they were "tired" and "cynical" about the future - part of what polling shows is a general grim mood across the country.
"In New Zealand as elsewhere, politics is splintering. But which parties ultimately benefit remains unclear for now," said Rashbrooke.
Final election results are expected on 27 November, with the official confirmation of MPs set for 3 December.

The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
- Published
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.

  - Published1 day ago
- How America voted in maps and charts 
  - Published1 day ago
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."

Vietnam withdrew on Monday a proposal allowing children aged 15 to 17 to donate their organs after death following public criticism in a country where deceased donor transplants remain limited.
The Southeast Asian country began kidney transplants in 1992 and performs the most annual transplants in the region, according to state media.
However, the vast majority of transplants in Vietnam rely on living donors. Transplants in many other nations mostly use organs from deceased donors, expanding their donor pool.
Officials in Vietnam say they are seeking to update a 2006 law on organ and tissue donation, aiming to increase life-saving transplants while safeguarding donors.
A draft submitted to the National Assembly last month proposed allowing 15- to 17-year-olds to donate their tissues, organs or bodies after death, provided the child's parent or legal representative consented.
But, after online backlash, officials removed the under-18 donor provision from a revised draft dated Sunday, with the government saying it had accepted recommendations from lawmakers that only legal adults should be permitted to donate their organs.
Dissent is heavily restricted in communist Vietnam, but opposition centred on whether parental consent could adequately protect child donors from pressure or exploitation.
Criticism also focused on a survey of schoolchildren as young as seven conducted in October to gather feedback on the draft law.
The poll prompted questions about whether minors could understand complex medical, legal and ethical issues, state outlet Tuoi Tre News said.
It said "the provision allowing minors to register as posthumous organ donors prompted considerable controversy and differing opinions among the public".
"Taking these concerns into account, the government has revised the draft," stipulating that only people aged 18 or older may donate their organs, Tuoi Tre said.
National Assembly deputy Pham Khanh Phong Lan urged lawmakers last month to oppose allowing child organ donors, saying: "You cannot sacrifice one child to save another."
One Threads user posted on Monday: "The power of public scrutiny has paid off. It is a relief to see this draft proposal rejected."
The newly revised draft still allows living minors to donate regenerative tissue, for bone marrow or stem cell transplants, to family members when no suitable adult donor is available.
The procedure would require health assessments, counselling and consent from both the child and their legal representative.
A draft law is expected to be approved this month.

A Royal Caribbean employee has been found by two Newport Beach fishermen treading water 20 miles off the California coast.
The cruise ship worker was rescued Friday after being spotted by Sean Norton and Grant Garrett, who had been fishing for marlin that morning.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat. Let's get all of our lines in,’” Garrett recalled in an interview with CBS Los Angeles.
The employee, whose name has not been revealed, told the fishermen he was a pianist on Royal Caribbean’s 14-deck Ovation of the Seas ship.
Norton said he and Grant lifted the man, adding that the pianist was “in total shock.”
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
Once the man was safely out of the water, the fishermen put out an emergency call, and Newport Beach lifeguards responded.
Local authorities believe the man may have gone overboard roughly nine hours before he was found.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean,” Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS LA.
A spokesperson for Royal Caribbean acknowledged the incident, telling The Independent, “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."
The rescue occurred during a particularly strong El Niño this fall that is keeping the Pacific Ocean warm off the coast of California.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees. A different year — no way he makes it,” Norton said.
The Coast Guard confirmed to The Independent that a “conscious individual” was rescued from the water. The man was reportedly hospitalized but is in stable condition, the Coast Guard said, adding that the incident is under investigation.
The Independent has reached out to the Newport Beach Fire Department for comment.

She lost her sight - now she is fighting to make history for Africa
- Published
Rukayat Taiwo Suleimon only took up sambo this year, but the Nigerian has already secured her place in the history of the martial art.
The sport shares strong roots with judo and wrestling, combining techniques such as hip and leg throws to take opponents to the mat, where they can be pinned.
Originally developed by the Soviet Union's Red Army in the 1920s, it was officially recognised as a combat sport by USSR officials in 1938.
Competing at the 2026 World Sambo Cup in Armenia, Suleimon defeated Uzbekistan's Charos Ortikova in the final of the women's 54kg category to claim victory on her international debut.
It was the first time that women with visual impairments had been included at the competition.
"Being the first female blind sambist in the world to win the gold medal makes me great," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"This is my first time in sambo and God crowned my efforts."
Suleimon's achievement was part of a breakthrough moment for African women in the sport. She and compatriot Elizabeth Aseso, who competed in the 59kg category, were among the pioneering sambists representing the continent in Yerevan.
For Suleimon, her gold medal is a reward for the hard work over many years which has seen her move from athletics to judo and now to the top of the international sambo podium.
"I really benefit a lot from sports and, despite my blindness, I achieve a lot," she said.
"If I [were] not blind, I don't think I would be at this level. I believe I will achieve even more."
From darkness to double glory
Suleimon's journey to becoming a champion has been marked by hardship and a determination to rebuild her life.
After failed surgeries she lost her sight in 2009 because of glaucoma, an eye condition that damages the optic nerve and can lead to permanent loss of vision.
The change in her circumstances affected her relationships, leaving her feeling isolated at a time when she needed support the most.
"People looked down on me. I would just stay indoors and cry," she explained.
"So many friends left me. They stopped communicating with me."
Her life began to take a different direction after she attended a vocational training centre for blind people in Lagos.
Through a friend, she was introduced to a para-athletics coach who helped her discover her potential in sport.
Since 2011, Suleimon has won more than 20 national medals across sprint events (alongside guide runner Stephen Oyelakin), discus and shot put.
She then began practicing judo and sambo.
"Since I [started] sports I have seen that where there is life, there is hope," she said.
"What sighted people can do, a blind person can do even better.
"I'm proud of myself because it's not easy to be a champion in athletics and in sambo. I don't want to lose the glory."
Her achievements have also become a source of pride for her family. Her twin sister Ganiyat Kehinde Suleimon says her sibling's disability has never defined her worth.
"She is someone we are all proud of. She is now a champion," Ganiyat told BBC Sport Africa.
"Her disability did not make her a liability to us."
For Nigerian sambo coach Olugbenga Adekahunsi, Suleimon's performance in Yerevan offered a glimpse of what she can accomplish with the right support and continued development.
"I see a lot of quality in her because she is very strong and the confidence is there," he told BBC Sport Africa.
"I believe she will become a great sambist."
'No support' for para-athletes
Suleimon says the recognition she has earned internationally has not been matched by adequate "support" at home.
However, her victory is the latest milestone in Nigeria's growing presence in the discipline.
Two years ago Samuel Oladele Kekere became the first blind African to compete at the World Sambo Championships in Kazakhstan, and Sodiq Ajibade followed that with a bronze medal at last year's edition in Kyrgyzstan.
"Despite making Nigeria and the whole of Africa proud, there is nothing to show for it," Suleimon said.
Her concerns reflect wider complaints from Nigerian para-athletes about limited funding, inadequate specialist facilities and insufficient institutional backing, despite their achievements.
Sherif Hammed, vice-president of the Sambo Association of Nigeria, says a lack of resources can prevent talented athletes from reaching their full potential.
"When athletes do not have facilities to train, they cannot compete at the world level," he said.
"It is quite disheartening and heartbreaking.
"People with disabilities, particularly visually impaired athletes, sometimes feel that because of their challenges, they have no purpose in life."
For Suleimon, a Lagos State judo champion, the journey to training is also an issue. Travelling across the city and covering transport costs make maintaining a demanding schedule difficult.
"I leave home at 5.30am to make it to training on time," she explained.
"It takes a lot of money and sacrifice."
Suleimon was unable to follow up her World Cup success at the World Sambo Championships in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where blind women were again scheduled to compete for the first time.
Beaten in Friday's opening round by Moldova's Ina Cernei, she still hopes her exploits on the global stage can inspire others.
"I want to encourage my fellow blind Africans to believe they can do it," said Suleimon. "And I want to make my country proud again."

As the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections rolled in, President Donald Trump — known for his frequent and brash social media posts — remained relatively muted, attributing the Democratic Party's sweeping victories to the fact that he himself wasn't on voters' ballots.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP," he posted to Truth Social, his social media platform, on election night.
But according to alleged screenshots some users shared on social media, Trump posted again later, ranting about how the voters had "failed" him and that there would be consequences to face as a result.
(X user @camolNFT)
The full text of Trump's supposed post read as follows:
THIS IS YOUR PRESIDENT SPEAKING. You read that right. YOUR PRESIDENT.
But since the woke mind doesn't want that, there's gonna be some changes around here. You failed me. There's consequences since you are an enemy of the greatest president to ever live.
American Crypto? Cancelled.
Super Intelligence? Cancelled.
Stimulus checks? Cancelled.
Epstein file releases? Cancelled.
Working to get gas prices lower? Cancelled.
Hope you like cancel culture. It seems like the liberal IDIOTS do. Why would you disrespect the greatest man to ever live. My son Barron came to my room upset. He is scared because he is a white man. Every white man should be scared. God bless some of you. PRESIDENT DONALD J FREEDOM TRUMP
Snopes readers asked us to investigate the legitimacy of the images being shared.
We found the supposed screenshots were fake.
Although the profile photo and handle matched Trump's real Truth Social account, the screenshot cut out the timestamp and engagement metrics. While legitimate screenshots of Truth Social posts do sometimes leave out that information (here's an example from an official Trump campaign account), omitting it for no apparent reason makes the post more difficult to verify. As a result we needed to look for additional information.
Searching Trump's Truth Social account turned up no results. We also checked multiple websites that archive the president's posts, even if they are deleted. Nothing matched there, either, confirming he never made such a post.
Additionally, Snopes frequently checks claims about fake Truth Social posts from the president, and as a result, we are very familiar with the his written voice — and we can check his word usage against archives of his real posts. While this fake post makes some effort to mimic his tone, it falls flat in a few spots. For example, Trump has not used the word "gonna" in a single post in 2026, while he has written "going to" dozens of times.
For further reading, we also fact-checked whether an image truly showed Trump fainting in response to the midterm results.

I don’t need to specifically tell you about WhatsApp’s popularity. It has billions of users worldwide, and it is the go-to messaging app for many people. Thanks to the network effect, most popular messaging apps haven’t replaced WhatsApp, even with better features and privacy.
One of the biggest reasons most people use WhatsApp, besides the fact that their friends or family are already on it, is that it is free to use. And since Meta owns it, free usually comes with a caveat. And that’s your data and how Meta tracks your WhatsApp chats. Although your chats are encrypted and Meta openly says it won’t use your data for advertising, you can talk to a friend on WhatsApp and still see relevant ads on other Meta platforms like Instagram instantly. Don’t you believe me? Just try it once.
Fortunately, WhatsApp also offers various privacy settings to keep your conversations private, prevent scams, and more. In this ultimate guide, we’ll cover all the privacy settings you need to enable on WhatsApp for maximum privacy. This guide includes all the methods, and I update it frequently and make changes if the features or flow change. Bookmark this page and revisit it anytime to keep your WhatsApp privacy settings up to date.
Table of Contents
WhatsApp Privacy Settings You Should Enable
Hide your Last Seen and Online status
If you care about your privacy and don’t want your people to know when you were online and when you last used the app, WhatsApp allows you to hide the last seen and online status completely
By default, WhatsApp shows the exact time when you last used the app and shows users when you are actually using the app
While these two features let others know when you use WhatsApp, they can also be a downside, especially if others are expecting an immediate reply when they see you online
Fortunately, WhatsApp lets you disable your last seen and completely hide your status. It also gives you more flexibility by letting you hide these from specific contacts, from your contacts, or disable them entirely for everyone.
Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.
However, you can silence unknown calls so that you won’t get notified of random spam calls.
How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on your profile picture, and tap on the privacy option
Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.
If you want to turn on disappearing messages for individual chats, open the new chat and tap on the three-dot menu on the top right corner of the screen, select disappearing messages, and select the timer
Keep WhatsApp photos out of your gallery
By default, WhatsApp saves all photos you receive to your media gallery, including sensitive and personal ones. Even if you lock WhatsApp, anyone can see the photos you received by opening your phone gallery. This also uses your data to automatically download them and increases your storage usage.
WhatsApp allows you to turn off automatic media download and also lets you stop showing media directly from your photos app
How to stop WhatsApp from automatically saving media
First, you can turn off automatic media downloads. To do that, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then scroll down and tap Storage and data.
From there, scroll down and tap Media auto-download, then select all three: when you are using mobile data, when you are connected to Wi-Fi, and when roaming. Then disable all download options, including photos, audio, video, and documents. This prevents files from auto-downloading on Wi-Fi, mobile data, or while roaming.
How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.
Here is how to set two-step verification with a password on WhatsApp
First, open your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, tap on account option, and tap on Password
Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.
Once you add two-factor authentication, remember to add a recovery email. This is especially useful if you lose your network; your email acts as a secondary verification method, where WhatsApp sends a code to your email instead of sending a verification SMS.
Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp on your phone. Tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Account. Scroll down, tap Security notifications, and turn on the option that says Show security notifications on this device.
Check linked devices and log out unknown sessions
WhatsApp lets you link and use your account on multiple devices. However, this could also mean someone could link your account to their device without you knowing. So, if you are suspicious about your account activity, you can check linked devices and sign out of any you don’t recognize.
How to check linked devices and log out of unknown devices on your WhatsApp account
Lock WhatsApp with your Biometrics
WhatsApp includes a native app lock feature that lets you lock it with your fingerprint or a pattern. WhatsApp also lets you lock immediately or after a set time. WhatsApp also recently rolled out a new feature to lock WhatsApp Web chats. So, I have made a detailed guide on how to lock WhatsApp on WhatsApp Web. You can watch the video below or follow the detailed steps in this guide.
How to lock your WhatsApp account with your fingerprint or Face ID
Lock and hide your most private chats
WhatsApp also lets you lock individual chats, not just the app. This way, you can lock or hide your most private chats. Here is how.
However, Locked Chat uses your device’s biometrics to lock chats. And if you cannot unlock the chat for any reason, you cannot get those messages back. Your only option is to clear the messages and unlock the chat, which you can do by going to Settings > Privacy, tapping Chat Lock, and tapping Clear Chat Lock. To lock the chats, follow the guide below.
Open WhatsApp on your device and, if you want to lock multiple chats on the home screen, select the chats you want to lock, tap the three-dot menu, and tap Lock chat. You can also do it for individual chats right here only.
Turn on Advanced chat privacy for sensitive chats
While disappearing messages remove your chat after a set period, you can turn on Advanced Chat Privacy for chats with sensitive content. This stops the other user from sharing or exporting your chats, and the media used in the chat won’t be saved in that person’s gallery. It also blocks the new Meta AI used in the chat itself.
Here is how to turn on Advanced Chat Privacy on WhatsApp
Hide your IP address in calls
WhatsApp also supports voice calls. Direct calls can connect your phone to another person’s phone, which can reveal your IP address and, in turn, your location. However, WhatsApp allows you to hide your IP during calls. Here is how.
How to protect your IP address in calls
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Privacy. Then scroll down, tap on Advanced, and enable the option that says ” Protect IP address in calls.
Disable link previews
WhatsApp also supports link previews, which show a preview of the website content. However, to do that, your phone connects to your website and sends a request from your IP address.
So it can easily reveal your phone’s IP address to the website, along with your location. You can also turn off link previews, which prevents those fancy images websites use for spam calls.
How to disable link previews on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Scroll down and tap on Privacy. From here, scroll down again, tap Advanced, and enable Disable link previews.
Block floods of messages from unknown accounts
WhatsApp also introduced a new feature that blocks messages from unknown accounts. It blocks unknown accounts that send you high volumes of messages, which is especially useful if you receive frequent spam texts or your WhatsApp is being bombed with multiple messages.
How to block a flood of messages from unknown accounts
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Tap Privacy, then tap Advanced again, and turn on the option that says Block unknown account messages.
Encrypt your chat backup
WhatsApp relies on Google Drive for your WhatsApp backup and iCloud on iPhone. However, by default, your chat backup isn’t encrypted.
You can turn on end-to-end encrypted backup with a passkey, password, or 64-digit key so third-party servers, including Google, can’t read your backup.
Here is how to encrypt your chat backup on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Chats. From here, scroll down and tap Chat backup, then scroll down again and tap End-to-end encrypted backup.
Here, you can turn it on and then use your passkey. Remember, you’ll need this passkey whenever you back up your WhatsApp with this data. You can also use a password or a 64-digit key.
Limit what Meta AI can do with your data
Like any other app, Meta also offers AI features that let you summarise and read messages and also chat with Meta AI. However, because these AI chatbots can’t use your data publicly, Meta uses Private Processing features, which it says process your data privately for those AI features.
However, both of the AI features, including Private Processing features and web search, where Meta AI can search the web based on your queries, are turned off by default. If you turn them on, you can turn them off by default to prevent Meta AI from using your data, even though it is processed privately.
Here is how to turn off the private messaging feature and that switch on WhatsApp
Reserve a username to keep your number private
Recently, WhatsApp introduced usernames on the platform, so instead of your phone number, you can create and share a username and let others contact you through it.
However, your phone number still verifies your account, but for better privacy, you don’t need to reveal it when sharing your WhatsApp account with others. You can also restrict who can message you using your username through a secondary verification method. I have covered in detail how to find your WhatsApp username.
How to reserve a username on WhatsApp?
Use Strict account settings if you’re a high-risk target
If you are a journalist, activist, or public figure, Meta offers Strict Account Settings to help protect your account’s security and privacy. Run the built-in Privacy Checkup
WhatsApp privacy settings can be confusing for beginners since the platform is used by people of all ages. However, WhatsApp also offers a built-in Privacy Checkup tool that provides a step-by-step process to help you enhance your WhatsApp account’s privacy.

In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe.
I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes.
Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off.
After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off.
The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well.
My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all.
Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do.
Since AI is often a lousy chef, giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk.
Earlier this year, the Times allowed AI to help with a recipe-scaling feature (modifying ingredient quantities so "serves 4" turns into "serves 6") and converting from imperial measurements to metric—cups, tablespoons, and Fahrenheit to grams, milliliters, and Celsius. Now, in the iOS-only beta, a "customize this recipe" field appears just above the ingredient list.
If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies.
"We put a lot of effort into trying to tell you when not to do something if it's no longer in the spirit of the recipe," says Camilla Velasquez, the general manager of NYT Cooking.
For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide, user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it."
She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end.
When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes."
So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more.
As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well.
I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original.
Once I started cooking, things went smoothly. I'm a recipe follower, not an improviser, and the Times’ recipes are easy to follow. The modifications were too. I was also impressed by how the app flagged that the chicken breast simmering time would be reduced because it cooks faster than thighs, and since they don't render as much fat as skin-on thighs do, it added some butter to the roux. These changes were incorporated into the right places in the recipe.
It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be.
This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option.
From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bowl into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice.
I'd been curious how it would handle batters, and it capably transformed Yewande Komolafe’s Toasted Sesame and Scallion Waffles into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang.
A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner.
Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original, saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch.
Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too.
It seems pretty natural that the Cooking section ran into some resistance when launching this feature. The NYT employs some of the best recipe creators in the business. Using AI to help us make substitutions is helpful, and the way the app integrates those changes into the recipes is impressive, but this tinkering with the original is essentially a subtractive process. How many of us are going to make substitutions and land on something better than Melissa Clark, Yewande Komolafe, or Francis Lam set out to make by design?
Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better.
It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms.
That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

The National Stock Exchange (NSE) on November 9 announced plans for a new headquarters in Mumbai, with renowned architect Hafeez Contractor set to design the proposed building. In a post on X, the exchange said the new headquarters would be located in Bandra Kurla Complex (BKC) and would represent a new addition to Mumbai's skyline. The proposed structure aims to symbolise innovation, ambition and India's growing stature in global financial markets. The building will come up on plots C-81 and C-82 in BKC's G Block, covering approximately 10,995 square metres. The Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) has allotted the land to NSE on an 80-year lease. An architectural video released alongside the announcement offers a glimpse of the proposed building's exterior and interiors. The design features a distinctive angular structure, a large blue globe displaying the NSE logo near the entrance, a glass-fronted facade and landscaped outdoor areas. It also includes separate drop-off zones for visitors and staff. The proposed interiors feature a spacious main reception area, a public atrium and an experience centre with open spaces, multiple levels and greenery. The visualisation also showcases a dedicated listing hall with a large display screen, arranged seating and a central presentation area. Other proposed facilities include office workstations with large windows and a market surveillance room equipped with multiple screens and monitoring desks. The video also offers a glimpse of open corridors, reception spaces and areas designed for visitors and employees. Regarded by The New York Times as "The Man Who Draws India", Hafeez Contractor is a Mumbai-based architect and urbanist known for his work across India's residential, commercial and public infrastructure landscape. He founded Architect Hafeez Contractor (AHC) in 1982 and has since led the firm into a team of more than 600 professionals. Its portfolio spans residential townships, business parks, educational campuses, hospitals, sports stadiums and several public projects. Contractor's architectural approach focuses on addressing India's infrastructure requirements while aspiring to meet global standards. His work includes several prominent developments, such as DY Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai, DLF Cyber City in Gurugram and Hiranandani Gardens in Powai, Mumbai. His residential projects across the country have also influenced the aspirations of India's growing middle class, particularly through the promotion of high-rise living and gated-community housing as defining features of urban development. Beyond architecture, Contractor's work has also influenced housing and urban policy in India. His collaboration with Shiv Shahi Punarvasan Prakalp Ltd. (SSPPL) helped establish a policy model that offered free housing to slum dwellers through developer incentives. This approach contributed to landmark high-rise developments in Mumbai, including the Imperial Towers, standing at 253 metres, and Minerva Towers, at 300 metres, according to his official website, Hafeez Contractor. Contractor's contributions to architecture have earned him two honorary doctorates: a Doctorate in Architecture in 2012 from Jawaharlal Nehru Architecture and Fine Arts University, Hyderabad, and a Doctorate in Housing in 2014 from Rai University, Ahmedabad. He has received more than 75 national and international awards, including the CWAB Architect of the Year award between 2006 and 2013 and the A+D Hall of Fame for the Decade Award. He has also been featured twice in India Today's Most Powerful Indians list over the last decade. His work across residential, commercial, educational and hospitality projects has earned him several awards. In 2016, Contractor was conferred the Padma Bhushan, one of India's highest civilian honours, in recognition of his contribution to architecture. Contractor pursued his Master's degree at Columbia University in New York, US, between 1976 and 1977. Before that, he completed his Bachelor's degree at the Academy of Architecture in Mumbai, where he studied from 1969 to 1976. His early education was at Boys Town School in Nashik, where he studied between 1957 and 1968. His academic qualifications and professional achievements include: Padma Bhushan: India's civilian honour for distinguished service of a high order, awarded in 2016. Doctorate in Housing (Honoris Causa): Rai University, Ahmedabad, 2014. Doctorate in Architecture (Honoris Causa): Jawaharlal Nehru Architecture and Fine Arts University, Hyderabad, 2012. It is preternaturally tough being a child cooped up in a cancer ward, a typical day filled with syringes, scans and chemo, when it ought to have been filled with play, play and more play, the room generously scattered with carelessly thrown toys. Even in the cancer ward, a toy can open up a cheerful vista beyond those grey walls for that child receiving it. For some children, that simple joy is a luxury, poverty queering the pitch already ravaged by cancer. Voluntary organisations working with children battling the double whammy of cancer and poverty seek to make room for those vistas of joy, relying on donations of used toys.
This intervention is two-fold as the voluntary organisation works in tandem with donors of used toys. Those donors are “us”: the general public that could be holding on to toys outgrown by the children of the house, but not by the adults who harvest nostalgia from those playthings. No censure here for latching on to those toys that are no more played with. A choice could be made between making those used toys really useful again by donating them to these underprivileged children or buying these kids new toys. As a society, this intervention is required of us. And this Children’s Day is the time to start it.
Two initiatives at ICH Egmore
Examples of this intervention are to be found at the Government Institute of Child Health and Hospital for Children (ICH), Egmore. Pephands Foundation, a voluntary organisation, runs what it calls PepCares Hub where play is promoted for these children with the help of volunteers as well as donors, particularly donors of toys. At pephands.org, a dedicated page invites old toys as donations to support its work among children with cancer in Chennai.
Also in ICH Egmore, there is what is called the Oncology Kitchen, being run by the voluntary organisation Myrtle Social Welfare Network (myrtleindia.org), to provide one nutritious meal from Monday to Friday to children undergoing cancer treatment at the hospital. In this manner, the NGO takes one worry off the parents’ plate. Williams, founder, notes that besides taking worries off the plate, his NGO is also focussed on placing joys in these children’s hands: toys, clothes and books.
Donations can be dropped off at three locations: the voluntary organisation’s Perambur office in Kennedy Square, Myrtle Women’s Shelter Home in Alwarpet, or at ICH’s A block, third floor. Williams emphasises that donated items should be in good condition, ensuring that children can really enjoy them.
A bank for toys
Early this year, The Toy Bank (toybank.in), headquartered in Delhi but active across India through partnerships with other NGOs and individual volunteers, lightened the murkiness engulfing the lives of children undergoing cancer in Chennai through what it calls the “giftofjoy” initiative. With the help of the Kodungaiyur-based Emmimah Charitable Trust (EMC Trust), it distributed toys and educational materials to underprivileged children battling cancer.
As one of its focus areas, EMC Trust works with children affected by cancer and accepts toys, books, and clothes for their young beneficiaries. According to Esther U, secretary of the trust, these gifts bring much-needed cheer to children spending a considerable amount of time in hospitals. The organisation regularly caters to around 80 young patients. The patients visit with their parents every month to collect the nutrition kits. For details, visit emctrust.org.
Online platforms
For those unsure about connecting directly with a voluntary organisation or want to have a wide choice of NGOS, online platforms might be the place to go. Among other things, they promote toy donations from the benefit of underprivileged children.
One such platform is Donateinkind.in which helps bridge the gap between prospective donors and NGOs. The website allows users to browse donation categories and find organisations across India, along with their addresses and contact details. It also features testimonials given by the users. They also provide guidelines for NGOs interested in getting listed. In the category “toy donation”, it entreats the public to “donate toys to children’s homes, toy banks and toy libraries run by Non Governmental Organisations”. For Chennai, it has listed ‘Toys for Tots’ Drive by HAPPY HANDS Spreading Smiles, noting that volunteers connected with the NGO collect toys for toy libraries. It adds that so far, seven toy libraries have been set up at primary schools in Chennai.
Share At Door Step (shareatdoorstep.com) is another platform that helps donors find a voluntary organisation engaged in a service they would like to support. In its bio, Share At Door Step (SADS) mentions toys among a prominent list of things that are donated for the welfare of the underprivileged. As its name implies, Share At Door Step provides the donor with the advantage of making the donation without leaving the comfort of their home. They can provide their location and seek a pickup slot. The website notes that a “convenience fee” would be applicable. Donors can also rack up what SADS calls “share points", by which they are eligible for rewards, all of which are listed on the website.
So, this Children’s Day, let us give them their childhood back by making it a little less about what they are going through and a little more about what they deserve to experience. Let us remember that the United Nations has declared an International Day of Play (June 11), asserting every child’s right to play, irrespective of their station in life. UNICEF promotes this day. After all, every child deserves the freedom to play, the joy of discovering something new, and the magic of simply being a child. Poverty and cancer should not be allowed to obstruct the delivery of this right.

Kashmiri food, phuljhadis from Old Delhi: Sonia Gandhi reminisces Diwali at ex-PM Indira's home
Remembering the Diwali celebrations at former PM Indira's home, Sonia said that the whole place would be lit up with diyas (earthen lamps).
On Diwali, senior Congress leader Sonia Gandhi shared profound memories of the festival at her mother-in-law, late Indira Gandhi's home – 1-Safdarjung Road. In a video shared on X on Sunday, Sonia is seen in a conversation with daughter Priyanka Gandhi and granddaughter Miraya Vadra in the garden of the house.
Remembering the Diwali celebrations at former PM Indira's home, Sonia said that the whole place would be lit up with diyas (earthen lamps). Kashmiri food would be cooked during festival time, Sonia reminisced.
Also read: CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke says he spent night at airport on way back from Kochi protest
“We would do the first lighting of the diyas by Ganeshji's murti. In those days we didn't have those little lights everywhere but we had diyas everywhere, around the pond, all along the roof, veranda and along the path. It was very pretty,” she can be heard saying in the candid conversation with her daughter and granddaughter.
Deep Dive
Priyanka also remembered celebrating festivals with her father Rajiv Gandhi at Indira's official residence. The mother-daughter also remembered how the weather used to be pleasant those days with skies blue and clear.
“Papa used to take us to Chandni Chowk to buy firecrackers,” Priyanka remembered her childhood ritual of going to Old Delhi for Diwali shopping.
Sonia also tells her granddaughter that people used to go "berserk" with firecrackers in those days, adding that she particularly liked fireworks like the 'phuljhadi'.
Also read: 'First Diwali when India is free from Naxalism': PM Modi marks festival in Bastar
Sharing the video on X and Instagram, Sonia said, "Revisiting my early memories of celebrating Diwali - the traditions, the festivities and the little moments that made it so special."
Sonia, whose memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love', recently made her social media debut with accounts on X and Instagram. The book is set to hit the stands on Tuesday, November 10.
In one of the excerpts from the book, Sonia recalls pleading with her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, not to become India's prime minister following the assassination of his mother, Indira, on October 31, 1984. In an edited extract from her memoir published by The Guardian, Sonia recounts the emotional moments after Indira Gandhi was shot dead by her bodyguards at her 1, Safdarjung Road residence in New Delhi.
Rajiv Gandhi was in West Bengal, attending a political rally, when he was informed that a serious incident had taken place in Delhi. He rushed back to the national capital and landed at around 3.30 pm before being driven straight to the hospital.

Recalling their meeting at the hospital, Sonia said she longed to be alone with her husband for a moment. However, she soon realised that Rajiv was about to tell her something she did not want to hear.
“We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn't want to hear. 'I have been asked; They want me to be sworn in as prime minister,'” she wrote.
Sonia said she was overwhelmed by anger and anguish at the prospect of Rajiv taking over as prime minister, fearing that he too could become a target.
“I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in,” she recalled.
