BALTIMORE/BOGOTA – For most people, the word “oligarch” conjures images of Russian elites who amassed huge fortunes in the wake of the Soviet Union’s collapse or, more recently, the tech billionaires who filled the front row at U.S. President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. But oligarchs are global, systemic and increasingly entrenched. They are a defining feature of the emerging world order.
We define oligarchs as actors who accumulate and fuse substantial wealth and consequential power (a criterion that, unlike Aristotle’s, does not require rule for the rich as a class). Today, some oligarchs, like Trump, start with wealth, which they use to acquire power (and yet more wealth). Others use power to accumulate immense wealth, as Russian President Vladimir Putin has done over the last quarter-century. Still others, like Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and Morocco’s King Mohammed VI, possess both from the start.
One need not be a billionaire to be an oligarch. We believe a net worth of $20 million, alongside evidence of wealth-power fusion, provides enough financial independence for an actor to build and exercise power without relying on others for the resources to do so. Applying this wealth threshold together with our wealth-power fusion criterion, we estimate that 59 heads of state or government today are oligarchs. Among them are leaders of eight of the world’s 20 largest economies (at purchasing-power parity, according to International Monetary Fund estimates for 2026).

- The claim that every calf birthed on a Texas ranch has been stillborn following the construction of a nearby artificial intelligence data center is unproven.
- The rumor has spread since at least May 2026. It appears to be based on an account shared by Clayton Tucker — the Democratic incoming Texas agriculture commissioner — who described a rancher in the state allegedly experiencing repeated cattle stillbirths after such a facility was built nearby.
- None of the versions of the story contain enough verifiable details to identify the rancher or the nearby facility. The accounts also differ regarding whether the plant is an AI data center or a battery energy storage system. The Texas Animal Health Commission said via email that it has not received any complaints or reports matching the account and has found no related investigations.
- It was not possible to find any scientific evidence linking noise or electromagnetic fields from data centers to cattle stillbirths.
- Snopes has reached out to Tucker — as well as veterinary and scientific experts specializing in cattle reproduction, noise and electromagnetic fields — for more information. We await replies to our inquiries and will update this article if additional information surfaces.
Throughout 2026, a claim circulated that every calf birthed on an unnamed Texas ranch has been stillborn following the construction of a nearby artificial intelligence data center.
For instance, one popular Instagram post (archived) from October features an image with text that says:
A Texas rancher says every calf born on his ranch has been stillborn since a data center was built next door.
They will call it anecdotal. A man burying calf after calf does not need a peer-reviewed study to know the building next door changed something.
(Instagram user @wonderzofthewild)
The caption attributes the story to Clayton Tucker — the Democratic candidate who won the 2026 midterms race to become the next Texas agriculture commissioner — and suggests "noise or vibrations" from the facility could be affecting the cattle.
Iterations of the rumor have spread widely on X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit and TikTok. One Instagram user posted about it in early June 2026 without mentioning any identifying details. Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether the story is true.
In short, it was not possible to find evidence confirming the rumor. None of the posts identify the rancher or the facility, while different versions of the story describe the facility as either a data center or a battery energy storage system. A spokesperson for the Texas Animal Health Commission said via email the agency has not received any reports or complaints about cattle stillbirths near data centers or battery storage facilities.
It was also not possible to find evidence that noise or electromagnetic fields from data centers cause cattle stillbirths.
Given the above and the lack of verifiable information, we have left this claim unrated.
Origin of rumor
The source of the claim, and the origin of the story at the heart of it, is unclear. Some of the earliest accounts come from Tucker, though it was not possible to establish when he first heard the alleged story.
Tucker discussed the supposed issue in a YouTube video posted on May 18, in which he said a farmer told him they had "not had a new calf in about two years" because of "ultra-low-frequency" noise and vibrations originating from a nearby AI data center.
He then told the story during a June 1 meeting of the Bell County Commissioners Court, at a July 7 Lubbock City Council meeting (around 1:33:51) — on that occasion citing numerous farmers — and during an August interview, in which he said a retired man bought a ranch in Fannin County, north of Dallas, but had to sell it for a loss due to a nearby data center causing multiple calf stillbirths.
Tucker's descriptions of the facility have, at times, differed. For instance, during an Aug. 24 podcast interview, he described the plant at the center of the story as a battery energy storage system (BESS), rather than an AI data center.
Local reporting confirms that a battery energy storage facility was built near Savoy, Fannin County. Meanwhile, reports from March describe plans for a data center in the area, but it was not possible to confirm that one was operating when Tucker began sharing the story. We also could not establish whether either one was the facility Tucker described.
Tucker shared posts repeating the allegation on Oct. 17 and Oct. 25. His captions acknowledge that "no veterinarian has confirmed the stillbirths" and that "no study has tied data center noise to livestock deaths," but still suggest data centers are to blame.
Separately, in April 2026 testimony (Page 42) to Texas lawmakers, Fannin County resident Cindy Tronzano reported that her cattle stopped grazing near a BESS facility and that her family had moved because of the noise. She did not mention stillbirths and it is unclear whether her account is connected to Tucker's story.
Snopes has contacted Tucker seeking more details about the stories he has repeatedly told. We will update this article if we receive a response.
A spokesperson for the Texas Animal Health Commission said via email that it has not received any reports or complaints about cattle stillbirths near data centers or battery storage facilities. The agency also said it has not found any investigations matching those circumstances.
Potential effects of data center noise on cattle
Data centers can produce continuous noise from cooling systems and other equipment, but it was not possible to locate evidence that such noise causes calf stillbirths, like the ones Tucker has discussed.
A 2023 scientific review published in "Annals of Animal Science" found that noise can cause stress in cattle and affect their behavior and health. It did not establish a connection between noise and stillbirths.
In early September 2026, French news agency Agence France-Presse investigated similar claims about data centers causing health problems and deaths among animals, including cattle and honeybees. Researcher Said Benaissa reportedly told AFP that studies do not support claims that electromagnetic fields from data centers cause cattle stillbirths. He reportedly said some studies have found small changes in fertility cycles and milk production.
It should be noted that electromagnetic fields and noise are different things. Therefore, these findings do not directly address the claims about low-frequency noise that social media posts cited.
What a September 2026 noise survey found
Some social media posts cite a survey that two nonprofit organizations, Quiet Communities and Science for Georgia, published in September 2026. Out of 103 people surveyed near data centers or cryptomining facilities, 83% reported hearing the noise they produce inside their homes. The organizations also note that some equipment can produce noise above 80 decibels.
The survey involved a small group and includes no reference to measuring noise at a Texas ranch. Only about 20% of respondents could answer questions about livestock, which was too little data to analyze. Therefore, the survey did not provide evidence linking data center noise to cattle stillbirths.
Snopes contacted experts in cattle reproduction, acoustics and electromagnetic fields for comment on the rumor about the calf stillbirths in Texas. We are awaiting their responses.
For further reading, we have previously investigated numerous other claims about data centers.

The US Food and Drug Administration has approved an India-made generic version of the world's only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV -- a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organisations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir.
The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy's Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
The drug is expected to cost USD 40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they're needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk.
People don't always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Perez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organisation Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.”
Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS -- and deaths. According to the WHO, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV programme for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organisation.
“And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.”
Generic lenacapavir can't be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is USD 28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that's similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent.
Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
“We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.”
Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection.
“For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.”
Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA.
“The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.”
Casa said she's optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV.
“Now,” she said, “we have the tools.”

Voters approved Question 1, which places protections for first- and second-trimester abortions in the state constitution. However, it also gives the state Legislature the power to pass some restrictions on abortions in the third trimester.
As the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections rolled in, posts on social media suggested that Virginia voters had approved an amendment to the state's constitution that would allow, as one X post put it, "the abortion of babies who are minutes from being born."
Snopes readers also contacted us looking for more information about the supposed vote.
The claim is false.
The posts used common anti-abortion framing to create a misleading description of a real proposal on the ballot, Question 1. The measure, which voters overwhelmingly approved, does enshrine in Virginia's constitution an individual's right to receive an abortion.
However, the measure explicitly contains an exception allowing the state Legislature to pass laws that restrict access to some abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy. Because this exception exists, Virginia voters did not approve "abortions up to birth."
It's also worth reviewing basic facts about abortions — doing so reveals that the anti-abortion posts are using dramatic language to attack a strawman argument they created.
The strawman argument
The misleading posts do not mention how far into their pregnancies women generally receive abortions. That's because the language of the claim relies on the idea that late-term abortions are a common practice, while the medical data shows they are quite uncommon.
According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the premier professional association for OB/GYNs in the U.S., less than 1% of abortions in the country are performed in the third trimester, and about 1% of abortions are performed after the woman has reached 21 weeks of pregnancy. The nonprofit Guttmacher Institute, a highly reputable source of information on abortion data, estimated that doctors performed 1.13 million abortion procedures throughout the country in 2025. Therefore, only about 11,300 abortions total were performed after the 21-week mark, still seven weeks shy of the third trimester.
In sum, late-term abortions are incredibly rare. The ACOG lists the following reasons why they are performed:
- As a result of a fetal diagnosis received later in pregnancy that may have a profound impact on the pregnancy's prognosis
- As a result of a diagnosis related to risks to their own health during pregnancy that did not present until later in pregnancy
- Not recognizing that they were pregnant until later in the pregnancy, which may delay them in presenting to start care
- Barriers to obtaining care earlier in pregnancy, including limited financial means, inability to travel, or work or childcare obligations
- A combination of any of the above
To put it another way, doctors, who take an oath to do no harm, perform late-term abortions because the baby is "life-limiting," the mother may not survive the pregnancy or the mother couldn't have the procedure earlier, even if she wanted to.
Question 1, explained
Question 1 enshrines the right to an abortion without any limitations through the first and second trimesters of pregnancy, amongst other reproductive care. This language reinforces the access currently available under Virginia law, according to reproductive healthcare nonprofit Planned Parenthood.
The amendment specifically permits the state Legislature to enact laws restricting abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy, with caveats. Those laws may not restrict abortions if "the patient's health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive," according to the wording on the ballot.
The following paragraph is the actual language of that caveat that will be added to the state constitution, according to Ballotpedia:
Notwithstanding the above, the Commonwealth may regulate the provision of abortion care in the third trimester, provided that in no circumstance shall the Commonwealth prohibit an abortion (i) that in the professional judgment of a physician is medically indicated to protect the life or physical or mental health of the pregnant individual or (ii) when in the professional judgment of a physician the fetus is not viable.
In addition, Question 1 also protects both patients and medical providers from punishment for providing or receiving abortion care.

Resource group for Education and Advocacy for Community Health (REACH), a not-for-profit organisation working to strengthen the tuberculosis (TB) response in India, has been awarded the Kochon Prize 2026, becoming the first civil society, non-profit organisation from India to receive this prestigious global recognition for its contributions to combating TB, a press release said.
Presented by the Kochon Foundation, an independent Korean non-profit foundation, in partnership with the Stop TB Partnership, the Kochon Prize recognises individuals and organisations that have made significant contributions to the fight against TB. The 2026 Kochon Prize is shared by REACH, the Centre for Health Solutions, Kenya, and the Marshall Islands TB Control Program. Previous winners from India include L.S. Chauhan (2006), head of the Revised National TB Control Programme, the Indian Council of Medical Research (2017) and Molbio Diagnostics (2024). The award was presented at the Stop TB Partnership Board Meeting held in Indonesia on November 5, 2026.
“Treat the person, not the disease - our journey with TB communities has been just that. We realised early on that overcoming barriers to care means addressing more than clinical needs - it means recognising social, community, family, mental health and situational challenges. That is the essence of integrated care: seeing the whole person, understanding their realities, and doing whatever it takes to ensure that no one is left behind,” said Nalini Krishnan, chairperson and co-founder, REACH.
“REACH is a remarkable and rare organisation that has been consistently ahead of the curve in terms of public health action, and particularly in the field of TB. A women-led organisation, they genuinely care about the people they’re supporting, beyond the numbers, data and reports to donor. However, they combine this with a robust scientific and technical approach and a shrewd understanding of the public health landscape in the country,” said Soumya Swaminathan, chairperson, M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation and former chief scientist, WHO, who nominated REACH for the award.
“This recognition is testimony to the dedication of the community health workers, TB Nanbans and TB Champions who work alongside us, and to the families affected by TB and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) who have placed their trust in us. We are deeply grateful to their unwavering commitment and fortitude, and are energised to do more to help facilitate equitable access to health,” said Ramya Ananthakrishnan, director, REACH.

In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.
"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.
The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.
Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.
Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.
Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.
And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.
And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.
"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.
When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Healthcare of last resort
Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.
But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)
Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.
Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.
"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."
And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.
Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.
Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.
For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.
"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."
Training elite clinicians
This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.
Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.
"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.
When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.
Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.
On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.
Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."
His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.
"What happened to you?" Horne asks.
"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.
A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.
Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.
Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.
Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.
Experiments
Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.
Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.
EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.
"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.
That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.
"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."
About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."
Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.
Today's trip
The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.
Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.
But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.
Merklin serves on a peer support team.
"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."
If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."
As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.
Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.
Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

Sean Penn isn’t exactly a fixture on the regional documentary festival circuit. But SFFILM’s Doc Stories has a way of attracting high-profile supporters.
On Saturday, Penn was at the fest’s Vogue Theatre in San Francisco to introduce James Marcus Haney’s “Black Sunflowers,” a documentary about a generation of young Ukrainians coming of age amid martial law and the demands of a country at war. Penn, an outspoken supporter of Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, signed on as the film’s executive producer before its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
“Who do you imagine yourself singing like if you could sing like somebody?” Penn told the packed theater. “This movie is the song I dreamed I could sing.”
Penn was one of several Oscar winners at the 12th edition of Doc Stories that concluded on Sunday.
Anne Lai, SFFILM executive director, said the organization’s mission, embodied by Doc Stories and the annual San Francisco Film Festival, is to keep independent voices alive by supporting filmmakers with distinctive work and helping them reach audiences.
“That means not only supporting films and filmmakers who are trying to put distinctive work out into the world, but also growing and sharing that work with audiences,” said Lai. “So as we talk about consolidations of studios and what happens on the margins, I think a lot about us as an organization is trying to look at what is in the margins because a lot of the most interesting things do not come through the mainstream.”
Academy Award-winner Laura Poitras attended the fest with her short “They’re Here,” about ICE agents’ descent on Minneapolis. It was one of 11 short documentaries that screened at Doc Stories.
Poitras and “They’re Here” co-director Rachel Lauren Mueller spoke in depth about making the film during the fest’s Doc Talks series.
“We describe (the film) as a horror documentary,” said Mueller, who is Minneapolis-based and shot most of the doc in January and February 2026 while residents were evading and resisting the paramilitary occupation of their city.
“Being in the occupation just as a human being and not even as a filmmaker was one of the most difficult experiences of my life,” Mueller said. “There were tanks rolling down my street. It was not the first time. That also happened after the murder of George Floyd, but this was different because the streets were filled with tear gas. They were kidnapping people from street corners right around my house.”
Poitras, known for her feature documentaries including “Citizenfour,” “All the Beauty and the Bloodshed” and “Cover-Up,” said that the gravity of the situation was one reason she and Mueller decided to make “They’re Here” a short film.
“I’ve worked in short form and long form, and the truth is feature-length documentaries often take longer, and I think we both felt a sense of urgency of making something that could be released in a more contemporaneous moment,” said Poitras.
“They’re Here” was one of several Oscar-qualified films that screened at Doc Stories. Others included Sam Pollard’s “Tutu,” J.M. Harper’s “Soul Patrol,” and Ava DuVernay‘s “14th.”
DuVernay said the Democrats’ midterm victory could make “14th” and its exploration of belonging and birthright citizenship even more resonant.
“The film goes far beyond this moment,” said DuVernay. “This film is about the structural challenges that we have had as a country, and until you know the machinery of elections, they are not going to get us to where we need to be. So, this is the right time for people to get past the vote, vote, vote of it all and into the OK, this is how we actually make systemic change.”
Doc Stories is considered an essential stop on the Oscar-season circuit because of its curation and the Bay Area’s concentration of AMPAS Documentary Branch and guild members. Its selections have a strong track record with the Academy. More than two dozen Doc Stories selections have earned Academy Award nominations, and several have won, including “No Other Land” and “Summer of Soul.”
“The doc community here is very engaged, committed, and vibrant, and they show up for each other,” said Jessie Fairbanks, SFFILM’s director of programming. “They want to see each other’s work and talk about what they are working on.
“There is usually some synergy just because of where we sit in the calendar year and the types of films that are campaigning, which is wonderful because it means we get a heightened profile for the festival. The doc community here is very engaged, committed, and vibrant, and they show up for each other. They want to see each other’s work and talk about what they are working on,” said Fairbanks.
Like DOC NYC’s annual Visionaries Luncheon, Doc Stories’ annual brunch brings together the who’s who of the doc community and lets filmmakers, producers, editors, cinematographers, and publicists schmooze with branch members before the Oscar Short List voting deadline. DuVernay and Netflix’s doc VP Adam Del Deo flew in for the lunch, as did the filmmakers behind “To Hold a Mountain” and Frontline’s Raney Aronson-Rath, who is campaigning for “One in a Million.”
Unlike for-profit DOC NYC, Doc Stories is a nonprofit festival, with a much smaller brunch than DOC NYC’s annual Visionaries Luncheon.
“Different organizations engage with the awards campaign in different ways,” said Fairbanks. “We don’t charge people a fee to be a part of our events. If you want access to the brunch, you can sponsor us, a nonprofit organization, and get access to the room; otherwise, you have to be a filmmaker who is a part of our organization, or you are an (AMPAS) voter. Monetizing that allows us to retain our independence when it comes to what we curate and what we put in front of audiences.”

MANCHESTER, ENGLAND – Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is facing another international window filled with uncertainty after his side slipped into the Premier League relegation zone despite a sensational comeback to claim a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa.
United is 18th on eight points after 10 games, one behind Coventry City, and for long periods of Sunday’s game looked like a disjointed, rudderless side, with collapses in concentration at the start of each half proving costly for Carrick’s men.

On Diwali day, as India celebrates the festival of lights, and firecrackers dazzle and explode, it’s perhaps timely to talk about health concerns related to festivals as well. The issue gains relevance, given that Delhi is already reeling under severe air pollution levels
In the 58th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss the public health concerns surrounding festivals, marking Diwali, including air pollution and AQI. Air pollution is now longer just a respiratory concern - research is increasingly linking it to several other health concerns including diabetes, heart disease and cancer. How to stay safe during both festive seasons, and all year around, are, therefore, important discussions to have.
With Ebola continuing to rage in parts of Africa, and the first death of a child in New York State of measles in 30 years, the issue of controlling the spread of infectious diseases has once again come into focus. Do watch for insights into how a One Health approach, which prioritises human, animal health, is the way forward, along with global cooperation and collaboration to tackling infectious diseases. And let’s not forget that vaccination remains crucial, and vital tool in our armamentarium.
Despite decades of progress, India still hasn’t fully been able to ensure quality maternal and child health care for all. Recent deaths of infants in tribal communities in Attapady, Keralam, have been in the news, calling for a deeper look at just why anaemia and malnutrition persist, and what interventions are needed to help tackle these issues.
The video also features a discussion on new research into Hepatitis B.

Dozens of global health and environmental organisations called on the World Health Organization on Tuesday to revise decades-old standards for nitrate levels in drinking water, arguing they do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.
In an open letter, 85 organisations, including Greenpeace International and the World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA), called on the United Nations health agency to include nitrate in an upcoming review of its drinking water guidelines.
The toxic effects of nitrates -- a residue left behind by intensive farming -- are widely recognised as particularly dangerous for children and pregnant women.
But the current WHO guidelines -- which set the maximum acceptable nitrate level in drinking water at 50 milligrammes per litre as nitrate or 11.3 milligrammes per litre as nitrate-nitrogen -- date back to 1958 and are "outdated", the organisations warned.
That level was set specifically to prevent so-called "blue-baby syndrome" -- a deadly blood disorder in which the blood's capacity for carrying oxygen is reduced.
But the limit "has not been updated in response to robust epidemiological evidence linking chronic, low-level nitrate exposure to long-term human health risks", Tuesday's letter said, pointing in particular to "colorectal cancer and adverse birth outcomes".
"Studies now link nitrate in drinking water, at levels well below the current WHO limit, to bowel cancer and premature birth," WONCA chair Pratyush Kumar said in a joint statement.
Decisive action
The letter was sent to coincide with WHO's annual One Health Day, which aims to raise awareness about the interconnected health of humans, animals, plants and shared ecosystems.
Surface water models indicate that hundreds of millions of people globally are exposed to elevated nitrate levels, the letter warned.
"Water should be life-giving, not life-threatening," Amanda Larsson, the global project lead for agriculture at Greenpeace, said in the statement.
"We cannot protect human health without protecting the groundwater and rivers that sustain us," she insisted.
"Governments must take decisive action to curb the growth of intensive livestock farming and actively support producers in transitioning to ecological farming practices -- ensuring that clean, safe drinking water isn't a luxury but a guarantee."
The organisations pointed to findings published last year by an expert panel commissioned by the Danish government indicating that the current international standard was insufficient to protect public health.
That expert panel recommended reducing the nitrate limit to 6.0 mg/L -- nearly 10 times below the current WHO benchmark -- something Denmark committed to earlier this year.
But most national governments base their drinking water standards on WHO guidelines, the organisations said, stressing that updating those guidelines was "vital for global policy reform".

One child succumbed to burn injuries, and 269 people were treated for firecracker-related burns across Tamil Nadu during the Deepavali festivities, according to official data tracking emergencies over a 24-hour window.
As per the official bulletin, the state 108 emergency ambulance network received 16,079 calls between 7 a.m. on November 7 and 7 a.m. on November 8.
Of the total distress calls, 2,475 were related to accidents, 396 for minor injuries, and 98 specifically for burn injuries.
To manage the festive emergency load, 1,283 ambulances were deployed on active duty across the State.
Statewide government hospitals recorded a total of 1,387 inpatient admissions during this period. The admissions included 956 for accidents, 321 for minor injuries or assaults, and 110 for burn injuries. One burn-related fatality was recorded, involving a child under the age of 15.
No adult deaths due to burns were reported during this timeframe.
Demographic data for burn injuries shows that men formed the largest group of victims, with 92 treated as outpatients and 76 admitted as inpatients.
Children under 15 were the second most affected demographic, with 48 outpatients and 17 inpatient admissions. Adult women accounted for 19 outpatients and 17 inpatients. In total, hospitals saw 159 outpatients and 110 inpatients for burn cases.
The Thanjavur Government Medical College Hospital recorded the highest patient volume for burns, accidents, and minor injuries, treating 36 outpatients and admitting 87 inpatients.
Other major medical centres handling the bulk of the emergency caseload included the Madurai Government Medical College Hospital with six outpatients and 84 inpatients, and the Chengalpattu Government Medical College Hospital with 85 inpatients.
The Periyar Nagar Government Hospital recorded one outpatient and 64 inpatients, while the Thoothukudi Government Medical College Hospital treated 46 outpatients and 13 inpatients.

CHICAGO — Sudden cardiac arrest statistics are chilling. In the United States, 350,000 people’s heartbeats, breathing, pulse, and blood circulation will all halt outside hospitals this year, seemingly out of the blue. These are not heart attacks. Only 1 in 10 people will survive them.
CPR and defibrillation can save their lives (and brains), but that depends on bystanders and emergency response systems being both nearby and prepared to step in — immediately. Survival chances drop by 10% for every minute that goes by without CPR.
Hints from observational studies suggested better, more comprehensive community training can help, which means educating 911 dispatchers, first responders, and potential bystanders. But results from a randomized controlled trial presented Sunday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Sunday show that approach has not worked, or at least not yet. But examples in Denmark may point the way forward.
“We performed an efficient, large, and high-quality trial engaging large segments of the community in emergency response, and in spite of this, survival remained low and unchanged,” Carolina Malta Hansen, the study’s lead author, said at a media briefing. “A multifaceted community and EMS implementation strategy did not improve survival with a favorable neurologic outcome for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. However, in the final year, there appeared to be an improvement in bystanders.”
Starting in 2021, researchers randomly assigned participants in 60 counties in North Carolina to receive intensive education on cardiac arrest intervention or to continue with standard practice. The intervention entailed training 911 dispatchers to improve their rapid recognition of cardiac arrest and better guide bystanders through CPR. First responders were educated on the use of automated external defibrillators before emergency services arrived. Community members in workplaces, religious groups, government offices, and other settings received training in CPR.
About 8.5 million people live in these counties. During the study’s five years, 22,459 adult residents experienced cardiac arrest outside the hospital. Their median age was 64; 37% were women, 33% were Black; and 29% lived in rural areas.
The numbers were split this way: 11,615 people experienced out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in counties that received intensive education, and 10,844 people had out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in communities that did not receive the intervention.
Amrish Deshmukh, a cardiac electrophysiologist who treats patients with heart rhythm disorders at the University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center, called the study results disappointing, but not surprising.
“Many interventions that have been studied in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and in post-arrest care unfortunately have not been shown to improve survival or neurologic outcomes,” he told STAT in an email. He was not involved in the new trial. “Prior studies have shown that mobile phone alerts, volunteer training, and increased automated external defibrillator (AEDs) availability can increase the performance of CPR and use of AEDs, but not all have shown improvements in survival.”
And yet, study author Malta Hansen, a cardiologist and clinical research associate professor at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital and Copenhagen EMS in Denmark, is hopeful. In the trial’s fourth year, an exploratory analysis showed the percentage of patients who underwent CPR performed by a bystander increased, suggesting that this component of the intervention was effective. More time may be needed to see which elements mattered and whether they affect survival.
“In light of the apparent improvement in CPR for the last year, further evaluation in the longer, more intense intervention is important,” she said.
Malta Hansen cites the case of Denmark, where rates of bystander CPR and survival are much higher than in the United States. The North Carolina study trained almost 5% of the population, at which point researchers started seeing a difference in delivery of CPR between the group that received training and the group that did not.
“Obviously, that’s not enough. We have observational evidence from other countries like Denmark, where 80% of the population is trained and 75% of patients receive high-speed care,” she said.
In Denmark, the defibrillation rate is 11%, compared to 2% in the U.S. In Denmark, survival is about 16%, compared to 10% in the U.S.
That CPR-trained rate in Denmark climbed from 20% in the early 2000s to 80% now, Malta Hansen said. “It’s not something that’s done in two or three years.”
Here’s what helps: To get your driver’s license in Denmark, you have to show that you have certification in CPR. “It’s just an incredibly efficient way to reach everybody,” she said.
Brahmajee Nallamothu, an interventional cardiologist and editor in chief of the AHA journal Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, had another theory on timing. Starting the trial right as Covid-19 was emerging could have affected educational efforts and could explain why effects of the training were delayed. He also asked if the educational intervention was the right approach.
“I don’t think anyone would argue with the importance of early treatment in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. When we think about bystander CPR, early defibrillation with AEDs, the challenge is: How do you translate that?” Nallamathu, who was not involved in the trial, said. “I think we still struggle with what’s the best way to train individuals so that they have sustained ability to understand and then utilize that tool when that situation arises, that’s an area that’s still complicated and still unknown.”
What’s next?
Malta Hansen’s team will follow this population in North Carolina for at least another year.
“We have established a fantastic infrastructure and network and collaboration, and everybody’s very excited to keep working on this,” she said. “What we need are communities who are very engaged and very eager to keep working on this. So we believe that future efforts to guide us will be successful.”
That won’t be easy, Michigan’s Deshmukh said.
“Implementation science is challenging (as evidenced by this and other negative trials), but is what I suspect will move the needle the most,” he wrote.

A video circulating on X, bearing the logo of M World, purports to show Russian foreign minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov saying that India is merely an oil-trading partner to Russia and that the two countries share only a commercial relationship. In the video, Lavrov is also heard claiming that India has no right to interfere in Russia’s foreign policy or advise Moscow on matters concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States or any other country.
Supreme Court advocate and activist Prashant Bhushan shared the video on his X account (@pbhushan1), which he later deleted. In his post, he criticized the Indian government and questioned what kind of advice external affairs minister S Jaishankar gave to Russia.
Another X account, Diya Kapoor, also shared the video with the similar claim of Sergey Lavrov drawing clear boundaries about the relationship with India.
🚨🇷🇺🇮🇳 RUSSIA DRAWS A CLEAR LINE!
“India is a trading partner, nothing more. We supply oil, and India pays for it. This commercial relationship does not give New Delhi the right to dictate or interfere in Russia’s foreign policy.”
Sergey Viktorovich ⚠️🌍 https://t.co/uX1x0adl0G
— Diya kapoor (@DiyaKapoor113) November 2, 2026
Some X accounts also shared this video with the claim of Sergey Lavrov dismissing India.
Fact Check
After a closer examination of the video, the movements of Sergey Lavrov while speaking appear unnatural and seem out of sync with the audio. This suggests that the clip may have been edited or manipulated. Using this as a lead, we performed a Google reverse image search on several keyframes from the video and found a video with the same background and clothing uploaded by M WORLD on October 31.
A comparison of the two videos shows that Sergey Lavrov’s clothing, background, head movements, and hand gestures are the same, with only the audio being different. Even the ‘M World’ YouTube channel logo appeared in both videos, confirming that the original video had been digitally manipulated. Both videos also feature the exact same glitch at the same moment.
In the original video, Sergey Lavrov is seen refusing the reports from Ukrainian officials claiming that Russian President Vladimir Putin refused to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and stating if Zelenskyy wants a direct meeting, he must travel to Moscow, where Russia will guarantee his safety and security.
Media outlet DW News posted the original video on October 31 showing the conversation about President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy meeting.
Furthermore, the official X account of the Russian Embassy in India, Russia in India (@RusEmbIndia) has also debunked the video. “Please stop copying silly AI fakes,” it said in a comment to the X post by Diya Kapoor.
@DiyaKapoor113 Please stop copying silly AI fakes
— Russia in India 🇷🇺 (@RusEmbIndia) November 3, 2026
Union government’s official MEA fact check account, too, flagged the post as fake.
Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨
The video of the Russian Foreign Minister being used in this post is fake! https://t.co/jpEX6qu19p
— MEA FactCheck (@MEAFactCheck) November 3, 2026
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov publicly dismissed India’s diplomatic standing is completely false and an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage contains a briefing regarding Russia-Ukraine relations, and there is no mention of India.
Twinkle Shrivastav is an intern at Alt News.

The parents of a 13-year-old girl have sued Google claiming she planned a potential suicide and funeral using its AI technology on a school-issued computer.
Filed Monday in a California court, the complaint is the first known case accusing Google of negligence related to AI integrations on Chromebooks, the tech giant's low-cost laptops used by millions of students in the United States and around the world.
The teenager was not able to access Google's Gemini app, nor OpenAI's ChatGPT, because they were blocked by her school. She was nonetheless still able to use Google's search engine, which contains AI-powered tools.
Those features were notably not among the tools that Google announced this week will be disabled by default for students.
"Schools should turn search off and keep it off until Google removes AI mode from search or ensures that every single student is always safe when they're interacting with AI," Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday.
The complaint alleges that the child had been a "happy 13-year-old girl" in North Carolina who received great grades, played music and participated in Girl Scouts.
Despite "no history" of mental illness, within months of using Google's AI-powered search on her school laptop, she began a "quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis" according to the complaint.
On March 17, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral," and the school notified her parents.
Her mother then saw the child writing a farewell letter in real-time after logging into her daughter's account, and her father intervened.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP.
Google argues that AI mode includes safeguards against self-harm and attempts to bypass them.
But the child "was able to keep going back over and over and over again," Liddle said. "Whatever safeguards they think they put in place were obviously insufficient."
Developers of fast-evolving AI technology are facing a litany of similar lawsuits in the US.
OpenAI faces several wrongful death suits, including from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, a teenager who committed suicide allegedly using methods advised by ChatGPT.
Google and the startup Character.AI agreed in January to settle several lawsuits filed by families of teenagers out of court.
On Wednesday, Google, TikTok and Meta each separately sued California to block a law that prohibits social media companies from providing addictive features to users under 16.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law in September, and it goes into effect on January 1, 2027.

Man Utd expected to sack head coach Carrick
- Published
Manchester United look increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick.
The club opted to stick with Carrick after the side's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October, with the intention of reassessing the situation during this month's international break.
Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that the board remain committed to that process, and that no final decision on Carrick's future has been made.
However, there is a growing expectation that chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will recommend to minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family for Carrick to be sacked.
The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.
BBC Sport reported in October that the club had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann over replacing Carrick.
Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is known to be keen on the role, while multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford.
Pochettino signed an extension to his contract as USA coach in August.
However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.
