- The claim that Apple Maps replaced current satellite imagery of Gaza with outdated imagery showing buildings still intact is unfounded.
- The rumor circulated on social media, with some posts comparing Apple Maps' imagery of the area with images from other services, such as Google Maps.
- We confirmed that Apple Maps does show outdated images of Gaza, but we found no indication that the service had ever hosted images of the area that captured the destruction that has taken place since October 2023. Rather, it appeared that Apple Maps simply lagged behind its competitors in terms of providing up-to-date imagery.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Apple seeking information regarding its satellite images of Gaza, as well as to a parody social media page that may have started the claim, and are waiting for responses.
As Israel's war on Gaza played a crucial role in some 2026 U.S. midterm election candidates' campaigns, a claim circulated online that Apple Maps had replaced current satellite imagery of Gaza with outdated imagery showing buildings still intact.
In the more than three years since militant group Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Israel has decimated Gaza's landscape and reportedly killed upwards of 74,000 people in what the United Nations has deemed a genocide. Social media users accused Apple Maps of "whitewashing" a genocide by presenting an inaccurate picture of the situation in Gaza.
One X post read, "Apple putting all the destroyed buildings back in Gaza on Maps isn't just wrong to do because it's an inaccurate depiction, it's terrifying. If a company with as much notoriety and influence as Apple wants to whitewash a genocide, what's next? Shame on you, Apple." Other posts expressed similar sentiments.
Although users claimed Apple had intentionally "replaced" current satellite imagery to make buildings appear they way they used to, this claim is unfounded. We did not find proof (such as a screenshot of Apple Maps imagery of Gaza showing the updated landscape) that Apple had updated the imagery at any point since at least October 2023, if not before.
As of this writing, Apple Maps imagery of Gaza is outdated compared to other services, such as Google Maps, but it has historically lagged in certain regions.
We did not find evidence that Apple Maps publicly dates its satellite imagery, but it's likely the imagery available as of this writing predates October 2023. We compared the current Apple Maps imagery to Google Earth imagery from August 2023 and October 2023, and some buildings that were destroyed by October 2023 still appear standing on Apple Maps.
(Apple Maps and Google Earth, Snopes illustration.)
We reached out to some of the social media users who circulated the claim, and they responded that they did not have definitive proof Apple had intentionally swapped out its imagery.
It's possible that the claim originated on a parody account. An X post (archived) from Nov. 1 by user @RabbiJeffx read: "JUST IN: Apple Maps has put all the buildings back in Gaza, because the easiest solution to a genocide is to pretend it isn't happening. Image on the right is from Google, showing the current reality." The user's bio describes itself as a parody account for memes and satire. We reached out to the account to ask if it was the origin of the claim and will update this story if we hear back.
Users have long noted the lack of Apple Maps' availability certain regions. We previously reported on Apple Maps' lack of updated global coverage when social media users claimed Apple Maps had removed the names of small towns and villages in Lebanon from its coverage amid Israel's bombing the small country to its north.
Snopes contacted Apple seeking information regarding its coverage of Gaza and did not immediately hear back. We will update this article if we receive a response.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.
The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.
Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable, is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.
Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.
Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.
Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.

- The claim that a Texas hospital attempted to kill a COVID-19 patient after learning she was unvaccinated is unproven.
- The rumor stems from the account of the patient, Gail Seiler, who is an anti-vaccination advocate.
- Seiler claimed in multiple interviews that she was abused and mistreated by the staff at Medical City Plano hospital, and alleged that they tried to kill her. We are unable to independently verify this without other primary evidence.
- Citing privacy laws, Medical City Plano declined to speak about Seiler's case, but it rejected "any suggestion that our hospital or its caregivers would intentionally harm a patient or withhold medically necessary care."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Seiler and are waiting for her response.
On Sept. 28, U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., held a roundtable discussion with former patients, hospital staff and families, detailing alleged mistreatment they experienced from "rigid hospital protocols" during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many people online shared the statement of one former patient, claiming a Texas hospital tried to kill her by denying her food and water, among other forms of mistreatment.
The clip, shared on Facebook and X (archived), showed Gail Seiler, a former COVID-19 patient, claiming she was mistreated and abused after hospital staff learned she was unvaccinated. One post stated: "A Texas hospital allegedly tried to kill unvaccinated patient Gail Seiler by starving her for 12 days, denying her water for 7 days, and telling her husband she was going to die."
In a recorded statement at Johnson's panel, Seiler described her 2021 stay at Medical City Plano hospital. She said she was denied food for 12 days and water for seven days, and that staff treated her as though her death was inevitable after finding out she was unvaccinated. In a separate interview from 2025, she accused the hospital staff of trying to kill her.
Because the allegation is based solely on Seiler's account and we do not have other primary evidence, we leave this claim unrated.
The hospital sent us the following statement over email:
Federal patient privacy laws prevent us from discussing or disclosing information about an individual's medical care or even confirming if someone was a patient.
However, we strongly reject any suggestion that our hospital or its caregivers would intentionally harm a patient or withhold medically necessary care. Such characterizations are fundamentally inconsistent with our mission, our clinical standards and the dedication of the physicians, nurses and other healthcare professionals who care for our patients.
Snopes also reached out to Seiler to learn more and will update this article accordingly.
During the September panel, Seiler and her husband shared the following testimony about her December 2021 visit to Medical City Plano, when she was hospitalized with COVID-19 (emphasis ours):
What I experienced [at the hospital] changed my life forever and exposed me to a system that abandoned individual patient care in favor of rigid protocols, coercion, isolation, and fear.
When the hospitalist in the ICU learned that I was unvaccinated, he looked directly at me and said, "I'm so sorry, Mrs. Seiler, but you're going to die." From that moment forward, I was treated as if my death was expected and inevitable.
When I was in the ER, the emergency room, the doctor and primary-care nurse said that they follow the FLCCC protocol [a nonstandard protocol developed by a fringe doctors' group that has dubious efficacy against COVID-19]. Once they discovered my vaccination status, however, my options became limited to remdesivir and a ventilator. I repeatedly requested treatments such as ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, budesonide, zinc, vitamin C and other early interventions, but those requests were denied. Instead, I faced aggressive pressure to take remdesivir, escalating oxygen protocols, and repeated pressure toward ventilation, even though I remained alert and did not require intubation. I refused sedatives and pain medications because I feared losing consciousness and the ability to advocate for myself. 
I was isolated from my family despite Texas legislation prohibiting these practices. I was denied access to my Catholic priest and my sacraments unless I received remdesivir. Believing I might die, I submitted to one round so that I could receive extreme unction. After my priest left, I refused any further doses.
During my hospitalization, I was denied food for 12 days, water for seven days. I was left naked and uncovered for extended period of time while staff observed me through the ICU windows instead of entering my room. I was designated a DNR or "do not resuscitate." That was against my wishes. I experienced physical, verbal and psychological abuse at the hands of some of the nurses because I was not vaccinated. My family was repeatedly told that I was unsavable and needed to be allowed to die.
My husband, Brad "Huckleberry" Seiler, a former ER nurse and former Army captain, became incredibly, increasingly alarmed by my condition. He believed the oxygen protocols were excessive and that the hospital's actions were accelerating my decline rather than helping me recover.
After I had been hospitalized for 12 days, Brad entered the ICU on Dec. 15, intending to get me out of the hospital and take me home. He was able to enter because the security guard was away from his desk and the ICU doors were standing wide open. Security and nurses followed him in demanding he leave, but Brad refused to leave without me. The hospital called the police in, resulting in a six-hour standoff as officers tried to persuade him to leave.
The day prior, my husband asked the police to perform a welfare check, and I had told the responding officer about the abuse and neglect I had experienced. He told me that they did not have a protocol for that, and he left me there. With the intervention of Col. Allen West and … Texas Sen. Bob Hall and our attorney, we were finally allowed to leave the hospital.
Doctors insisted that my lungs were permanently damaged and that I would not survive outside their care. They were wrong. With the help of Dr. Richard Bartlett, my husband and my daughter, they cared for me at home using treatments that the hospital had previously refused me, and I fully recovered.
Footage of her testimony is available on YouTube and X:
In 2025, Seiler described the same experience in more depth during a video interview hosted by Betrayal Project USA — a nonprofit group led by Seiler — who, before her hospitalization had protested vaccine mandates — to "defend medical freedom." She described taking offense at being asked by a doctor whether she was vaccinated: "As if that had something to do with the treatment." She also said she was not going to take the vaccine — which she called a "clot shot," referring to the debunked conspiracy theory that the COVID-19 vaccine caused blood clots.
She said that after the hospitalist allegedly told her she was going to die, "I knew that they were going to kill me or they were going to try to kill me."
It is unclear whether Seiler pursued legal action against the hospital. A search of Texas court records found no such lawsuits.
Johnson, the senator who hosted the September roundtable, has spread anti-vaccine misinformation, including falsely claiming thousands of deaths are connected to the COVID-19 vaccine, saying thathe was "sticking up for people who choose not to get vaccinated."
Snopes has previously debunked numerous claims about COVID-19 vaccines, including that the AstraZeneca vaccine causes blood clots and that countries' vaccination rates corresponded with their excess death rates.

In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, captured 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains by winning 19 seats, elevating them to a potential “kingmaker” role. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results and opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video (here, here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that Muslim MPs are performing Namaz together in the Israeli parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of Muslim MPs performing Namaz together inside the Israeli parliament.
Fact: The video shows Jordanian MPs performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the Jordanian parliament in Amman on 03 November 2026. There are no reports of Muslim MPs performing namaz in the Israeli parliament. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we searched for reports of any such act happening in the Israeli Knesset recently but couldn’t find any credible reports to support it. Moreover, the parliament announced that Israel’s newly elected Knesset will hold its inaugural session on 10 November 2026, during which lawmakers will be sworn in, and the speaker will be elected.
Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same visuals published by BBC News Arabic and Jordanian media outlets (here, here & here). These reports state that the footage shows members of parliament performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the House of Representatives of Jordan (the Jordanian Parliament) in Amman on 03 November 2026.
The prayer was reportedly led by MP Dr. Ahmad Al-Raqab right before a scheduled legislative session to elect members of the parliament’s permanent bureau. He can be seen leading the prayer in the extended video published by some media outlets.
Furthermore, the presence of Jordan’s national emblem in the viral video, along with matching interior visuals, conclusively proves that the footage is from the Jordanian parliament and not the Israeli parliament.
To sum it up, the video from Jordan’s parliament is being falsely shared with the claim that it shows Muslim MPs performing Namaz in the Israeli parliament.

Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

On 02 November 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah participated in the BJP’s ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha Padayatra in Hyderabad. Organised by the Telangana unit of the BJP, the march began near the Dr Babu Jagjivan Ram statue in Basheerbagh and concluded at Moazzam Jahi Market. Shah was accompanied by Union Ministers G Kishan Reddy and Bandi Sanjay Kumar, Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao, and other party leaders and workers. The march was organised as part of the BJP’s campaign against the INDIA bloc’s allegations concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls (here, here, and here).
Amid this incident, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows people protesting against Union Home Minister Amit Shah and chasing him away during the BJP’s Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha padayatra in Telangana on 02 November 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows people chasing Union Home Minister Amit Shah away during his Telangana padayatra on 02 November 2026.
Fact: The video dates back to July 2023 and shows Rahul Gandhi travelling in a car amid a crowd waving Congress flags in Khammam, Telangana. Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha’ in Khammam on 02 July 2023. On the same day, Amit Shah attended a programme in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, after virtually inaugurating the Akshar River Cruise in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. We found no reports of him visiting Hyderabad that day. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an X post (archived) dated 4 July 2023, featuring a clearer version of the same video. Rahul Gandhi is clearly visible inside the VIP car, with people waving Congress flags. The post’s caption identifies the location as Khammam district in Telangana and states that Rahul Gandhi was returning after delivering a speech. This suggests that the video is from a Congress event held in Telangana.
On 02 July 2023, Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha‘ in Khammam, Telangana, as part of the Congress party’s campaign ahead of the Telangana Assembly elections. Rahul Gandhi also shared videos from the event on his official YouTube channel, while the Congress party issued a press release about the programme.
To verify whether Amit Shah was in Hyderabad on 2 July 2023, we conducted a Google search and found that he was scheduled to attend the ‘Jan-Swabhiman Divas‘ programme at the Indira Gandhi Pratishthan in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, organised to mark the 74th birth anniversary of Dr Sonelal Patel. He attended the event as the chief guest and addressed the gathering between 2:30 pm and 4:30 pm. Earlier that day, he had virtually inaugurated the Akshar River Cruise at the Sabarmati Riverfront in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, through video conferencing. These reports indicate that Amit Shah was engaged in public programmes in Ahmedabad and Lucknow on 2 July 2023; However, we found no reports indicating that he visited Hyderabad that day.
To sum up, this viral video does not show Union Home Minister Amit Shah being chased away during the Hyderabad padayatra on 02 November 2026.

Delivery of various services in government hospitals and health centres across Keralam are likely to get affected in the coming days as the job contracts of 1,495 temporary staff working under the National Health Mission (NHM) have been terminated from October 31.
According to sources, those who lost their jobs include doctors, nurses, pharmacists, accountants, physiotherapists, lab technicians, and the staff who coordinate the activities of Accredited Social Health Activists. The services of special newborn units in district hospitals and activities of ‘Ashadhara’ project, the digital and decentralised healthcare initiative launched by the government through the NHM to manage haemophilia and other rare genetic bleeding and coagulation disorders, may be hit. Functioning of urban health centres and labs and pharmacies in many hospitals and other healthcare institutions too may get affected.
Leaders of the Centre of Indian Trade Unions-affiliated NHM Employees Federation say that the highest number of the affected staff are in Ernakulam and Thrissur districts, 183 and 180, respectively. Ninety-nine people have lost their jobs in Kozhikode district alone.
Assembly elections
Meera Nimeesh, State general secretary of the federation, says that the contract staff are appointed for a one-year period from April to March. However, this year, the contract was extended till May, because of the model code of conduct for the Assembly elections. After the new government assumed office, their tenure was extended twice, till October 31. Ms. Nimeesh adds that though the staff had earlier undergone one round of performance appraisal in May, they were asked to do it again in October. Following this, their services were terminated.
Ms. Nimeesh claims that even those with close to 20 years of experience, who have consistently recorded good performance, found themselves jobless one fine morning. She alleges that the government’s action is politically motivated as those who don’t align themselves with the United Democratic Front government have been singled out and terminated.
In a statement, the federation says that the services provided by NHM staff—spanning areas such as immunisation, maternal and child care, communicable disease control, management of lifestyle diseases, palliative care, laboratory services, day-to-day operations of hospitals, and field-level health activities—constitute an integral part of the healthcare system. Meanwhile, it is learnt that the Health department has issued a notification for the appointment of new staff.

Armed Maoists eliminated, but ‘dimagi Naxals’ remain a threat: PM Modi
He described the elimination of armed Maoists as a victory for the government’s policies and strong political will
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday warned that the threat of Naxalism persists despite the elimination of armed Maoists, alleging that ideological supporters of the movement, whom he described as “dimagi Naxals”, have infiltrated political parties and various organisations to instigate people against the Constitution and democracy.
Addressing security personnel during Diwali celebrations at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) camp in Karanpur in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district, Modi said identifying and defeating such elements was essential to securing the country.
He described the elimination of armed Maoists as a victory for the government’s policies and strong political will, but cautioned against complacency.
“Amid the successes, we must remember one more thing. Naxalites have been eliminated, but the threat is not over yet. Armed Naxalites have disappeared from the forests, but ‘dimagi Naxals’ have taken control of several organisations,” he said.
Also Read:‘First Diwali when India is free from Naxalism’: PM Modi marks festival in Bastar
He alleged that such elements continued to instigate people against the country’s Constitution and democratic institutions and had infiltrated several political parties and organisations.
“We must identify and defeat them and secure the country,” the Prime Minister said.
Modi said his government had taken several decisions to deal a major blow to the funding networks of Naxalites and separatists. He alleged that previous governments had restricted the operational freedom of security forces, preventing them from responding effectively to Maoist attacks.
“We gave security forces the freedom to take all necessary decisions,” he said.
He also said his government had worked to dismantle the support system that Left-Wing Extremism allegedly enjoyed from certain sections of the government and administration.
Modi said the government’s objective was to ensure that no mother lost her child, no family was pushed into devastation, no child took up arms and no young person’s future was destroyed.
Also Read: History of Diwali celebrations at White House, and Indian diaspora’s political profile in US
“We remained committed to this resolve until the goal was achieved. Without publicity or showmanship, we worked with sensitivity and broke the backbone of Maoist terrorists. We transformed the lives of people in Naxal-affected areas through a spirit of service, which led those suffering from Naxalism to stand firmly with the government and security forces,” he said.
Modi said government action had destroyed counterfeit currency networks and disrupted the supply lines of Naxalites and separatists.
Describing the fight against Maoist violence as a major challenge, he said more than 230 districts across nearly 20 states were once affected by Naxalism.
“To take the country forward, its enemies must be crushed with unwavering determination and a well-planned strategy,” he said.
Modi said the lack of political will to tackle the menace had been addressed in 2014, when people gave him an opportunity to serve the country.
He also said that, for the first time in 47 years, not a single Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel had been killed in the line of duty during the preceding year.
Bastar, once considered the epicentre of Left-Wing Extremism in Chhattisgarh, has witnessed significant change in recent years following intensified anti-Maoist operations, large-scale surrenders and the expansion of development initiatives.

Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.
It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.

In her Tribeca Festival documentary Linda Perry: Let It Die Here, Linda Perry fans were treated to a rare POV of the 4 Non Blondes frontwoman’s life and musical process.
At Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film, the five-time Grammy nominee performed “What Lies with You” from her fourth solo album Let It Die Here, and recounted writing the song after going through “one long meltdown” following her mother’s death, as well as letting director Don Hardy Jr. shoot a four-hour jam session where “the song came to life in the film” after she wrote it the night before.
“Don and I worked on a film called Citizen Penn for Sean Penn, and then we just kind of became friends, and he asked me, ‘You know, you’re super interesting. Can I just come in your studio and film your process?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah!’ And then, I thought I would just get some good Instagram content, because I’m terrible at it. I mean, swear to f*cking god,” Perry told the Sound & Screen audience.
“And then, as it always happens when a camera shows up, things start happening,” she added. “And I was struggling a lot, I was just having such a hard time figuring out how to write a song for myself.”
Perry continued, “And then Don came and said, ‘Hey, you know, the footage I’ve been shooting, I think there’s a documentary here. I’m seeing it kind of clear.’ And I was just like, ‘I don’t wanna hear about it. Don’t tell me about it. I don’t wanna f*cking know about it.’ And then, he’s like, ‘But you understand it would be about you?’ And I’m like, ‘I get it. If I said it, I said it. If I did it, i did it. But don’t bring it up to me.’ And that’s kind of how it happened.”
In Linda Perry: Let It Die Here, now available to stream on Hulu and Disney+, the artist provides an intimate look at her life, career and personal struggles.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.
Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.
“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.
As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.
Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.
“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.
“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

After months of skirmishing, the Trump administration removed WuXi AppTec, a key contract developer and manufacturer for the pharmaceutical industry, from its list of “Chinese military companies” operating in the U.S.
The Department of Defense took this step to comply with a court ruling last August, according to a notice with the Federal Register. At the time, a U.S. District Court judge temporarily blocked the administration from pursuing the designation after WuXi filed a lawsuit arguing it was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Two months earlier, the administration had placed WuXi AppTec on the list over concerns that the company has ties to the Chinese government and military, and that U.S. biotech leadership is at risk due to growing competition from Chinese companies. WuXi is seen by China hawks in Washington as a rising threat to national security.

New Delhi, Nov 09: Delhi recorded its most polluted Diwali in five years with average Air Quality Index at 376 and the morning after was only marginally better at 371 recorded at 10 am on Monday when a blanket of smog and fog blanketed the city.
The overall AQI stood at 371 at 10 am on Monday, also the highest for a post-Diwali day since 2021.
Of the 51 monitoring stations that recorded data, 14 were in the 'severe' category, four in the 'poor' category and the remaining 33 in the 'very poor' category. Delhi Technological University (DTU) recorded the worst reading of 439. Earlier in the morning, the overall AQI stood at 370 at 8 am.
According to CPCB data, the Diwali-day AQI of 376 was the highest recorded on the day of the festival since 2021, when it was recorded at 382.
It is worth noting that Diwali falls on different days in October or November every year. It was on November 8 this year, on October 20 in 2025, October 31 in 2024, November 12 in 2023, October 24 in 2022 and November 4 in 2021.
The average AQI on Diwali stood at 345 in 2025, 328 in 2024, 218 in 2023 and 312 in 2022, compared with 382 in 2021 and 376 this year.
The pollution levels remained high on the day after the festival as well. The full-day average AQI on the day after Diwali was 351 in 2025, 338 in 2024, 360 in 2023, 302 in 2022 and 462 in 2021.
The city woke up to a thick layer of smog and fog on Monday, with visibility dropping sharply at both of Delhi's major weather stations during the early morning hours.
At Safdarjung, visibility dropped to 50 metres at 6.30 am, placing it in the dense fog category, compared with 700 metres a day earlier. At Palam, visibility stood at 400 metres, indicating moderate fog, against 800 metres on Sunday.
At 8.30 am, visibility improved to 100 metres at Safdarjung and 600 metres at Palam. It subsequently improved to 500 metres and 900 metres, respectively, by 9 am, with both stations reporting shallow fog, according to India Meteorological Department (IMD) data.
At Safdarjung, shallow fog was observed between 10.30 pm and 2.30 am before dense fog set in from 2.30 am to 9 am, lasting six hours and 30 minutes. Shallow fog was reported again from 9 am.
At Palam, shallow fog was recorded between midnight and 5 am, followed by moderate fog from 5 am to 8.30 am, lasting three hours and 30 minutes. Shallow fog was subsequently reported from 8.30 am.
"It is smog along with fog," IMD officials said.
The officials attributed the drop in AQI from last night and the hazy conditions to dry weather and calm winds. Winds remained calm over Safdarjung and Palam during the previous evening, they said.
Meanwhile, Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir placed Delhi's air quality in the 'very unhealthy' category on Monday morning, recording an AQI of 245 at 8.30 am.
According to IQAir, the concentration of PM2.5 stood at 170 micrograms per cubic metre, around 34 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline value.
The concentration of PM10 was recorded at 126 micrograms per cubic metre, while ozone levels stood at 31, nitrogen dioxide at 44.6 and sulphur dioxide at 32. Carbon monoxide concentration was recorded at 1,461.5 micrograms per cubic metre.
PM2.5, fine particulate matter capable of penetrating deep into the lungs and entering the bloodstream, is among the major pollutants of concern due to its adverse health effects.
IQAir's dashboard also showed a prominent air quality alert for Delhi, with data from 32 monitoring stations provided by 12 contributors.
Meanwhile, real-time readings on AQI.in showed that Delhi's AQI had climbed to 2,283 after Diwali. Six other Indian cities also recorded AQI levels above 1,000 at 9 pm on Sunday, according to the platform.
On Monday morning, AQI.in recorded Delhi's air quality at 637, classifying it as 'hazardous'.
Several areas, including Bawana, Burari, Jahangirpuri, Sonia Vihar, Punjabi Bagh, Okhla and Rohini, continued to record severe air quality on Monday, with pollution levels remaining high since Sunday night.
Despite restrictions on firecracker bursting, several parts of Delhi continued to witness fireworks on Sunday evening, with reports emerging from areas including Pitampura, Burari, Mayur Vihar and parts of Lutyens' Delhi.
The District Magistrate (East), in an order, had permitted the bursting of green firecrackers only on November 7 and 8, between 6 am and 7 am and 8 pm and 10 pm.
However, residents reported that firecrackers continued to be burst beyond the permitted evening window. In outer Delhi's Pitampura and Burari, Mayur Vihar, the intensity of fireworks was particularly high.
The DM's order also prohibited the bursting of firecrackers within 300 metres of hospitals, nursing homes, health centres, old-age homes, educational institutions and other notified silence zones.
Only CSIR-NEERI-certified green firecrackers were permitted for sale, exclusively at locations designated by the Delhi Police in coordination with the district administration, which had also announced joint patrolling and enforcement teams to check unauthorised sale and use of prohibited firecrackers.
According to the Air Quality Early Warning System (EWS), Delhi's air quality is likely to remain in the severe category over the subsequent few days.
A ventilation index below 6,000 square metres per second, coupled with an average wind speed of less than 10 kilometres per hour, is unfavourable for the effective dispersion of pollutants, according to the EWS.
Unfavourable meteorological conditions, vehicular emissions, Diwali celebrations and the ongoing peak stubble-burning season in neighbouring states are among the factors expected to contribute to the deterioration.
According to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), an AQI between 0 and 50 is classified as good, 51 and 100 as satisfactory, 101 and 200 as moderate, 201 and 300 as poor, 301 and 400 as very poor, and 401 and 500 as severe.

The late Ronald Graham wore two hats. He was a renowned mathematician and, at one time, president of the American Mathematical Society. He was also a serious juggler and president of the International Jugglers’ Association. “He loved tricks,” said Fan Chung, a mathematician at UC San Diego who was married to Graham. “You know, spinning a ball, spinning a coat hanger, spinning several balls together, throwing pens against the wall.”
Sometimes Graham wore both hats at once. “It’s interesting, in fact, that many mathematicians and computer scientists have an interest in juggling,” he said in a 1980 television interview. “I think it’s the search for patterns and structure that is responsible for this.”
He would go on to write numerous papers, some with Chung, on the mathematics of juggling. But back in 1971, decades before he made that connection explicit, he posed a question that some mathematicians now say might have been inspired by juggling, too.
Start with a random set of different integers, not including zero. Can you always rearrange them so that if you add up the first two numbers, then the first three, then the first four, and so on, every “partial sum” turns out different? In the language of juggling, this would mean that if each ball stays in the air for a different amount of time, you can always find an order to throw them in such that two balls won’t come crashing down on the same beat—which would ruin the act.
If the numbers are all positive, then the answer to Graham’s question is obviously yes: The sums will always grow larger as you add more numbers. Similarly, if there are both positive and negative numbers in the mix, the answer is also known to be yes. But what if the numbers live in a finite world—like numbers wrapped around a clock, which repeat after a certain count?
That’s what Graham wanted to know. He conjectured that the answer should still be yes. It often happens, he figured, that even when dealing with rigid constraints, you can still find enough flexibility to construct special patterns or structures—just as it’s usually possible to find a valid sudoku board or Latin square (another kind of puzzle) despite their many rules. “It fits nicely in all these questions about designs and about very symmetric structures,” said Noga Alon, a mathematician at Princeton University. But for decades, no one could prove Graham’s intuition to be true.
That changed recently, when several young mathematicians picked up the balls. In a proof that spanned four papers and various fields of mathematics, they finally resolved Graham’s rearrangement conjecture. The final paper, by Lisa Sauermann of the University of Bonn and Huy Tuan Pham of the University of Chicago, appeared in February 2026, officially closing the problem.
Across the papers, one theme prevailed: the power of randomness to draw out patterns. As Alon put it, “It’s the power of collaboration, the power of the young generation, the power of probabilistic methods” that solved the problem.
Alp Müyesser, a mathematician at the University of Oxford, often finds himself drawn to problems whose solutions need two ingredients: a random process and something extra as well. After solving one such problem in 2022 while he was still a graduate student, he encountered Graham’s conjecture and realized that his just-finished proof could help there, too.
The conjecture is set in the world of clock arithmetic. You start by placing the whole numbers on a number line, then you wrap the line around the face of a clock so that the numbers repeat after some prime number, p. Say p is 7, for instance. In this setting, 0, 7, 14, and all other multiples of 7 are equivalent—meaning that you can add two positive numbers (like 3 and 4) and get zero.
Graham asked the following: If you pick any set of nonzero numbers off this number line (for any p), can you always rearrange them so that the partial sums you get are all different?
The challenge depends on how big your set is compared to p. The more numbers you pick, the more sums there are to manage. But if you choose fewer numbers, there will be fewer ways to rearrange them. These different cases inspire different approaches.
Müyesser, along with his former adviser, Alexey Pokrovskiy of University College London, tackled the case where your set includes almost every possible number up to p. With sets this large, it can be extremely hard to construct a valid ordering. But it turned out that starting with a random ordering can bring you most of the way there.
“Computer scientists often call this a ‘finding the hay in the haystack’ problem,” Müyesser said. You might know that lots of good orderings are out there, but actually finding one is hard. “If you do it randomly, it’s likely going to work, but it’s hard to explicitly describe what the solution is supposed to look like.”
Müyesser and Pokrovskiy needed to ensure that no sequence of numbers anywhere in the ordering added up to zero. Otherwise, adding those numbers to the previous partial sum would repeat that sum.
A completely random ordering might have a few of these troublesome sequences. So Müyesser and Pokrovskiy first set aside a few specially chosen numbers from the set, then randomly scrambled the rest. They scanned their random ordering for any problems; if they came across an interval that added up to zero, they could insert one of the spare numbers to change it. In 2022, they posted their solution, though it was hidden in a paper that focused on applying the same technique to a more general problem.
A couple of years later, Noah Kravitz of Oxford, unaware of Müyesser and Pokrovskiy’s solution, stumbled on Graham’s conjecture in an online archive of unsolved problems. “I saw there was an open problem, and I was like, it’s embarrassing for humanity that we don’t know this,” Kravitz said. “This situation just had to be rectified.”
He decided to approach the conjecture from the opposite end. Together with Benjamin Bedert of Oxford, he considered the case where the set of numbers is tiny compared to p—for instance, Alon said, if you have a set of 100 numbers where p is 1 billion.
Kravitz and Bedert solved Graham’s conjecture for those cases and posted their proof in September 2024. Müyesser saw it and reached out, sharing his own work; the three of them (plus two other colleagues) then teamed up to extend Müyesser’s original approach.
“It was a pretty unlikely combination of people,” Kravitz said. He and Müyesser come from two areas of combinatorics that don’t typically collaborate. “Different sections have completely different techniques,” he said.
Their paper, which they posted in August 2025, handled more cases where the set of numbers is relatively large compared to p. But between those cases and the small-set cases that Kravitz and Bedert had covered, a gap remained. No one could figure out what to do about medium-size sets, such as those that include roughly half as many numbers as p. “Our methods didn’t work there, and there were clear reasons that they would not have worked,” Müyesser said.
It seemed as though research on the problem might enter another long hiatus. Then, in February 2026, a surprise appeared online.
Lisa Sauermann and Huy Tuan Pham were old friends. The two mathematicians had met in 2015 at Stanford University, where Sauermann was a graduate student and Pham an undergraduate. Today they live on different continents—Sauermann in Bonn, Germany, and Pham in Chicago. But a conference in Germany in September 2025 provided a rare chance for them to share a chalkboard again, and afterward Pham followed Sauermann to Bonn for a short visit. All they needed was a problem to work on.
At the conference, they heard two talks on Graham’s conjecture by mathematicians who had attempted but failed to bridge the gap. They were intrigued. And as it later turned out, Sauermann had encountered a closely related problem in the International Mathematical Olympiad as a high school student. She solved it correctly, and by the time she finished high school, she’d won a gold medal in the prestigious competition four times. (Most likely, it was Chung who placed the problem on that year’s exam, as she was on the committee that wrote the questions, and she frequently took inspiration from Graham’s many puzzles.)
By the end of their three-day visit, Sauermann and Pham had a plan for how to crack the case.
It hinged on a technically demanding method called anti-concentration. Here, an anti-concentration statement asserts that some event has a particularly low chance of happening. But the mechanics of proving these kinds of statements are so intricate that, though Kravitz and others were aware that such an anti-concentration approach might succeed, “we just hadn’t had the guts to actually try it,” he said.
First, though, Sauermann and Pham began the way their predecessors had. They randomly reordered their set of numbers and came up with a procedure to fix any problems—that is, any sequences that add up to zero. Any time they found a zero-sum sequence, they swapped out the last number in the sequence with another one.
This procedure often went without a hitch. But three types of “bad events” would cause it to fail. One: A zero-sum sequence might occur toward the end of the entire arrangement; then there would be no other numbers to swap in. Two: Many zero-sum sequences might appear too close together, making it impossible to fix them all. And three: Fixing one bad sequence might create another zero-sum sequence down the line.
Sauermann and Pham hoped to prove, using anti-concentration, that each of these bad events was sufficiently unlikely. Then there would have to be a way to rearrange the set of numbers to satisfy the conjecture.
To do this, the duo used Fourier analysis—an area of math that lets you rewrite functions as sums of simple waves—to show that in general, when you add up random sets of numbers, no one sum is especially likely to appear. They then used this insight to carefully estimate the probability that each bad event would occur, ultimately showing that the total chance of getting a bad event was less than 100 percent. That was enough to settle the conjecture.
A few months after their stint in Germany, Sauermann and Pham posted their 27-page proof online. They had shown not only that a satisfactory rearrangement was always possible, but that a random ordering could be rearranged to eliminate bad events at least 90% of the time—a massive success rate.
The mathematicians who had previously worked on the problem were surprised to see the remaining case closed so quickly. “Their approach is just completely different,” Müyesser said.
Together, the four papers prove Graham’s conjecture for sets of all sizes. But they all assume that p is very large; though no one has calculated its exact value, think along the lines of 10 raised to the 100th power. To mathematicians, that’s fine—the salient point is that you’re working in the setting of clock arithmetic. But another aspect of the problem technically remains unsolved—you might still try to resolve the conjecture for all p. And if you want to use the result to choreograph a real juggling routine, you’re out of luck: To correspond to such a large p, the routine would have to be much too long.
The proof confirms that even within these strange, limited number settings, “there are some nice structures that always exist,” Alon said. You can always achieve some degree of flexibility, shuffling the numbers in your set around to avoid revisiting the same partial sums.
“To pose a good problem is really an art,” Chung said. “I think Ron would be extremely happy to see the problem solved.”

It’s notoriously hard to govern Los Angeles, a city that gives its mayor less direct authority over the government than in a city like New York or Chicago. But even so, it’d be hard to do much worse than Karen Bass.
Los Angeles is about to test a new kind of housing politics
The city ousts its NIMBY mayor for a democratic socialist YIMBY.
Elected mayor of LA in 2022, Bass campaigned on promises to solve the city’s homelessness and housing affordability crises (which are really part of the same underlying crisis). She then spent her term undermining her own administration’s affordable housing policy and fighting the state of California’s efforts to compel cities to allow more housing production. She lost her bid for reelection this week to Nithya Raman, an LA City Council member, rising progressive star, and nationally prominent YIMBY.
Los Angeles has the highest ratio of home price to household income of any large city in America, and the second fewest homes per adult of any major city. It has a highly suburbanized and car-oriented fabric, like much of the rest of the country — all of which makes it a kind of proving ground for whether America’s sprawling cities can build their way out of their housing shortages.
Everyone in the city’s political leadership notionally agrees that LA needs to permit a lot more homes to meet demand — the only true way to make housing affordable — but not all of them have evidently had the policy discipline to follow through.
Raman may be different. She has gained a following in housing reform circles over the last few years with her brisk, direct-to-camera social videos explaining how LA’s housing shortage drives up rents and criticizing city policies that make it so difficult to build more homes (perhaps it’s no surprise that she has plenty of friends in Hollywood).
“There has been an overall lack of urgency in addressing housing supply in [Bass’s] administration,” Raman told me in an interview in July. How best to accommodate LA’s need for more housing, she said, is “a question that the city has actually turned away from.”
Even given LA’s relatively weak mayoralty, Bass’s failures on housing were often a matter of political choice. As The Atlantic’s Marc Novicoff put it, “Bass seems to have gone out of her way to exercise as little power as possible.” Where she did go out of her way to wield her influence, it was often to stop denser housing from being built. Some of her bewildering housing policy choices while in office include:
- Days into her term, Bass signed her first executive order, known as ED1, to fast-track housing developments where 100 percent of the apartments are affordable. Applications for these projects were to get approvals within 60 days instead of being dragged through excruciating permitting processes. It was a good idea — and it seemed to be working, quickly attracting developer applications to build thousands of affordable apartments. It was working so well, in fact, that a backlash from vocal NIMBYs followed. Less than six months after signing ED1, in June 2023, Bass weakened it to exclude projects in single-family neighborhoods — which make up three-quarters of LA’s residential land — from the fast-track approval process. Her administration even tried to apply that restriction retroactively to developments that had already applied to build in single-family areas under ED1, a breathtaking display of bureaucratic dysfunction; a judge later ruled that this violated California law. Bass has since added more restrictions to the ED1, and one observer has described it as “functionally gutted” for many developers. To be fair to Bass, even after she weakened it, the program has still resulted in more than 7,700 affordable apartments under construction, according to her campaign.
- Bass opposed SB 79, a landmark California law that passed in 2025 requiring cities and suburbs to allow construction of denser housing near transit stops. Permitting apartments near public transit is one of the most basic principles of sensible urban planning. But in LA, it was controversial enough that Bass urged Gov. Gavin Newsom to veto it. After he signed SB 79 into law anyway, Bass worked with LA’s city council to delay much of the law’s most ambitious upzoning until 2030, while permitting smaller apartment buildings near some transit stops.
- After the devastating January 2025 fires, some property owners whose homes had burned down in the Pacific Palisades had applied to rebuild under SB 9, another important California law that allows single-family lots to be modestly densified into up to four housing units. In response to backlash from some neighbors, Bass reportedly pressed Newsom to restrict SB 9 in fire-damaged areas; she then banned SB 9 applications in parts of the Palisades. (There are certainly legitimate questions about whether rebuilding in such a fire-prone area is a good idea at all. But Bass offered no publicly available analysis that the modest increase in density allowed by SB 9 posed a special danger, even as she worked to accelerate the rebuilding of single-family homes.)
All of these point to a leader who is not serious about changing the conditions that led to LA’s housing shortage, and lacks the courage to take on what is arguably the city’s most defining political challenge.
Raman has promised to fundamentally break from that approach. That will make her mayoralty an important experiment for the rest of the country. Even modest progress in a city as resistant to housing as LA could help crack open a way forward for new approaches to housing in the many other cities that face affordability crises.
This won’t be easy for her — she’ll face the same anti-building political pressures, and will need to maintain a cooperative relationship with the city council. When I spoke to Raman over the summer, I noticed that she treaded gingerly around the topic of adding density to single-family neighborhoods. Because of the uniquely American obsession with keeping single-family homes segregated from other types of development, it can be a real political third rail in LA and nationwide. But research has suggested the city can’t fill its housing shortage without building more in those neighborhoods. Raman will, at least, have an important ally in California’s newly elected governor, Xavier Becerra, who is also a strong YIMBY.
Raman’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) makes her emblematic of a fusion that’s been emerging in Democratic politics, between supply-side abundance and left-wing economic populism. It’s also evident in politicians like Zohran Mamdani and some of the young Democrats who won elections across the country this week.
From talking to Raman, I have the sense that she’s more at home with the YIMBY part of her politics than the DSA part. Her relationship with the DSA’s LA chapter has been strained (though it did endorse her candidacy). But her social-democratic commitments are also sincere — she’s been a strong champion of rent control and tenant protections in LA, for example, and helped shape a stronger rent stabilization law the city adopted last year.
The new political syntheses taking shape on the American left are exciting and intriguing. Whether it will finally make a breakthrough in LA’s — and California’s, and America’s — housing crisis, of course, remains to be tested. But it’s a welcome sign that American politics need not remain trapped in the same orthodoxies and failures.

Society expects women to do everything but fails to respect them: NCW chief
New Delhi, Society expects women to manage homes, earn livelihoods, support families and provide emotional strength, but continues to discriminate against them, NCW Chairperson Vijaya Rahatkar has said, calling for a fundamental change in attitudes towards women.
In an interview with PTI, the National Commission for Women chief said governments have introduced several laws to protect women, but these alone cannot bring the necessary transformation.
"I also find it a bit surprising that society expects everything from women. Whether taking care of the home, it should be the mother, wife, sister, or daughter. She should stand firm in everything, stand on her own feet, earn, support everyone, do household chores, and provide emotional support. She must do all this; we cannot function without her," Rahatkar said.
Deep Dive
Despite the significant contribution women make to their families and society, discrimination and violence against them remain a concern, she said.
"Sometimes I feel very surprised and saddened that in a country that has respected women so much, not just today but for centuries, discrimination against women still occurs sometimes. This bothers me deeply," the NCW chief said.

Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say

Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.
The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.
Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.
Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.
But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.
A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.
Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.
While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".
"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."
For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.
The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.
The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.
Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.
The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."
Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace.
Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.
"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.
Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.
Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."
