If they decide to remove Carrick from his position, they want to avoid having an interim head coach take over, but as yet, there have been no substantive talks with other potential candidates.
Sky Sports News understands the club's hierarchy are planning to use the international break to fully evaluate the season so far and reassess their options.
Carrick and the players have all had Monday off after rescuing a late point against Villa on Sunday, but the head coach and his staff are due back into Carrington on Tuesday.
With most players away on international duty and no first-team training sessions planned in the coming days, that has bought some breathing space for a full re-evaluation of the season.
One win in 11 games, 30 goals conceded so far in all competitions, the worst record of any team in the top-five European leagues, and a worst-ever start to a Premier League season has ramped up the pressure on Carrick.
Those problems have outweighed the positivity brought about by the comebacks of the last two matches.
It is thought the United hierarchy feel Carrick over-achieved last season, with a third-placed League finish earning Champions League football.
But it is equally clear the bosses are adamant that the club's current crop of players have woefully under-achieved so far this season.
Sky Sports News understands there are three key reasons why United are not rushing a decision over the head coach position - all of which have given Carrick an extended stay of execution.
Firstly, the supporters are not singing for him to be sacked. It is unlikely that will ever happen, such is the affection of the fanbase for a legendary player who won 11 major trophies with United, including the Champions League and five Premier League titles.
As such, the pressure to change the boss which other clubs often experience from the stands has not materialised at Old Trafford.
Secondly, there is a feeling in the boardroom that Carrick and his coaching staff still retain the support of the players.
Despite the chaotic nature of the last two games, they have produced a Champions League win against Roma and a draw against a good Villa side - with notable comebacks in both.
As such, the assessment seems to be that the players have not downed tools, and they are still fighting for Carrick.
Thirdly, United's bosses remain unconvinced at this stage that changing the head coach will solve the team's problems.
If they did believe that, they could have already made a move to sack Carrick and appoint a candidate such as Julian Nagelsmann or Eddie Howe - both of whom are out of work, available, and thought to be keen to talk to United if a vacancy becomes available.
'It doesn't matter who's in charge at Man Utd'
Sky Sports News chief reporter Kaveh Solhekol:
"The club needs to become Manchester United again. They need to turn into a club who are capable of winning the title regularly, winning the European Cup again.
"It doesn't matter who's in charge, in my opinion. You could have Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. But with the present ownership structure, I don't think things are going to change.
"You could bring in another manager but you would just paper over the cracks. We're talking about a club that used to rub shoulders with Barcelona and Real Madrid.
"If things carry on as they are at the moment, they'll be rubbing shoulders with Lincoln and QPR. There's a circus around the club, everyone talking about what's going wrong and how it can be changed.
"But I think most Man Utd fans think that unless you change the owners, nothing is going to change."

In a significant development in the case of the murders of seven members of a family, which has sent shockwaves across Karnataka, the police have now successfully recovered all seven bodies. The recovery of the bodies was a crucial step in the probe into the ghastly murders, to build a strong case.
The latest breakthrough came on Monday (November 9, 2026), with the police recovering two more bodies from Shiradi Ghat, in the Western Ghats of Karnataka. The bodies have been identified as those of Shankar, the accused Indushekhar’s brother-in-law and his wife, Nalini, who were among the seven victims.
The development comes a day after the police recovered two bodies of the accused’s brother-in-law, Shivakumar and his wife, Divya, from the foothills of Chamundi Hills on Sunday (November 8, 2026). A day before that, the police had recovered two more bodies of the accused’s wife, Sunita and her mother, Roopavathi, from Salem, Tamil Nadu. On November 6, they had recovered the body of a minor boy, Puneeth, 7, from the foothills of Nandi Hills.
The families have decided to conduct the last rites for all seven together in one place. The bodies, most of them found in a highly decomposed state, will be handed over to the family after autopsies have been conducted.
Following a missing complaint by the deceased Nalini’s mother, Tungamma, the Srirampura police on November 5 detained Indushekhar and his 17-year-old minor daughter and rescued an 11-year-old boy from them. The duo confessed to having killed seven members of their family. Indushekhar’s wife, mother-in-law, two brothers-in-law, and their families. The accused has reportedly claimed that marital discord and humiliation by his wife’s family spurred him to take revenge.
Probe
Meanwhile, police teams investigating the ghastly murders are tracking down shops from which the accused allegedly purchased materials used to dispose of the bodies. Investigators are checking CCTV footage from these shops and recording statements from shop owners and staff to establish the purchases made by the accused and reconstruct his movements before and after the murders.

Karnataka to increase Urdu Academy grants, hold meeting with minority groups
D K Shivakumar promised additional Urdu Academy grants and a minority leaders' meeting. The initiative underscores Karnataka's commitment to constitutional rights, linguistic diversity and social unity.
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar has promised additional funding for the Karnataka Urdu Academy and announced a separate meeting with minority community representatives next week to discuss their concerns, reaffirming the government's commitment to protecting constitutional rights and promoting social harmony.
Shivakumar made the announcements on Sunday while inaugurating the Karnataka Urdu Academy's annual awards ceremony, book release and 'Jashn-e-Urdu' programme at Puttanna Chetty Town Hall in Bengaluru. He also presented awards to 20 people for their contributions to Urdu language, literature and culture.
The Chief Minister said the government would hold discussions with leaders and legislators representing minority communities, including Christians, Muslims, Jains and Buddhists. The views and concerns of legislators from Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) would also be heard.
"It is our responsibility to fulfil the promises made in our election manifesto, as well as the assurances given to various communities on different occasions. We are holding meetings with the objective of resolving issues while respecting everyone's sentiments and ensuring that no one is hurt. We will safeguard the rights and the dignity guaranteed under the Constitution," he said.
URDU ACADEMY TO RECEIVE ADDITIONAL GRANTS
Shivakumar said the proposal to increase grants for the Urdu Academy had already been discussed with the ministers concerned and that the government would assess its requirements before extending support.
"Whatever the academy requires will be reviewed and supported. The government will stand behind the growth of Urdu language, literature and culture," he said.
He also defended the government's commitment to minority welfare, saying a department could not be shut down simply because some people lacked faith in minority communities.
"Our government exists to protect the interests of minorities and to be their voice. We are committed to ensuring that no community faces injustice," he said.
'GOVERNMENT COMMITTED TO PROTECTING CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS'
The Chief Minister said the state government would function strictly within the framework of the Constitution and ensure equal respect and protection for people across castes and religions.
"All of us, including Rahul Gandhi, took our oath holding the Constitution in hand. Preserving the Constitution and upholding its ideals by offering equal respect and protection to all castes and religions is the government's commitment," he said.
Shivakumar said the government and the Congress party believed in bringing society together rather than creating divisions.
'URDU IS THE LANGUAGE OF THE HEART'
Describing Urdu as a language that transcends community boundaries, Shivakumar said it had the power to connect people through literature, poetry and shayari.
"Urdu is not a language limited to just one community; it is the language of the heart. This language knows no boundaries. Everyone should respect the Urdu language and culture, which have earned global recognition," he said.
Recalling an Urdu poetry event during the Mysuru Dasara celebrations, the Chief Minister said he had spent nearly an hour listening to shayari and found the experience deeply enriching.
He said the audience included Muslims, Jains, Brahmins, Kannadigas, Hindi speakers and people from different religious and linguistic backgrounds, all listening to the poetry with keen interest.
"This is a fine example of how language can connect people," he said.
Shivakumar also emphasised that knowledge should be respected irrespective of the language in which it was expressed, adding that no language, including English, should be treated with disrespect.
"Language is a medium of communication. Everyone should love and respect their mother tongue and recognise the importance of one's mother and mother tongue," he said.
'LET US WORK LIKE A NEEDLE THAT BINDS PEOPLE'
In an appeal for social harmony, Shivakumar used the analogy of scissors and needles to underline the importance of unity.
"Our languages may differ, but human emotions are the same. Humanity is our caste, humanity is our religion. Both scissors and needles can be made from iron. We do not need the work of cutting. Let us work like a needle that stitches and binds people together," he said.
"Our government and party work to unite society; we have no interest in dividing it," he added.
The Chief Minister also congratulated 20 award recipients for their contributions to Urdu language, literature and culture, praising the academy's efforts to promote Urdu.

In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. “This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.”
In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth’s mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet’s interior.
Ice and sea
The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.
The leading explanation was glaciation. Between roughly 720 and 635 million years ago, glaciers reached the tropics, and some scientists think the entire planet froze over, a scenario called Snowball Earth. “Ice sheets are very good at grinding, scouring, scraping the surface,” Flament explains. He said that glaciers are about 10 times more effective than rivers at eroding rock away. But if the whole planet froze, the Great Unconformity should be found everywhere. And it’s not.
Other explanations included rifting, pulling and stretching of Earth’s crust, and a global drop in sea levels. But rifting acts mostly on the edges of continents, and a sea level change should have affected all continents alike. “There’s no doubt that there was extensive glaciation. There’s no doubt that there have been sea-level changes throughout time. The question is, was that enough to put the Great Unconformity puzzle together?” Flament says.
A fourth idea held that the mantle itself was moving continents up and down, a process called dynamic topography. “It had been proposed, but it hadn’t been quantitatively tested,” Flament says. So, his team set out to do so.
Lava lamp planet
From roughly 100 to 200 kilometers beneath the surface down to nearly 3,000 kilometers, Earth’s mantle slowly convects. “An analogy would be a lava lamp, where some stuff comes up and some stuff comes down,” Flament explains. “Cold rock sinks and hot rock rises.”
The mantle is solid, yet a piece of rock can slowly travel from the surface to the deep Earth over some 200 million years. That motion tugs on the surface. Where cold slabs of ocean floor sink into the mantle at subduction zones, the ground gets pulled down; where hot mantle rises, it gets pushed up. The amplitude of this up and down motion is still debated, though. “The short of it is several hundreds of meters, and it’s still to be worked out exactly what that [precise value] is,” Flament says.
Dhungana and Flament ran six simulations of mantle convection going back 1 billion years, driven by reconstructions of how tectonic plates moved over that time. Then they grouped regions where the ground rose and fell in similar ways to find where the unconformity should have formed, and where it should have survived to the present. Flament, however, says the starting configuration of these simulations remains uncertain.
Magnetic records in ancient rocks reveal how far continents were from the equator, but not their longitude. “It’s possible that some continents may be in the wrong hemisphere,” Flament admits. The ancient ocean floor, long since recycled into the mantle, had to be invented entirely from scratch in the models. Still, the simulations produced a consistent story.
Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, had little or no subduction along its margins between about 930 and 510 million years ago, much like Africa today, so it sat above some rising mantle and was pushed up. Five of the six models showed this pattern of Laurentia seeing long uplift followed by sinking in the Cambrian. For northern Europe and North China, this pattern showed up in four.
But the uplift alone, Flament’s team concluded, was too gentle to strip away enough rock to create the Great Unconformity.
Glacial grind
“The uplift could create a tilt for the whole continent, but it’s not great at creating a steep slope,” Flament says. The missing piece of the puzzle, he argues, were glaciers that ground through rock even on low ground and gentle slopes. The models show the uplift was still building when Snowball Earth hit. “This gentle uplift that’s continuous, and then that glacial erosion that comes on top, work together,” Flament explains. “They’re not coupled. They just happen to coincide in time.” When the continents sank in the Cambrian, seas flooded in and buried the eroded surface.
The models made by Flament’s team also explain why the gap is so obvious in North America but hard to find elsewhere. Compared with records of sediment preserved on each continent, North America and Eurasia show one long rise followed by one long fall, which the researchers interpret as the ideal recipe for the Great Unconformity.
South America and Australia, on the other hand, went through two cycles. “This would form potentially two unconformities, and then the Great Unconformity would be more difficult to see,” Flament says. Africa was a different case altogether—hemmed in by mountain belts at the time, its erosion and sediment were shaped by the mountains rather than by the mantle beneath.
But if the mantle goes through such up and down cycles on a regular basis, the remaining question was why we can see only one Great Unconformity, and not many.
One of a kind
The team says the Great Unconformity is unique in the geological record because of a combination of a rise-and-fall cycle lasting over 900 million years, a near-global glaciation that happened at the right moment, and rock records that get harder to read farther back in time.
Flament suspects there may be an older candidate, tied to a glaciation 2.4 billion years ago, but rocks that old lack the fossils that make younger sediments easier to date. “Having life in sediments makes it a lot easier to have a sense of time,” he says. His work, however, may help explain what happens right after the Great Unconformity formed.
The intense erosion that carved the Great Unconformity washed rock material into the oceans, possibly fertilizing them just before the Cambrian explosion, when calcium became abundant in seawater. “That’s when life learns to mobilize calcium and create skeletons and shells,” Flament says. He admits, though, that mantle dynamics likely wasn’t the only process that enabled the Cambrian explosion. “I think it would be misleading to say the mantle set the pace here. But I think it was one of the forces that worked together.”

Welcome back to Power Play! Senior writer Molly Taft has been tackling topics around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. With the elections over, Power Play will be going on hiatus. But if you’ve got a question or thought for a story, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
If there’s any incoming congressional freshman who understands how voter anger about data centers supercharged this week’s election, it’s Will Lawrence.
A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America who helped found the Sunrise Movement, Lawrence centered his campaign on opposition to data centers from the beginning, months before many other candidates had caught on. It helped him win a challenging primary in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District against much-better-funded opponents, and this week, he defeated incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive House races in the country. (Elon Musk’s America PAC chipped in $340,000 against Lawrence.)
For this last edition of Power Play, I caught up with Lawrence about what the future holds for data center developers and for voters concerned about them, and what his plans are when he gets to Washington, DC, next year.
MOLLY TAFT: I’ve seen some post-election takes that data centers weren’t as big of a factor for voters as media coverage may suggest. I’m curious as to what you heard from voters in the last weeks of the campaign about how data centers may be competing with other big issues in this election.
WILL LAWRENCE: What are the two headlines on the election? It's been about costs, and it’s about corruption. Data centers speak directly to costs and to the legalized corruption that's become ordinary business in our rigged economy. They’re taking tax breaks, they’re sucking up water, they’re proposing to use double or triple the total capacity of the grid in Michigan, they’re threatening people’s home values.
All of this is being done because the playing field is fundamentally slanted away from local communities and towards these mega corporations. People have attempted to exert community control and local oversight, and they've been challenged in court by these Silicon Valley companies.
You see an economy and a political order that is favoring the wealthy few over the many. It really makes a mockery of democracy itself. Why is it that we keep having to play whack-a-mole against these individual projects? It shows that people in Silicon Valley and Wall Street and DC have made these decisions for us, and it speaks of the lack of economic democracy.
There have been a lot of announcements from big tech companies in recent weeks, making promises to be more transparent, to use less water, to not use NDAs—OpenAI released a bunch of commitments the day after the election. Do you think these compromises are enough to sway people?
I haven’t seen any of the specific proposals. But if they’re feeling the heat, that’s good. What they've offered so far has been completely inadequate, and it's going to take a lot to win back trust.
There was just a new hyperscale data center proposed in the last week before the election in Delhi Township, south of Lansing, close to Mason. There was an announcement made by a local economic development agency and a would-be developer. They said, “This is going to be different. We're going to do a six-month community engagement process before we even decide if we are going to build a data center, but if we do, it's going to have all these protections. And we want to hear from you.”
The township board scrambled [to put together] an emergency meeting. Two hundred fifty people showed up, probably more than that—it was overflowing. And people said, OK, the answer is still no. It’s going to take a lot of work [from the companies] to convince anybody that anything has actually changed.
Have any tech companies reached out to you?
I haven’t spoken to any of these companies.
When you go to Washington in January, what are some of the first policies you’re going to try and work on around data centers?
I'm going to fight for a federal data center moratorium, and along with it, a pause on advanced AI development. The risks simply do not match up to the benefits at this time. We've got to have a conversation across all of the different stakeholders to determine what an appropriate regulatory agenda looks like.
Would that be a pause similar to what Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed, where it's contingent on AI safety regulations?
Yes. Safety here also means making sure that we're not sacrificing people and the planet to build data centers. We need to have appropriate regulations on both of those aspects.
What about using oversight or investigatory levers?
Certainly—it makes sense. We build cars here in Michigan. If GM put a car on the market that had a 1 percent chance of exploding on the highway and killing everybody inside, it would never go to market. If it did, they would be sued out of existence.
But these Silicon Valley companies, they tell us that they're actively developing a product that has a 10 percent chance of killing everybody on planet Earth. I mean, what are we talking about? This is obviously reckless endangerment, according to any existing standard of consumer protection law. There should be investigations into that, and there should be suits filed to provide a sanction against companies for engaging in unacceptable risks that are a public hazard.
What We’re Writing
It’s been a busy week for the WIRED newsroom! My colleague Tori Elliott and I tackled how data centers factored into the blue tsunami that swept the country on Tuesday. (Spoiler alert: Voters really, really want regulations on data centers.) Over on the Business desk, Caroline Haskins looked at how the election results are sending tech bros scrambling to find other locations to build data centers—including in space.
And earlier this week, WIRED’s global editorial director, Katie Drummond, sat down with New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani to talk about his first year in office. He told her that the movement against data centers gives him “a real sense of hope.” Read more from Katie and the mayor here.
What We’re Reading
- The Hill got a scoop that some environmental groups have begun to talk with tech companies about setting standards for data centers on everything from emissions to community engagement.
- ProPublica reports on how interior secretary Doug Burgum stands to gain from a possible data center build-out on public lands.
- Anti-data-center activists broke into a Microsoft data center construction site in Amsterdam on Friday as part of a wave of planned protests across Europe. Reuters has more.

Travel-focused SaaS company RateGain reported a 46.5% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹51 Cr a year ago. Operating revenue jumped 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr, reflecting the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, which RateGain acquired for $250 Mn in November last year. Sequentially, net profit declined 21.3% from ₹94.9 Cr, while operating revenue fell 5% from ₹785 Cr. RateGain reported negative other income of ₹26.2 Lakh, taking its total income to ₹745.1 Cr. Total expenses rose about 158% YoY to ₹647.7 Cr. Adjusted for deferred deal consideration related to the Sojern acquisition, RateGain said its net profit rose 78% YoY to ₹90.8 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to ₹169.1 Cr. For H1 FY27, operating revenue increased 169.5% YoY to ₹1,530.4 Cr from ₹568 Cr. Reported EBITDA rose 214.2% to ₹324.5 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA increased 250.9% to ₹362.5 Cr. The company said its reported H1 EBITDA had already exceeded its full-year FY26 EBITDA. Sojern Integration And Debt The Sojern acquisition expanded RateGain’s travel marketing business, particularly its presence among destination marketing organisations (DMOs), hotels, and other travel businesses. To finance the acquisition, RateGain’s UK subsidiary secured a $125 Mn debt facility from HSBC and Citibank, backed by a corporate guarantee from the Indian parent. Including a repayment of $46.3 Mn today, the subsidiary has repaid $93.8 Mn, or 75%, of the original facility. Its outstanding debt now stands at $31.3 Mn. Alongside the expansion in revenue, RateGain said the Sojern integration helped broaden its customer base. It had 14,538 customers at the end of September, about 4.5X the 3,224 customers it had at the end of FY25. Its customers include hospitality companies, online travel agencies (OTAs), airlines, car rental companies, and DMOs. Marketing Drives Business Mix RateGain operates across three verticals: data as a service (DaaS), distribution, and marketing technology. Its offerings span competitive pricing and demand intelligence, hotel distribution, digital marketing, and guest engagement. Marketing technology now accounts for 80.2% of revenue, followed by DaaS at 13.2% and distribution at 6.6%. By customer industry, hospitality contributed 48.6% of H1 revenue, followed by DMOs at 30.9%, OTAs at 7.2%, airlines at 3.7%, and car rentals at 2.3%. North America accounted for 63.7% of H1 revenue, followed by Europe at 21.5%, Asia-Pacific at 12.3%, and other markets at 2.5%. The company’s client roster includes 33 of the world’s top 40 hotel chains, four of the top five airlines, and seven of the top 10 car rental companies. RateGain also highlighted its AI products. Chairman and MD Bhanu Chopra said shifting travel demand is increasing customers’ reliance on data and AI. He said RateGain’s priorities included adding customers, increasing their use of its platform, and extending AI into more of their daily operations. In H2 FY27, the company plans to take the combined RateGain and Sojern offering to more customers. RateGain reported a total pipeline of ₹660 Cr and new contract wins worth ₹277.7 Cr. The company’s employee headcount stood at 1,244 at the end of September, up 42.8% YoY. Shares of RateGain ended today’s trading session 3.3% higher at ₹819.50 apiece on the BSE.

Sri Lanka’s sports ministry has reversed an earlier decision to abandon the proposed cricket ground in Jaffna, with construction set to begin next week.
Sports Minister Sunil Kumara Gamage, who visited the proposed site at Mandathivu in Jaffna, told reporters that all necessary approvals have been secured and construction contracts awarded.
“We have obtained all necessary approvals. Contracts for construction have been awarded,” Gamage was quoted as saying in a ministry release.
In late June, the interim committee appointed by Gamage to administer Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) had announced that the project would not go ahead, citing a shortage of funds.
The foundation stone for the proposed facility was laid by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in September 2025, during the tenure of the previous SLC administration headed by Shammi Silva.

Former Australia cricketer David Warner lent his full support to Usman Khawaja’s revelations regarding the sandpaper gate and thanked his ex-opening partner for revealing the truth.
Warner was among the three, including Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, to get bans after the Australian players were found using sandpaper to shine the ball during the 2018 South Africa Test series.
While Warner and Smith were handed 12 months ban, Bancroft was given a nine-month ban.
Recently, Khawaja reignited the discussions where in his autobiography, Sabr, he claimed everyone knew about using the sandpaper.
Warner in an Instagram post on Monday said it was about time the truth came out. “It’s been eight years since I’ve spoken on this topic, and Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you,” he said in a video.
“I thank you for what you’ve done; it’s 100 per cent accurate what you’ve said, now everyone knows the truth.”

“This is for everyone in Australia; it’s been the question everyone has been asking. Uzzie wrote down every single thing from that day on, you said how it is and it’s 100 per cent accurate.
“It’s been a tough time for my family and for Steven (Smith) and Cameron (Bancroft), no doubt, but this is what needed to come out; I fully support that.”
Even while bowlers like current Australian captain Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc have denied having knowledge about players using illegal methods to shine the ball, Warner said the investigation was “botched” by those in charge.
“We’re not here to point fingers, and we’re not opening old wounds. It’s about accountability, transparency, ensuring that the truth is properly examined,” he continued.
“Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched, but Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft. Uzzie was not interviewed; how is that a thorough investigation? It baffles me.
“There were a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media, by people, and there were a lot of people who stayed silent,” Warner said.
Warner added that people should stop scrutinising person asking for accountability. “One thing I told my girls was to tell the truth because lies will eventually get out.
“This is Usman’s story; this is what Usman believes. Uzzie, thank you.”

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.
Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.
Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.
India's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city's already hazardous air.
Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.
"Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes," he said.
New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world's most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.
After harvesting rice, farmers often burn leftover stalks to clear their fields for the next planting season. The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.
The problem becomes particularly acute in late October and November, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.
Authorities in New Delhi have implemented a set of measures to curb pollution, which include limits on construction activity and restrictions on diesel generators, while courts have sough restrictions on firecrackers. But the measures have not prevented the return of severe pollution each year.
Environmentalists say long-term solutions, such as cleaner energy and stricter controls on vehicle emissions, are needed to prevent the annual crisis.
Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, described the government's response so far as "knee-jerk" and "temporary."
"A lot of interventions happen only because the government is pressured or pushed in a corner to do something," she said.

Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.
But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.
“[The government] cut off the supply of medications, special foods and diapers. They haven’t delivered any since last November. The matter is in court,” said the facility’s coordinator, Fernando Montero. The pope and Milei, he said, “have completely opposing ideologies”, arguing that the pope teaches that a person’s worth is not measured by whether they are productive, whereas Milei is a “hyper-capitalist” who believes only “those who compete the most should be rewarded”.
Pope Leo’s three days here – he began a three-country trip through South America in Uruguay on Friday, and will finish with six days in Peru – will be the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987. His predecessor, Pope Francis, who was Argentine, never returned during his papacy.
The trip could prove uncomfortable for Milei. A far-right libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as the symbol of his promised spending cuts, Milei called Francis an “imbecile” and “the representative of the Evil One on Earth” in 2020, and accused him of promoting communism, saying social justice was theft. Milei claims to have apologised when he met Francis in the Vatican in February 2024.
Since taking office the previous December, he has slashed public spending, which the government says was needed to curb inflation. The cost, however, was high. The thinktank Mate estimates that retirees on the minimum pension – 63% of the total – have lost about 30% of their purchasing power. Last Wednesday at the weekly retirees’ march outside Congress, a man held up a cardboard sign reading, “Save us Pope Leo XIV – Milei is killing us.”
Last month, Buenos Aires archbishop Jorge García Cuerva said Leo XIV would find “a divided Argentina and a large number of very poor brothers and sisters.”
But the differences between the pope and the president go beyond typical social issues. In May, Leo XIV called for “disarming” artificial intelligence, while Milei has said he would not regulate AI technology and has instead presented bills to build datacentres across the country and to grant legal status to “no-human corporations”. Federico Sturzenegger, a minister in charge of state cuts, says he has used AI to draft legislation.
Milagros Miceli, a sociologist and computer scientist who leads the Critical AI Lab in Berlin, said the “contradiction” between the two is “pretty evident”. She welcomed Leo’s visit, celebrating how the “powerful figure” of the pope intends to put “human beings at the centre by stripping these technologies of the values that are presented to us as taking precedence over humanity.”
Juan Grabois, a left-wing Peronist deputy and social leader who served in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, said: “The idea of absolute deregulation is at the heart of the president’s agenda, and the replacement of the human element with these forms of algorithmic power has clearly also become a policy priority for the government.”
Disability funding has been a flashpoint between church and state. As Milei has clashed with Congress over a funding law that remains in limbo, Argentina’s conference of bishops wrote to the health minister, Mario Lugones, on 1 April, denouncing “the serious situation facing numerous institutions dedicated to the care and support of people with disabilities in our country”. The ministry has met the bishops twice since, in April and again on 5 October, but without resolving the impasse.
The government is trying to downplay potential tensions. “There’s no way the pope is going to come here to comment on local politics,” Sandra Pettovello, the minister overseeing social policy, said recently. Amnesty International, meanwhile, has written to the pope about Argentina, warning of its “concern about government decisions that affect the exercise of fundamental rights”.
All of this will be top of mind when Milei receives the pope at the airport on Sunday. From the disability home, the pope will go on to Buenos Aires and meet business and union leaders; then on Tuesday he will celebrate Mass at the grounds of FAdeA, the state-owned military aircraft factory in Córdoba, whose workers have protested against Milei’s cuts. Juan Cruz Esquivel, director of Buenos Aires University’s Barometer of Religions and Beliefs, says the itinerary speaks for itself.
“I don’t want to speculate [about what the pope will say], but clearly any mention of defending domestic production, labour, disability or social justice in the pope’s rhetoric naturally clashes with the ideology that Milei’s government has been promoting,” says Esquivel.
Mariano Oberlin, a Catholic priest in an impoverished neighbourhood of Córdoba, expects the clash to play out diplomatically. “Pope Leo has been saying it without confronting, but he keeps upholding the church’s social doctrine as the key axis of his ministry,” Oberlin said. “If Milei wants to use him, he’ll probably have to do a lot of juggling to make him say the opposite of what he’s been saying – and of what he’ll surely say when he comes: that the Gospel invites us to feel like brothers, to respect each person’s deep, inherent dignity, and to fight so that this dignity becomes real in access to rights.”
Since Francis’s tenure, social movements in Latin America have come closer to the Catholic church, and Argentina is no exception. Grabois, who was part of that process, sees the relationship as a two-way exchange. “[Francis] wasn’t the ‘good priest’ who came to help the poor,” he says, arguing that the exchanges helped Francis “develop his social thinking”. “Without the cartoneros (cardboard pickers) and the villeros (people from impoverished neighbourhoods), Francis would not have been Francis.”
To Grabois, the same is true for Leo. “Francis took notice of Leo because he saw him supporting the Peruvian indigenous movement.”
That doesn’t mean all Argentine social movements support the pope. On Saturday, a day before the visit, the LGBTQIA+ community will hold the 35th Pride March in Buenos Aires. María Rachid from the march’s organising committee said: “The church’s dogma regarding our families has not changed at any time, neither under the previous pope nor under this one”, though she notes that Francis’s words on gay rights “brought some relief to many families and their communities”.
But a new development is the rise of evangelical churches, while Catholic identification falls. Buenos Aires University found 57.7% of Argentines identify as Catholic and 17.4% as evangelical, compared with 76.5% and 9% nearly 20 years ago. Last week, Milei inaugurated an evangelical temple in Neuquén and gave a nakedly political speech promising to seek re-election next year. Although Catholicism remains Argentina’s majority religion, it has lost its cultural hegemony and its influence on legislative agenda, Esquivel said.
Nevertheless, a majority of Argentines expect a “message from the pope focused on the social and humanitarian agenda”. People who, 10 years ago, held views that were very, very hostile toward the church,” he said. “I even see them as more fervent [about the visit] than typical churchgoers who attend Sunday Mass.” For Grabois, “in the face of dehumanisation, ordinary people are taking refuge in the only global voice that’s speaking out about this today – which is Francis and Leo’s.”

Labubu hype seemed unstoppable, now the fluffy monster mania is dying
- Published
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.
Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.
Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.
The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.
Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".
He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.
But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."
Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.
It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.
Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.
The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.
The rise and fall
Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.
The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.
One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.
Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys. The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.
They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu.
A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find, with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.
Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.
Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.
For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.
"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.
Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.
Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.
Rivals take over
As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.
Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.
Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.
"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year. "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."
Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.
That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.
Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.
But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."
'Now I only buy what I like'
After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular."
Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls.
His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles."
Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases.
"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out."
But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans.
Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines.
There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.
For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.
"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

This woman defied lethal cancer. Can mRNA vaccines make that possible for others?
Donna Gustafson is living a cancer patient's fantasy.
At 72, the retired accountant hikes, travels, lifts weights, and exchanges adoring glances with Ed, the husband she married 50 years ago. All these moments are happening while she shows zero evidence of the Stage II pancreatic cancer that was supposed to kill her years ago.
"I have had 100% quality of life; I am back to where I was prior," Gustafson says.
"She's better than that," her husband interjects. "She's sassier, and she's in the best shape of her life — there's no question about that."
Seven years ago, Gustafson became the world's first recipient of an mRNA vaccine designed to treat pancreatic cancer, a highly lethal disease diagnosed in about 70,000 Americans every year. There are few effective treatments for the disease, but Gustafson's was a personalized version, created using samples of her tumor, aiming to reprogram her immune cells — training them, essentially, to recognize distinctive mutant proteins on cancerous cells and kill them.
mRNA vaccines having a moment
It's been a big year for cancer vaccines using mRNA, especially after drugmakers Merck and Moderna released results last month from the first major successful trial of mRNA vaccines for skin cancer, showing a 42% reduction in recurrence and death over two years.
A combination of technologies using mRNA, genomics and AI, helped create these vaccines, which are also being tested on lung, kidney, bladder and brain cancers. But researchers don't yet understand why some trials have failed, while others show eye-popping results in the form of people like Gustafson.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Gustafson, who splits her time between New Jersey and Florida, says she wasn't scared to be first to test this concept against pancreatic cancer. She credits her three grown daughters for finding and getting her into the trial. "It was a no brainer," she says. "I knew that statistically, the odds of my survival were low, and I was very happy to be offered some type of hope."
Gustafson received nine doses of the vaccine, along with surgery and chemotherapy. She was part of a small clinical trial involving 16 pancreatic cancer patients. The vaccine worked on half of the patients, and seven of those eight are still alive today.
For patients on these vaccines, treatment is also an easier option. It does not compare to chemotherapy, which requires hours of infusion and comes with after-effects that were "barbaric" for his wife, Ed Gustafson says with a shudder.
By contrast: The shots felt like nothing, Donna Gustafson says. "I had no symptoms, no side effects — to the point where I was actually worried that maybe it was not helping."
But it was. Very swiftly.
Surgeon and scientist Vinod Balachandran ran the trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City. The vaccine used in his research is made in an expansive lab made up of hallways of freezers, desks, centrifuges and cytometers. Patients' responses to the treatment are measured in the lab. The oncologists and mathematicians who work there are dedicated to decoding pancreatic cancer, then reverse engineering the mRNA necessary to fight it.
A research analyst pulls up a graph on her computer, showing dozens of superimposed green lines — each representing the number of times an immune cell reproduces, Balachandran explains.
Looking at the graph representing Donna Gustafson's immune cell count, Balachandran notes how the lines shoot up, then remain high and flat — "a 10,000-fold increase" — reflecting how her immune system mass produced cancer-attacking cells and sustained it, for years beyond her last shot. "It just tells us that this response lasts," Balachandran says.
Balachandran says it was the strength and durability of such responses in half of the patients that, for him, blew open the possibility of mRNA vaccines. "Well, if you could generate such a strong immune response in the toughest of cancers, could this similarly develop cancer vaccines for a broad array of human cancers?," he says.
Promising future
This technology is now at an inflection point — with patients, doctors, researchers and investors. The National Cancer Institute, for example, is working on a partnership with private companies to fast-track research and development of more mRNA cancer vaccines. Balachandran and Sloan Kettering are part of that, with plans to expand production of personalized vaccines for patients on site.
Donna Gustafson says she and her husband have felt overwhelmingly lucky over the past seven years.
"I saw two more grandchildren be born and grow, many birthdays, holidays and Christmases with my family," she says.
With her husband, she's created and ticked off many items off her bucket list: skydiving, summiting, celebrating their 50th anniversary with the expectation of many more to come.
"We've done so many things — we probably have done so much more," Ed Gustafson says, before his wife picks up his sentence, "...if we had not had this experience."
"We live so much more for the day now," Ed Gustafson says, looking at his wife.

I Tested 30 Pairs of Computer Speakers. Here’s My Comprehensive Guide to Buying the Best Ones
Featured in this article
Good computer speakers can make for a quick desktop upgrade. Sound is often overlooked when people buy a PC. Some folks prefer headphones, others stick with those old, battered speakers they inherited, and some rely on the awful built-in speaker in their monitor. With any of the speakers in this list, you can enhance voices in video calls and movies, tease out greater depth in your favorite music, and provide spatial awareness in games. After several months of testing, I've narrowed my selection across various budgets and preferences. Whether you want a soundbar for your computer, a pair of speakers, or a surround sound system, you can find it here.
Be sure to check out our many other audio guides, like the Best Soundbars, Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Wireless Headphones, Best Gaming Headsets, and Best Bookshelf Speakers.
Updated November 2026: I added speakers from Creative, a mention for speakers from Pioneer, and updated prices.
Other Computer Speakers I Liked
There are tons of computer speakers on the market, and many of the ones I tested are perfectly fine, but don't deserve a spot above for one reason or another.
Pioneer DJ DM-40D-BT for $239: Designed as entry-level speakers for bedroom DJs, the Pioneer DJ DM-40D-BTs sport a molded black plastic front with an MDF cabinet, but they feel well-built and solid. There’s a 4-inch fiberglass woofer with a 0.75-inch soft‑dome tweeter, and a class‑D amplifier with DSP (digital signal processing). Input options are RCA, 3.5-mm stereo mini, or Bluetooth 5.0, with a 3.5-mm headphone port in front, a simple volume knob, and a Bluetooth button. On the back of the control speaker, there’s a DJ/Production switch, which dials up the boomy bass. The sound quality is decent for the money, but they’re a bit too big for my desktop. If you need a budget option for music production to pair with a laptop, they might be a good shout, though the IK Multimedia iLoud Micro Monitors above are better if you can find the extra cash.
Edifier M60 for $200: Close to matching my top picks in sound quality, but significantly cheaper, the Edifier M60 speakers produce a rich, clear sound that persists when you crank the volume. The bass is decent, considering the lack of a subwoofer, but it can get muddy and a bit rattly. You have three connection options, including USB-C, 3.5 mm, or Bluetooth 5.3. My test music playlist sounded great on these speakers, and only the rumbly bass distracted me in games and movies, though they come with angled stands that point them at your ears and reduce vibrations. The M60 speakers are also the perfect size for most desktops. On the downside, the touch controls are a little annoying (you have to hold down for three seconds to power on/off or change mode), and the Edifier ConneX app for Android (also available on iOS) was a little flaky, though it offered some handy customization options and a six-band equalizer. Overall, these speakers are a solid option if this is your budget.
Creative Pebble Nova for $266: These eye-catching orb-shaped speakers with RGB rings around the base are a statement piece for your desk. They are big, angled at 45 degrees, and you have the choice of a flat base or elevated stands. They light up, produce a pleasant sound that’s rich across the board and with real depth, and can, frankly, get far too loud for your desktop. I was also impressed by the virtual surround sound for gaming. Don’t make the mistake of thinking the Creative App is superfluous, because it’s packed with options, from an equalizer to dialogue enhancement to RGB lighting controls. While I love the stand, it made them too tall for my desk because of my dual monitors. I also found the touch controls a bit finicky, and I advise switching off the power saving mode.
Ruark MR1 MK3 for $599: Perfect for a retro vibe, the styling includes a fabric front, and black finish with a dial on top. With a fluid and expansive soundstage, music sounds great on these speakers, and even without a subwoofer, there’s a decent rumble of bass. I found Ruark’s speakers equally pleasing for watching movies and video calls, as voice clarity is excellent, though I experienced some slight distortion with deep voices during meetings. They are also quite large, maybe too large for some desks.
OXS Thunder Pro for $600: With a compact design, sci-fi styling that includes RGB lighting, and no separate subwoofer, I was unsure what to expect from this soundbar. The Thunder Pro is 24 inches long and just 3 inches tall, so slotted into place perfectly under my monitor. It comes with a wired control dial, a remote control, and extra feet in the box to angle it. I was immediately impressed when the bass of Dead Prez’s “Hip-Hop” kicked in, bouncing the passive radiators up and down. The sound is expansive, the bass is far better than it has any right to be without a large subwoofer, and the highs are surprisingly crisp. This soundbar is Dolby Atmos-certified and has three distinct gaming modes. The first-person shooter mode offered excellent spatial sound, allowing me to hear the footsteps and grunts of a cloaked Elite in Halo Infinite just in time to avoid being impaled. Connectivity is comprehensive with USB-A and USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, Bluetooth 5.0, two HDMI ports (one eARC), a mic-in port, and a headphone jack. All that’s missing is the option to hook up a subwoofer. The wired control unit lights up, acts as a volume dial and power button, and has EQ and mode buttons on the back. Razer Nommo V2 Pro for $438: Stick to one brand for all your gaming gear, and it’s easier to achieve harmony. Plus, you only need one app to configure everything. The wireless control puck acts as a volume dial, and you can press it to mute, play, or skip. While Razer Chroma RGB now supports more than 300 games, offers various effects, and an ambient awareness mode that reacts to your screen, there are only two lighting zones (one for each speaker). Unfortunately, the Razer Synapse software is the only way to get at some settings, and it feels bloated and sometimes hogs system resources.
Logitech G560 Lightsync for $250: Folks who prefer Logitech gear should consider the G560 Lightsync. This 2.1 system comprises a huge subwoofer and two speakers with an attractive curved loop design. For movies and gaming, the G560 does better, with DTS:X Ultra virtual surround sound to emulate larger systems. Majority DX10 Desktop Speakers for £13: They lack bass and general clarity, but these USB-powered speakers are the cheapest I’ve tried. Only available in the UK, they could be enough if your budget is very tight.
Edifier G2000 Pro for $212: A spruced-up version of the G2000 above, the Pro is an upgrade to 64-watt power, 3-inch full-range drivers, and virtual 7.1 surround sound. Creative Pebble X Plus for $123: If our budget pick isn’t quite doing it for you, Creative’s Pebble X Plus adds a cube-shaped subwoofer under your desk. Onkyo Creator GX-10DB for $250: Capable of producing a warm and rich sound, Onkyo’s speakers are the perfect size for your desktop and come with angled stands (though they are plastic). Logitech Z407 for $110: A complete 2.1 system at this price is no mean feat. These speakers connect via USB, 3.5-mm aux, or Bluetooth, and there’s a wireless remote volume dial. These are the computer speakers that had deal-breaking flaws for me.

House of Marley Get Together Duo for $170: Sporting an attractive and eco-friendly blend of bamboo and fabric, the Get Together Duo from House of Marley is affordable. The battery-powered right speaker can also double as a portable speaker, and you can use these as bookshelf speakers, but as computer speakers, they are just OK.
SteelSeries Arena 3 for $150: Sporting a nice pear-shaped design with tiltable speakers and subtle branding, the entry-level Arena 3 from SteelSeries can get loud. They don’t have lighting, USB, or any other extras.
Logitech Z906 5.1 Surround Sound Speaker System for $450: This 5.1 system is THX-certified and comes with a huge subwoofer, five speakers, and a central control unit. The design feels dated, maybe even a bit ugly, and you need to run cables around your room. The surround sound effect is solid, and you can even convert stereo with the 3D mode, but overall, it’s a bass-heavy system.
Are Computer Speakers Worth It?
Budget is a deciding factor for most folks, but even cheap desktop speakers offer far better sound than your monitor. Headphones are a great alternative, but not everyone wants to wear headphones all the time. You can spend as much as you like on audio gear, but I have focused on reasonably affordable desktop systems here, starting from as low as $35 and not exceeding $700.
What Should I Look for in Computer Speakers?
It depends. There’s plenty to weigh when shopping for a set of computer speakers, so it’s vital to start by deciding what’s most important to you. For example, I work and play on the same desktop PC, so I need speakers that perform well for video calls, long gaming sessions, listening to music, and watching movies. I also have a standing desk, and my monitor setup doesn’t leave much room, so I prefer compact all-rounders with long cables.
Sound quality: The top consideration for most folks, you want the best sound quality you can afford. A good set of speakers will offer a balance of clear vocals, rich treble, and rumbling bass. If you crave bass you feel in the pit of your stomach, a subwoofer is essential, though it might not be a good idea for folks who have downstairs neighbors. For accurate positional sound, you might want to look at a surround sound system with multiple speakers.
Design: Consider the finish. Your speakers will be on show, so you’ll want to pick something that fits your decor.
Brand: Gamers with devices from an existing brand might lean toward the same brand of speakers because they can be configured in the same software. This is particularly important with speakers that have built-in lights, so you can sync up your entire setup.
Extras: Some people will consider these superfluous, but if you want a remote control for kicking back or RGB lighting to bring a splash of color to your desk, these are extra perks on higher-end speakers. Snag speakers with a decent range of connectivity, and you can always repurpose them later. Most speakers come with all the cables you need, but it’s worth checking before you buy. I have listed what you will find in the box with all the computer speakers I recommend.
Where Should I Position My Desktop Speakers?
You ideally want the speakers to be angled slightly up (around 15 degrees) and pointed at your ears. Since you know the exact spot you’ll be in when listening, you can tweak the position of your speakers for the best results. Don’t just chuck them on the desk and leave it at that. Try moving and angling them until you find that sweet spot.
Do I Need Speaker Stands?
Speaker stands can maximize sound quality by helping to reduce vibrations from your desktop that can muddy the sound. Angled speaker stands are also a good way to direct the sound toward your ears. Some manufacturers, such as Edifier and Onkyo, include stands; IK Multimedia and Razer include adjustable bases or fold-out feet; Audioengine sells stands separately. You will also find a wide choice of third-party stands online.
What Size Speakers Should I Get?
If space is limited, a compact set of speakers will work best. The trade-off is power and volume, as small speakers generally don’t produce as big or high-quality a sound as large speakers. If you opt for a subwoofer, you will want a suitable space under your desk. For surround sound systems, you must run cables and find suitable spots for speakers behind you. If you have a wide monitor on a mount, a compact soundbar beneath it could be the best fit. Check the dimensions carefully and measure the space on your desk before you buy.
What’s the Best Way to Connect My Speakers to My Computer?
Speakers can come with a multitude of ports and connectivity options. USB connections usually sound best because they output the digital signal for the digital-to-analog converter (DAC) in the speakers, which is likely to be better unless you have a good sound card. But the best way to be sure is to try both and see which sounds better. If you want to be able to connect a phone or laptop wirelessly, then Bluetooth is paramount. Most speakers have a 3.5-mm aux input, and some have an output for headphones. Just make sure your preferred speakers support the connectivity you want. You should also make sure that you have the necessary free ports on your PC or laptop, though you can always add more with a USB hub.
How I Test Computer Speakers
Every set of speakers in this guide was tested for at least a week, sometimes longer. I don’t use headphones, so they were all used for video calls throughout my work day, listening to music and podcasts, and for movies and games in the evening. While I played several games, watched many movies or shows, and listened to lots of music and podcasts, I ran through a specific list of test content with every speaker system to make it easier to compare them.
My test content included the game Halo Infinite, the movie Dune, and a music playlist including “Hip-Hop” (Dead Prez), “The National Anthem” (Radiohead), “All Along the Watchtower” (Jimi Hendrix), “Hey” (Pixies), “Sabotage” (Beastie Boys), “A Day in the Life” (the Beatles), “Nothing Compares 2 U” (Sinéad O'Connor), and “Only God Knows” (Young Fathers).

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) calculates it using eight pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide.

‘Had to accept her wish’: Row over Vedic rituals at wedding of DMK general secretary's granddaughter
The wedding of DMK leader Duraimurugan's granddaughter drew objections from DK chief Veeramani, who questioned the use of religious rituals at the wedding.
The conduct of Vedic traditions and Sanskrit chants at DMK general secretary Duraimurugan’s granddaughter’s wedding has sparked a controversy in Tamil Nadu.
According to news agency PTI, the senior DMK leader has expressed regret over the incident and said that the ceremony was conducted as per his granddaughter's preferences.
Senthamarai, the granddaughter of Duraimurugan, and Deepak Ravi, son of film producer Kannan Ravi, got married on November 1 in Chennai.
The guest list included former Tamil Nadu chief minister MK Stalin, actors Dhanush and Sivakarthikeyan, as well as several well-known figures from the film industry.
Vedic wedding draws flak from DK prez Veeramani
The event drew sharp objections from Dravidar Kazhagam president K Veeramani, who questioned the use of religious rituals at the wedding in a family associated with the Dravidian movement.
Veeramani criticised Duraimurugan, arguing that such personal decisions should not contradict the movement’s founding ideals of rationalism. Following the backlash, the DMK leader expressed regret.
Veeramani also questioned the contrast between the wedding invitation, which carried photographs of Dravidian movement icons and DMK leaders, and the ceremony itself, where priests performed rituals. Citing Duraimurugan’s post in the party, he called on DMK chief MK Stalin to take steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Duraimurugan says he gave in to granddaughter’s wishes
Speaking to the media on November 6, Duraimurugan explained that the wedding was conducted according to his granddaughter’s preferences. He said she had pursued her education overseas and married outside her caste, and had specifically wanted a traditional ceremony performed by priests.
The DMK leader said he eventually agreed to her request.

"I had to accept my granddaughter's wish due to her insistence. I regret the incident. No one needs to make this a political issue or turn it into a subject of debate," Duraimurugan said, as quoted by PTI.
Reiterating his commitment to party principles, Duraimurugan said his own wedding and that of his son, Kathir Anand, had been solemnised by then CM and late DMK patriarch M Karunanidhi without such rituals.
