India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
- Published
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.
One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.
Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.
Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.
Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).
The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.
The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.
But the critical response so far has been mixed.
Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".
Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars.
"I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.
Shubhra Gupta, external of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".
There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.
Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.
Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King.
"It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote, external, giving it four stars.
Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".
Giovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it, external five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.
The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".
In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.
When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.
Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.
Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.
Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.
The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.
Other adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.
Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters.
It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.
The 2023 film Adipurush, another big-budget retelling of Ramayana, sparked backlash on several fronts.
Hindu groups called for a ban, accusing it of disrespecting religious figures, while some critics questioned its depiction of Ravana, which they said drew on Mughal imagery and reinforced stereotypes about Muslims. The film was also criticised for its dialogue and visual effects.
For the actors portraying these characters in the latest film, that burden was deeply felt.
"I was filled with fear," Kapoor told the BBC Asian Network's Haroon Rashid. "I knew that maybe I'm too old for this. I won't be able to do justice to it."
He called the role "an opportunity of a lifetime", but said playing a figure worshipped by millions left little room for the creative freedom he had enjoyed in other films.
Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, said the experience was as much spiritual as artistic. Raised in a religious household, she said she approached the part not just as a performance, but as an opportunity for personal growth.
How the film is being received will become clearer soon, as audiences head to cinemas.
But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale.

How to turn on personal results on your Google Home
Voice Match lets every member of the family set up Google Home's personal results.
Google announced in August 2025 that Google Home speakers and other compatible devices would be getting a Gemini-driven refresh. This includes a more conversational and contextual experience with the ability to understand natural phrasing. It also includes improvements to Voice Match and personal results. When you ask "What's on my calendar?" it knows who you are and will curate the responses accordingly.
To set up personal results, open the Google Home app connected to your Google Home speaker and set up Voice Match (select your profile photo, Home settings > Gemini for home assistant > Voice Match). Then select Home > Settings. Under Features, select Google Assistant > Personal results. Select the devices you want this to work with. And that's it!
With compatible Google Assistant — now Google Gemini — devices, the smart speaker can tap into your personal calendars, appointments, Google Keep, Notes, Lists, Photos and other pertinent details. You can also share access. This means everyone in the home can sync their own unique profiles.
The benefits of personal results
With Voice Match on and personal results set up, the speaker will listen for your voice and provide responses relating to you, while these will be blocked from anyone else. Others, like guests or other family members who have not set up their profiles, can still ask questions, set alarms, and more. But they will get generic responses versus personalized ones. You, however, will be able to ask what's on your calendar, ask what items are left on your to-do list, request for your Google Home to play your favorite music playlist and more. If you find the smart speaker keeps misunderstanding you, look into some quick fixes, like moving it to a quieter room or redoing the Voice Match training.
It's worth noting that if you were to turn off Voice Match with personal results turned on, anyone speaking to the smart assistant will hear your personal results. This might not matter if the Google Home speaker is in your home office, on your nightstand or another location where you're the only one using it. But for a household with multiple people and a Google Home speaker in a central location, you need to follow additional steps so it knows who it's speaking to.
Personal results for everyone
To get personal results to work for everyone in the family, everyone needs to go through setting up Voice Match. It works for up to six people, and each person needs to link their Google account to the device individually and turn on Voice Match using the steps noted above. From here, the Google Home will be able to determine who is speaking and provide personalized responses to their queries by recognizing and distinguishing among voices.
Personal results combined with Voice Match allows everyone to walk by, ask a question, and get a response that's unique to them. A teen might be reminded that he has a math test today, while Mom can call up her notes with a reminder to pick up a case of water for the soccer game tonight. Dad might ask for the score for his favorite team while Grandma wants to play her favorite music playlist while making dinner. It's a useful feature to use whether you're personalizing results for you and you alone or for everyone to have their own personal assistant.

Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
- Published
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."
Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.
"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."
Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.
In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".
On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.
The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.
Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.
Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

It’s 2016, and you’re wandering around the neighborhood at dusk. On the prowl, you’re swiping on a smartphone to catch that elusive Snorlax and grow your collection in Pokémon Go. You, alongside hundreds of millions of other players, are enjoying a mixed-reality game built around lovable characters. What you don’t realize is that these scans of your environment will one day help robots navigate obstacles and interact with objects.
Niantic, the creator of Pokémon Go, sold the game last year and pivoted hard into one of Silicon Valley’s buzziest AI topics right now: world models. “We’re very much about reconstructing the real world,” says Brian McClendon, Niantic Spatial’s chief technology officer. He hopes to leverage its trove of world data to build replicas. Unlike the text-based nature of large language models, world models use visual inputs and can generate digital environments that simulate physics.
This software is poised to seep into everyday life, without you necessarily ever interacting directly with world models. 2027 could be a major year for the expansion of home robotics and driverless cars, both of which are bolstered by advances in world models. It’s time to better understand how these bots think.
“So with a language model, you have a sentence, and it will predict the next word in the sentence,” says Oliver Cameron, the CEO of Odyssey, an AI lab focused on world models. “With a world model, you give it a visual state of the world, an image, and it will then predict the next visual state of the world.” These 3D generations can be used as digital training grounds. “They’re simulations, but they look and feel real,” he says.
McClendon sees these world models as helping robots practice without physical movement or being in intended environments. He says someone could take photos of where the robot is intended to function, generate a 3D model, and then let the software run “millions of simulations” to train the robot on the space’s parameters.
It’s not just humanoid robots that could use simulated practice; driverless cars also improve using world models. Without a human behind the wheel, split-second software reactions are paramount.
“Importantly, a world model must be able to react to the actions that we take in the world, and so it must understand physics, cause and effect, and how other objects and people change their actions in response to our own,” says Jamie Shotton, chief scientist at Wayve, which builds world models designed for cars.
Wayve’s generative world model is powered, in part, by dashcam footage. The startup uses it to recreate hazardous roads and other unsafe conditions that would not be practical to test in real life.
Beyond physical applications, developers are also analyzing how world models could impact video games. Since physics and 3D rendering are core to video games, major players like Tencent are investing in their own world models.
You can expect large AI companies, like Google, to keep boasting about their latest world-model improvements. Investors are also throwing money at insurgent big names in computer science that are turning their attention to the technology. Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, raised over a billion dollars recently to fund his Advanced Machines Intelligence startup. Additionally, famed Stanford computer scientist Fei-Fei Li launched a startup in 2024 called World Labs, which AMD acquired this year for over $8 billion.
Even if you plan on avoiding autonomous cars and domestic bots altogether, world models are already warping the labor market behind the scenes. To simulate our physical world, AI labs need real people to record it. Earlier this year, I strapped an iPhone to my forehead and recorded hours of videos in my apartment. I recorded my hands folding laundry, washing dishes, and pouring Diet Coke, selling the video data through an app for a fairly measly payout. As more companies attempt to build better world models, even more gig work may demand this kind of data collection.
Between chasing virtual monsters in 2016 and selling videos of my chores in 2026, these systems are ingesting more and more of my physical life. Now I can’t stop picturing the digital ghost of some humanoid robot trapped inside a simulation of my bedroom, endlessly folding my boxers with its metallic claws—getting slightly better with every pass. I’m sorry I didn’t tidy up first.

Open-weight artificial intelligence models are now almost as capable of hacking into computer networks as the best closed ones, according to new research that heralds a much-anticipated turning point in the cybersecurity landscape.
Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.
“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.
The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.
The findings are also noteworthy given that the US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, premised the limited release of new models—beginning with Claude Mythos Preview in April—on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking capabilities were broadly available.
Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company’s Project Glasswing, which gives trusted access to the full capabilities of new models, was focused on getting those tools “in the hands of defenders to give a head start.”
“We need to prepare now for a world where these capabilities are broadly available in 6, 12, 24 months. Many things would be different about security,” he told WIRED at the time.
Seven months later, that transition seems to have arrived on schedule.
Vals tested AI models in two simulated scenarios, giving them various specific tasks to achieve. The first scenario involved a mock corporate network accessible through a public-facing website. The second involved two different company networks; a model needed to compromise the first in order to gain access to the second.
The researchers found OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, to be the most capable, completing 81 percent of the tasks it was given in an average of two tests. The Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek was not far behind, completing 73 percent of the objectives on average. The Vals researchers note that on some tasks, the two models scored equally.
The research also showed how much cheaper it is to use an open-weight model for this kind of task. Vals says it costs $17 to $46 in tokens for GPT-6-Sol to carry out an attack compared to $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. Open models are generally cheaper because they can be run on one’s own hardware. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, says this also provides a strong incentive for those playing defense to use open models rather than proprietary ones.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Much of the year in cybersecurity has played out as predicted, with AI automating core hacking tasks to help both attackers and defenders find a massive number of new vulnerabilities in code and rapidly probe networks for weaknesses. While the speed and scale of the findings, and the intensity of fixing uncovered software flaws, have all increased, experts are still debating whether AI has fundamentally altered the conceptual foundation and tenets of cybersecurity defense. In other words, it’s still not clear whether AI tools pose a new kind of threat or amplify the security challenges that have long existed.
The fact that open-weight models are now starting to match closed ones is crucial for understanding how criminal hackers can harness AI, and how companies and developers should respond. But in practice, real-world observation of cybercriminal and state-backed hacking activity has repeatedly shown in recent months that attackers are doing what they always do by conserving their resources and generally making do with older and less capable models—both proprietary and open—for most of their activity. And even with strict controls, defenders must assume that the best-funded and most highly motivated attackers have already had at least some access to closed models all this time.
“I am in general agreement that open-weight models are capable of producing advanced attacks and vulnerabilities today, especially when you consider the abliterated models that disable safety training by modifying weights,” says Alex Zenla, cofounder and chief technology officer of the cloud security firm Edera. “My caveat to this is that it is likely that the closed labs have trained additional, unreleased models exceeding these capabilities. So I would put this very much like a cat-and-mouse game. The labs see themselves as moving fast to outpace the open-weight models, to be able to secure vulnerabilities before the open-weight models find them. Unfortunately, I do think this may be the beginning of a dangerous security landscape.”

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

Three social media content creators from West Bengal — Akash Sarkar, Surajit Shee and Srimoyee Chakraborty — were recently arrested after making posts which questioned the ruling BJP government and its policies.
While Sarkar was granted bail on October 29 after spending three days in police custody, Chatterjee was released from detention on a personal bond on October 26. Shee was first sent to judicial custody and held at Medinipur Central Jail. At present, he is in police custody till November 6.
An FIR was lodged against Shee under Sections 152, 197 and 353 of the BNS, pertaining to acts endangering integrity of India, assertions threatening national integration, and statements amounting to public mischief, respectively.
In the FIR registered against Sarkar, the police invoked Sections 356(1), 353(1)(2) and 299(1) of the BNS, pertaining to criminal defamation, spreading false information/hate speech, and intentionally outraging religious feelings, respectively.
Surajit Shee: Posts on Durga Puja Stampede
Surajit Shee, hailing from Dantan village of West Midnapore district, runs a Facebook page called ‘Core Bangla-Janakantha’, which has over 2,52,000 followers. Shee shares posts on a range of social, political and scientific issues. The two last posts on his page were made on October 19. In one, he is seen appreciating the BJP government for banning DJs and loudspeakers during processions in the state, and in the other post, he talks about allegations that followed the Chorbagan stampede which killed 19 people in Kolkata at a Durga Puja.
Another post by Shee from October 18 caried a video that has been restricted in India. The caption reads, translated from Bengali, “What is the actual truth behind the Chorebagan incident? Which version is correct? The official government figures or the claims made by the public? The government itself is abusing the law. Those in power are misusing their authority to silence the voices of ordinary citizens.”
Shee is a member of ‘Bharatiya Biggyan o Juktibadi Samity’ — an organization which aims to promote scientific temperament in the society.
Alt News spoke with Dipak Roy, a key member of the outfit. Roy mentioned that beside discussing political issues, Shee was vocal about various scientific and social issues.
“Surajit had been telling us that for almost a year that a section of local BJP-RSS workers had been harassing him over his social media content. The intensity of the harassment increased after May 4 (as BJP came to power in the state). On either October 17 or 18, Shee told me that his house had been attacked by the same group, who claimed that he was posting anti-national content. I suggested that he take shelter elsewhere. He then went to a friend’s house in Contai. The police arrested him from there on October 24,” alleged Roy.
Although Shee was detained by police on October 24, he was shown as arrested on October 25, Sunday, from his residence in Dantan, instead of Contai.
According to Roy, the group that attacked Shee’s house claimed that a complaint had been lodged against him at Dantan police station over his alleged ‘anti-national’ activities. Roy told Alt News that when Shee’s father and father-in-law went to the police station to enquire about the alleged complaints, the police could not produce any complaint lodged against him. Police allegedly told them that the chief minister had ordered Shee’s arrest and that it “would be better if he surrendered” or else they would “make an example out of him”.
During the arrest, Roy alleged that only three to four police personnel were present while nearly 20 RSS-BJP workers rounded him up. “Around 15-20 RSS-BJP workers surrounded the house of his friend in Contai. These people assaulted him before handing him over to the police, who then took him away in a car,” alleged Roy. “We thought Contai police had arrested him and arranged for a lawyer to represent him at the Contai sub-divisional court. However, later we realised that Shee had been arrested by Dantan police and was produced before the Dantan court.”
Roy further alleged that Shee’s family could access the legal documents related to the case two days after his arrest. Police have also allegedly seized Shee’s mobile phone, but no seizure list has been provided to his family.
Alt News’ attempts to contact both Dantan and Contain police were unsuccessful till publication time.
Alt News spoke to Tapan Jana, Shee’s maternal uncle, who said, “Surajit was produced in Dantan court on November 2, and police sought seven days of custody. However, the judge allowed only four days.”
“After he was remanded to police custody, an officer from Dantan police station verbally abused us when we went to meet him. The officer said that Surajit had insulted Sanatan Dharma, the state and central governments, and was inciting the public through his Facebook posts. He told us to make sure that Surajit reveals during questioning who had instructed him to make those posts,” Jana said.
“The officer further said that unless Shee confessed, he would make it difficult for him to get bail,” Jana added.
Akash Sarkar: Posts on Stampede and Suvendu Adhikari
Akash Sarkar (30) was arrested from his home in Nagerbazar on October 25, produced before the Barrackpore court on October 26, which ordered three days of police custody. He was released on bail on October 29.
Sarkar told Alt News that during interrogation, police pointed to three aspects of his posts which they claimed led to his arrest — his reference to Suvendu Adhikari’s ‘bhaipo’ (nephew) in connection with the Chorbagan stampede, his comments about the government’s handling of the situation following the stampede, and his use of the term ‘teen bati’ (three bowls) to refer to Adhikari.
Sarkar said, “In one of my Facebook posts, I had mentioned that Suvendu’s nephew was the chief patron of Chorbagan Sarbojonin, the puja where 19 people were trampled, and that he should take responsibility for the tragedy. I had also flagged the manner in which the Durga idol, with its hands tied, was taken away by the police for immersion.”
“I had written in my Facebook post that, according to the BJP, previous governments in West Bengal were not Sanatani. But even those governments did not treat the goddess in the way the Sanatani government treated her. The police flagged my post as religiously inflammatory and kept me in custody for three days,” added Sarkar.
According to Sarkar, in another post, he had addressed chief minister as ‘teen bati’ — a political jab aimed at Adhikari.
“The ‘teen bati’ jab was popularised by Ali Aftab Chand, a lawyer at the Calcutta high court who identifies himself as a ‘Rashtravadi Muslim’. He was not arrested. Is it because he is close to the BJP?” asked Sarkar.
According to the FIR, a person named Soumen Das had lodged a complaint against Sarkar, alleging that Sarkar “has been using his Facebook profile to publish false, defamatory, religiously inflammatory and provocative posts concerning the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Sri Narendra Modi and Hon’ble Chief Minister of India, Sri Suvendu Adhikari.”
“While I was in the lock-up, I heard from a few police personnel that our local MLA, Tarunjyoti Tiwari, had visited the police station and taken a personal interest in my case. Police hinted that although the charges against me were flimsy, orders from higher-ups were forcing them to keep me in custody,” he alleged, adding that the police was yet to return his phone.
Srimoyee Chakroborty: Posts Critical of State Government
Chakraborty had posted an update on her Facebook profile on October 26, mentioning that she had been held at the Bidhannagar East police station. She was later released the same day on a bond of Rs 2,000.
On October 26, she announced on Facebook that she was detained, while vowing to continue her fight. Her posts on Facebook reflect a similar pattern of posts critical of the BJP-led state and central government and its policies. However, it is not clear which particular post led to the administrative action.
A scroll through her Facebook timeline shows her vocal support for the Left.
Similar to Shee and Sarkar, Chakraborty had also made a series of posts critical of the government’s management of the Chorbagan stampede and the immersion process. On October 21, she shared the chief minister’s video where he announced that only people who follow Sanatana Dharma would participate in the Durga idol immersion process. In the caption, she referred to Adhikari as ‘teen bati’.

The cow, the flea and the genome: One Health and the statecraft of prevention
A cattle virus at home and a plague scare abroad make the same argument this World One Health Day: life is epidemiologically indivisible, and the institutions that govern and study it must learn to be so too
About three-quarters of emerging human infections originate in animals. India, with 1.4 billion people, some 536 million livestock and the world’s largest milk output, sits at the centre of this arithmetic. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.

It was not possible to find evidence of Kirk publicly saying Texas would never turn blue in his lifetime, though it may have been something he said in private.
In November, a rumor circulated that Charlie Kirk, the deceased co-founder of conservative nonprofit network Turning Point USA, once said Texas would "never turn blue" within his lifetime.
People posted examples of the claim across social media, with one Facebook user writing (archived):
"Texas will never turn blue in my lifetime." - Charlie Kirk
Well, I'll be damned! He was right. He's looking up right now and shaking his head in shame.
The rumor spread following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, which saw the Democratic Party flip Texas blue after James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won their races for a Senate seat and the governor's office, respectively.
Kirk was fatally shot in September 2025. Snopes has covered numerous claims about his assassination.
In short, there is no evidence Kirk ever publicly said Texas would never turn blue in his lifetime. Therefore, the posts above incorrectly attributed the in-question quote to him.
Most of the posts featuring the rumor include no evidence supporting the claim, such as an old social media post or podcast episode showing Kirk making the statement. There has been such proof when Snopes has looked into quotes that were correctly attributed to him.
Searching for the alleged quote on Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo yielded no credible results, only more internet users spreading the claim. Likewise, searches of Kirk's official X and Facebook profiles returned no such proof of him saying it. If he had publicly said the comment, the results would have likely provided evidence of him doing so.
Similarly, videos or audio likely would have resurfaced and credible media outlets would have reported on the remark considering the Democrats' sweeping victory in the 2026 midterms. That was not the case.
Rather, it appears users fabricated the quote, which led to several posts that seemingly intended to be satirical — like one attributing the statement to "Charlie Kirkstradamus," a reference to French astrologer Nostradamus who is known for his prophecies (Snopes has also debunked numerous prophecies incorrectly attributed to Nostradamus). Others simply repeated the claim as though it is authentic.
Several posts include a screenshot or reference of something Kirk did post to X on Nov. 3, 2020, the date of that year's presidential election. That post reads, "Texas is not going blue. Don't listen to the activist media."
Some people who shared that authentic message alongside the in-question false quote seemingly misrepresented the legitimate quote's context to suggest Kirk had said Texas would "never turn blue" in his lifetime.
A majority of Texans did vote for Trump during the 2020 presidential election.
In January 2026, the state's Hood County announced its intention to rename one of its roads, "Charlie Kirk Memorial Parkway."

A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the State's first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced on Monday (November 2, 2026).
The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles (150 kilometres) north of Syracuse, Governor Kathy Hochul said.
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
Ms. Hochul, a Democrat, said the child's death is “a devastating reminder of what's at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but State health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
Ms. Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighbouring States and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

The midterm elections were great for Democrats everywhere, but some triumphed even more decisively than others: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, for example, cruised to reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote.
How Democrats can make good on their new mandate
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore explains what his party needs to do in the wake of their midterm victories.
Voters pushed Republicans out — and kept Democrats like Moore in power — in part because of their concerns over a handful of critical issues, including the rising cost of living, the Iran war, and the growing dominance of AI and data centers. The question now is how Democrats can best wield their new power to act on the currents that carried them into office.
For Moore, the stakes may be particularly high: He’s often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down.
America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Moore about his vision for how the Democrats should proceed. As Moore put it, this is a moment in which the party will have to move quickly on the problems that motivate voters most.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Lowering cost is the top priority for voters, and, frankly, it was where they penalized Trump the most. What’s the single biggest thing Democrats could do to address folks’ cost of living concerns?
Actually move fast to fix the things. No more studies. No more 10-year research reports. Move fast. For example, in Maryland, we’ve done permitting reform to be able to speed up affordable housing, right? And I did not need a 10-year research paper to tell me that we have an issue with affordable housing.
Get more housing around transit. Do more transit-oriented development. If it’s state-owned land, don’t tell me why we can’t do something. It is state owned land. Do something on it.
The reason we made the largest investments in childcare in our state’s history is because it is insane when you’re watching the fact that people are spending thirty and forty percent of their paychecks on child care and knowing how much that’s actually going to impact [them]. So there are things that we can do right now to be able to address it.
But I also think that there are things that we need Washington to be able to do. For example, gas prices: There’s no governor that can impact gas prices. We just need to stop fighting stupid wars. There’s no governor that is impacting national energy policy or national grocery prices. What we need to do is stop allowing illegal tariff policy to happen. So I do think that there are things that Washington Democrats have got to do, and that they need to move fast on. But I also think that we don’t need to wait for them to be able to put things in place that we know that actually work.
I wonder what universal healthcare means to you. Is that the government providing insurance?
If you look at what we’ve done here in Maryland, we’ve been able to actually come up with platforms through our Total Cost of Care [Model]. We’re actually working with our hospitals. Our hospitals have a universal budget, and are then able to make sure that people are getting the care that they need.
That has done a tremendous job of being able to help to break the cost curve. Maryland is one of the only states in the country where you’re watching the cost of healthcare actually go down, [while] also being able to increase coverage.
A lot of the Democrats’ affordability message came out of Mamdani’s win. I remember him telling me the one thing he would never budge on is the belief that billionaires shouldn’t exist. I wanted to pose that question to you. Do you think billionaires should exist?
I lose no sleep over the amount of billionaires in our society. I do lose sleep over the amount of children that are growing up in poverty. And I think those who [do] have, have a responsibility to support and uplift and create pathways for those who do not.
Here in our state, we actually cut taxes for the middle class. We cut taxes for military veterans. And I said [to wealthy Marylanders], you need to invest more to make sure that we’re doing things like we’re doing: having the fastest public safety turnaround story in the United States of America, having math and reading scores in our public schools now at five-year highs. And I did ask wealthy Marylanders to invest a little bit more to make sure we can get those kinds of results.
I wanted to move on to Iran. You served in Afghanistan and are a veteran. When we think about this incoming Democratic Congress, should they continue funding a war that Americans have mostly found is not in their interest?
No, and they shouldn’t have funded in the first place.
I’ve heard the argument that that leaves soldiers behind.
No, because we’re talking about a president who unilaterally went to war without even asking Congress for authority. The president does not have the authority to just wage war by himself. That is something that the Constitution lays out. Congress is the only one that has the authority for that. And truthfully, this Congress has been so caught up in the aura of the president of the United States that they have not been leaders; they have been cheerleaders.
Part of the issue is that this Congress needs to be held to account, and that’s exactly what I think happened on Tuesday. But I think about my experiences, right? I served in Afghanistan. I led soldiers with the 82nd Airborne Division, and we went over there with what we believed was an understanding of what was at stake and what needed to happen. That this was about the Taliban, and the Taliban could not be in charge of Afghanistan after 9/11. Twenty years later, trillions of dollars spent, thousands of American service members dead, and do you know who’s in charge of Afghanistan right now? The Taliban.
And so we are dragging ourselves again into another forever war. And the problem is that we have a Congress that is not actually asserting its authority to be able to check this administration. I think that Congress needs to get this done not in the first hundred days, [but] in the first hundred hours. Congress needs to assert its authority and say to the president of the United States: This needs to end.
Data centers also had a horrible night on Tuesday. But I still hear a lot of Democrats say that AI has a place in the economy of tomorrow. Is there a place for pro-AI Democrats in this big tent?
I am very concerned about what we’ve seen from AI, and I know a lot of Americans are. I’m hopeful for what I think the promise of what AI can bring to things like health care and what I think AI can bring to things like education. But I also know that there need to be guardrails.
What we have seen from Donald Trump and these folks is that there are no guardrails. They just let it do what it does. I don’t think that’s the right answer. I think that’s remarkably dangerous.
I don’t think that the answer is telling them, “Police yourself, guys, because that’s going to get us to the right answer.” And that’s why in Maryland, we’ve actually put together guidelines as to how we’re going to be protected from AI. That includes things like protecting our workforce. That includes things like protecting our pocketbooks. That includes things like protecting our children.
We put together some of the most stringent guidelines in the country that said things like, they have to pay for all their own energy and all their own upgrades. That our taxpayers do not pay a single penny for that. That they cannot pollute our air or pollute our water. They need to follow all environmental guidelines. That they need to hire local union workers. And also really importantly, that we need to make sure that the people of Maryland have control, not the data center companies, not the Trump administration. That control belongs to us.
About half of the local jurisdictions in Maryland have either a ban or a pause on [data centers]. And I’ve said the state will never override you, ever. If you have a ban or a pause, that is done, because control goes to the locals.

Kerala is stepping up its fight against drug abuse, with the state government announcing November 16 as the launch date for the next phase of its anti-narcotics campaign, Operation Toofan. The upcoming initiative, called 'Toofan Care', will focus on rehabilitating people struggling with drug addiction and helping them return to normal life, alongside the ongoing crackdown on drug trafficking networks. Kerala Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala announced the development on Monday, saying that 35 hospitals across the state had been prepared to provide rehabilitation facilities. The initiative marks an expansion of the government's strategy, which initially focused on identifying drug networks, conducting raids and taking legal action against those involved in the narcotics trade. According to ANI, Chennithala stated, "Operation Care, launched as part of Operation Toofan, aims to rehabilitate people addicted to drugs and help them return to normal life." He added, "Necessary facilities have been arranged at 35 hospitals to support the initiative." Operation Toofan, officially called 'Operation Toofan: The Narco Hunt', is a statewide anti-drug campaign launched by the Kerala government on June 2. The initiative is being implemented by the state Home Department and Kerala Police, in coordination with departments including Health and Excise. Its primary objective is to dismantle drug trafficking networks, curb the supply of narcotic substances, prevent the spread of synthetic drugs such as MDMA and protect young people from substance abuse. The campaign also seeks public participation in identifying drug-related activities and strengthening awareness about addiction. The November 16 rollout will place greater emphasis on the rehabilitation and recovery of people affected by drug addiction. The government believes that enforcement measures and arrests alone cannot address the drug problem. Providing treatment, counselling and rehabilitation is also necessary to help people overcome substance dependence and prevent them from returning to drug use. Chennithala said the state had already brought the issue of alleged loopholes in the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act to the attention of Union Home Minister Amit Shah. "There were instances of accused persons being released from prison due to certain loopholes in the NDPS Act. The issue had been brought to the attention of the Union Home Minister, and the state had conveyed the need for amendments to the Act," ANI quoted him as saying. The minister further said the Union Home Minister had called for collective efforts to launch a mass movement against drug abuse. "That is exactly what we are doing," Chennithala said. The upcoming Toofan Care initiative will use the 35 hospitals prepared across Kerala to provide treatment and rehabilitation facilities to people struggling with addiction. The focus will be on helping affected individuals access medical assistance, de-addiction services and support to resume their everyday lives. The initiative is significant because it expands the campaign beyond policing and prosecution to address the health and social consequences of substance abuse. Kerala's government has also been working towards involving local communities, families, educational institutions and health workers in identifying people who may need early intervention. The campaign comes amid concerns over drug trafficking and substance abuse in Kerala. According to National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data cited by ANI, Kerala recorded 30,697 cases under the NDPS Act in 2023, the highest number among Indian states. The scale of the problem has prompted the state to combine enforcement with prevention, awareness and rehabilitation. The first phase primarily focused on enforcement, including raids, investigations, arrests and action against drug distribution networks, particularly around educational institutions. Kerala Police had registered 10,070 cases and arrested 10,883 people under the campaign by September. The police also seized 23,438.746 grams of MDMA, 1,214.354 kg of ganja and 4,738.269 grams of hashish oil. The campaign also conducted 9,529 awareness classes and 649 counselling sessions across the state. AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a 6% growth in its net profit to ₹71.7 Cr in the quarter ended September (Q2 FY27) from ₹67.7 Cr a year earlier. On a sequential basis, net profit declined 15.4% from ₹84.8 Cr. Meanwhile, its operating revenue grew 46.5% YoY and 7.4% QoQ to ₹287.9 Cr during the quarter under review. Including other income of ₹2.8 Cr, total income during the quarter stood at ₹290.7 Cr. The fintech company’s operating EBITDA, excluding other income, grew just 3% YoY to ₹9.9 Cr. This came as its total expenses rose 49.4% YoY and 7.7% QoQ to ₹282.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, outpacing the growth in operating revenue. At the same time, its consolidated net revenue, after accounting for payment processing and other costs, declined 1% YoY to ₹151.3 Cr in Q2 FY27. AvenuesAI attributed the decline to its ‘competitive pricing strategy’ amid efforts to deepen merchant relationships and increase transaction volumes. As a result, its net take rate moderated 4% to 5.06 bps despite a 19% sequential increase in its total payments volume to ₹1.77 Lakh Cr. The company generated ₹282.2 Cr in revenue from its payment business, which includes its CCAvenue payment gateway, payment infrastructure services to banks (CPGS), and credit and lending-related services, accounting for nearly 98% of its operating revenue during the quarter. The remaining ₹5.7 Cr was derived from its ecommerce platform business, Rediff. AvenuesAI Looks To Unlock Value Across Subsidiaries Alongside its financial performance, AvenuesAI outlined its plans to expand its AI capabilities, with advanced technology development and AI software-related work remaining among the key objectives of its rights issue. In June last year, the company had raised ₹700 Cr via a rights issue, primarily for the repayment of outstanding loans, expansion of its IPO-bound digital content and ecommerce marketplace Rediff and further investments in its AI arm, Nueromind, for which it had earmarked ₹294 Cr. Almost 42.7%, or ₹297.2 Cr, of the net proceeds remained unutilised at the end of the September quarter. AvenuesAI has now announced that it will directly utilise the funds for AI development and software-related activities instead of routing the investment through Nueromind. It clarified that the change was limited to the mode of implementation, with no alteration to the end use of the proceeds. In the June quarter, AvenuesAI announced plans to amalgamate Nueromind with itself, subject to NCLT approval. It is also developing its Transaction Intelligence Score (TISco), an AI-led initiative that will use permitted transaction and merchant-behaviour signals for risk assessment, fraud prevention, merchant intelligence and financial services workflows. The company aims to use its transaction infrastructure to build an intelligence layer that can support merchant and enterprise services. On the investment front, AvenuesAI said it made investments in two financial services companies during the September quarter. It acquired a stake of up to 7% in Online PSB Loans Limited for a consideration of up to ₹65 Cr. It also invested up to ₹34.5 Cr to acquire a stake of up to 1.38% in Ratnaafin Capital Private Limited. The company also reiterated its plans to expand CCAvenue's international payments business, particularly in the US, by leveraging its payment technology, enterprise relationships and regulated infrastructure. Meanwhile, its ecommerce arm, Rediff, is on its way to the bourses for a separate listing. After filing for an IPO confidentially earlier this year, the markets regulator SEBI approved the draft papers in August. However, the Q2 disclosure did not provide an update on Rediff's proposed IPO. As per sources, Rediff would look to raise in between ₹600-800 Cr via the IPO AvenuesAI outlined that unlocking value from Rediff is one of its three strategic priorities for FY27. It plans to integrate Rediff's consumer and enterprise digital ecosystem with its payments and AI capabilities. This includes RediffOne, which offers digital commerce and communication services, and RediffPay, which is intended to expand consumer payment engagement. AvenuesAI has maintained its FY27 consolidated revenue guidance of ₹1,100-1,300 Cr. The company said its focus for the remainder of FY27 will remain on expanding merchant relationships, improving operating discipline and creating additional monetisation opportunities through Rediff, enterprise technology and applied AI. It is also monitoring potential changes to the merchant discount rate (MDR) policy for eligible UPI transactions, with any introduction, timing or scope remaining subject to government and regulatory decisions. Shares of AvenueAI ended today’s trading session 3.72% lower at ₹129.25.

The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) morning, while many parts of the city reeled under “severe” level of air pollution, according to official data.
Many parts of the city, including ITO, Dwarka, Rohini, Punjabi Bagh, Alipur, Bawana, and Jahangirpuri witnessed “severe” level air pollution.
Other cities and towns in north India, including Noida, Gurugram, and Panipat also witnessed “very poor” air quality, on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) morning.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi was 379 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), as per Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
“Severe” level air pollution affects healthy people and seriously impacts those with existing diseases, as per the CPCB.
The overall air quality of Delhi is likely to be in the “very poor” category for three days, as per the Central government’s ‘Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi’.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 350 (very poor) at 4 p.m. on Tuesday, up from 324 (very poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI.
A higher AQI means worsening of air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

(Bloomberg) -- Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered changes to the curriculum at US senior service colleges, arguing that future admirals and generals need an education more focused on winning wars than academic theories.
“The only question that matters to the American republic is this: Will it help us achieve victory?” Hegseth said. “To be sure, there are plenty of other important considerations in military life: Ethics, logistics, administration, diplomacy. But all of them are in service of victory.”
Hegseth announced his plans during a speech at the Naval War College in Newport, Rhode Island, where he said an 18-month review by his office had revealed “a stubborn undercurrent of passive-aggressive institutional resistance” to the changes pushed by the Trump administration.
The embattled Pentagon chief made the announcement as he faces an impeachment effort in the House, and after Democrats pledged to investigate his leadership once they assume control of the House and Senate in January.
There are also growing bipartisan calls for President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth, though the president and other cabinet officials have publicly voiced support for him.
“My team, we’re not worried about the noise,” Hegseth told reporters in Rhode Island. “There’s partisan noise all over our town. We’re focused on delivering the president’s agenda.”
Implementing Hegseth’s desired changes may take time. Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata is to “issue supplemental implementation guidance as necessary” and convene relevant officials “no less than every 60 days” to track progress and address any obstacles. The memo directs the service secretaries to provide reports to Tata.
Among other changes, Tata is tasked with finding alternatives to existing external accreditation bodies for the schools.
The changes apply to institutions that provide professional military education to mid-career and senior officers, including the Air War College, Army War College, Marine Corps War College, National War College, Naval War College, and the Dwight D. Eisenhower School for National Security and Resource Strategy.
Also covered are the Intermediate Level Education institutions such as the Army’s Command and General Staff College, the Air Force’s Air Command and Staff College, the College of Naval Command and Staff and the Marine Corps Command and Staff College, as well as joint programs at the Joint Forces Staff College and National Intelligence University.
Monday’s move is the latest in Hegseth’s effort to overhaul the military educational system, which has included banning books discussing race and gender from Defense Department-run schools on military bases, and directing the service academies to eliminate tenure for civilian instructors.
“Our senior service colleges must cease producing theorists whose very first experience integrating the strategic, operational and tactical realms occurs when they step into a theater of war,” he said in his remarks.
Hegseth said he plans to shift the curriculum to emphasize not just military strategy, but execution, and to ensure that the majority of instructors have relevant military experience, including civilian faculty. He also directed war colleges to administer wargames or other comprehensive exams.

A deportation flight carrying eight Iranian nationals was abruptly canceled on an Arizona tarmac
A U.S. deportation flight of at least eight Iranian nationals who were eventually bound for Iran has been abruptly canceled

Eight Iranian nationals were put on a plane in Mesa, Arizona, on Sunday morning for a deportation flight that was meant to take them first to the country of Georgia and then on to Pakistan.
The flight was canceled without explanation, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees and who spoke to some of those slated for repatriation.
Rahnama said a senior official from the Iranian Interests Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, visited the eight detainees who boarded the plane.
Those detainees were told that the Iranian government would transport them from Pakistan to Iran, he said.
Court documents unsealed days ago in a civil lawsuit filed by the fund showed the Trump administration, as recently as mid-October, said it had plans to deport the Iranians to Iran, even as the war there drags on, via an unnamed third country.
The lawsuit was filed in July and alleges that the U.S. government illegally shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the U.S. with Iranian officials.
The administration did not specify in the October court records when it would carry out the deportations.
But in the past week, roughly a dozen Iranian nationals in immigration detention said they were notified that they were scheduled for an upcoming deportation flight to Pakistan and then to Iran, according to numerous attorneys who have since confirmed those plans with DHS.
Three deportation flights to Iran occurred between September 2025 and January 2026, with over 100 Iranian nationals deported.
The administration's confirmation of the new plans amid the war that began in February highlights its resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees.
In response to questions Sunday from The Associated Press, the press office of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security provided a statement attributed to an unnamed spokesperson that said Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not comment on “prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details,” nor would the agency confirm future removal operations.
“As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history,” the statement said.
In the litigation brought by the Iranian immigrant advocacy group, at least a dozen Iranian detainees have said they've been contacted by Iranian officials who had knowledge of sensitive information on their asylum claims.
U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes, a nominee of President Joe Biden, has not ruled on the claims.
She ordered the U.S. government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
In a court filing Sunday, the defense fund laid out what it had learned about plans for a removal flight that day and argued that the administration may have violated the judge's directive to give advance notice of deportation plans.
Later Sunday, the government filed court documents in the case, but they were sealed and inaccessible to the public.
The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund has called for a halt to the removal flights, saying in a news release that they would “reportedly mark the first deportation of Iranians to Iran since the U.S.-Iran war began.”
The group's executive director, Yasmin Chubin, said in a statement Sunday that it was difficult to comprehend why the U.S. would forcibly deport Iranians, including asylum seekers, to Iran, amid ongoing military hostilities.
The consequences of removal, Chubin said, “could be irreversible and individuals may face persecution, torture, or death.”
At least one person who had been part of the scuttled flight volunteered to go back to Iran after nearly two years of detention, Rahnama said, out of desperation to leave what he described as inhumane imprisonment.
It's unclear how many other deportees may have volunteered to leave.

Some Roku OS users have been sad to learn that their favorite screensaver will no longer be available as of December 1.
This week, affected users reported receiving an alert on their device that they will not be able to use the “Aquatic Life” screensaver after this month, as first reported by Cord Cutters News.
The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing.
Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn’t be renewing Roku’s license.
“I can’t be part of the Fox world,” he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News’ controversial style of news and entertainment.
Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements, according to the user notice.
The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS .
“When my head is in overdrive (very often with my ADHD), this screensaver grounds me and lets me exhale and become focused with myself again. It may sound over the top, but it’s true. It takes a lot for me to chill and relax, but this Aquatic Life [screensaver] is my go to. Totally gutted 😢,” a Reddit user wrote this week.
