Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.
Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying
The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.
At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.
And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.
There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.
The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.
When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

Technology share prices clawed back last week's sharp losses on Monday (November 9, 2026), despite a plunge in Nvidia following a probe into its boss Jensen Huang over claims of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Oil prices fell over 5% on hopes for diplomatic talks aimed at ending the U.S.-Iran war, before paring losses.
Chipmakers and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence boom took a hammering in the days after last Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep both chambers of Congress, leading to speculation lawmakers would seek to rein in tech firms.
But Wall Street on Monday (November 9, 2026) rebounded, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing more than 2%.
Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare said the rebound in equities was due to more than just the drop in oil prices.
"What we also have this morning is an inclination to buy into last week's weakness, and specifically into the large losses seen in the AI trade," he said in a note to clients.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which includes major chipmakers and AI firms, jumped more than 6%.
But the gains did not extend to Nvidia, which saw its shares slump more than 8% as trading got under way in New York, but recovered to stand down more than 5% in early afternoon trading.
Mr. O'Hare said Nvidia was being treated as a one-off story by investors for the moment.
"In other words, the stock is being penalized for Jensen Huang's personal transgression, which has invited a great deal of uncertainty into the mix, but the market isn't caught up in the notion that this situation is going to have a systemic domino effect," he said.
The news that Nvidia's board would investigate whether Mr. Huang had been targeted in a foreign espionage plot, following his admission he was unfaithful to his wife, brought fresh uncertainty in the markets.
The New York Times last month reported that U.S. intelligence officials concluded a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed had been funnelling information to Beijing.
The executive, Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Mr. Jensen Huang — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said.
In a message to company employees released to media on Sunday (November 8, 2026), Mr. Huang acknowledged having an affair and apologised to his family and company staff.
Nvidia is a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models and one of the world's most valuable companies, and last year became the first to reach a market capitalisation of $5 trillion.
Technology analyst Dan Ives, at the investment bank Yorkville Ives, said the crisis would at the very least spark congressional inquiries and "create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons".
China on Monday (November 9, 2026) said the claims that it had spied on Mr. Huang were "baseless".
Europe's main stock markets rose following gains across much of Asia.
The dollar fell against its main rivals.
Oil prices continued to slide as Iran and the United States continued talking instead of fighting.
"Two month lows in oil have done much to bolster bruised sentiment in global markets, and the admittedly small signs of progress in peace talks adds to downward move," said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at online trading and investing platform IG.

When was the last time you had to call customer support with a problem? Can you remember how it went?
You’re going to hate shopping in an AI economy
Why AI agents will make the “rage economy” worse.
If you’re like most Americans, the answer is “probably not very well.” And that may be understating it: As of 2025, according to the “National Customer Rage Survey” — yes, it’s a real thing — nearly 80 percent of Americans ran into a “product or service problem” in the past year, and nearly two-thirds experienced “rage” in attempting to resolve it.
We have, in short, entered into a rage economy, where high prices and inflation have made everyday products unaffordable at the same time as our experiences buying those products have filled us with fury.
The landscape isn’t really improving, either: As a consumer, you’re faced with terrible customer service, unhelpful chatbots, and products that are worse than they used to be.
If you listen to the big AI companies, however, there’s a light on the horizon: AI agents, which can step in and do the things you don’t want to (like waiting on hold or dueling it out with aforementioned unhelpful chatbots). But are AI agents really the key to fixing our rage economy? Or will they just be what brings it deeper into chaos?
Charlie Warzel, a staff writer at The Atlantic, recently went deep on what happens when we bring AI agents into our already contentious consumer experience (along with his colleague Matteo Wong).
Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Warzel about how AI agents are being used for the grating parts of our lives, what happens when companies use their own AI agents to deal with consumers, and where this all might leave us.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Charlie, we spoke about how the economy and how customer service works is making everyone rage out. Are AI agents going to make it better or worse?
In the early time, it’s probably going to make it a lot worse. What we are essentially seeing right now is that these agents are inundating the internet with persistence.
These are relentless things that are tasked to do the onerous activities that we don’t want to do. And they’re already flooding call centers. They’re flooding restaurant reservations. They’re flooding plumbers and people who run small businesses with requests and queries. And they’re not people.
It’s going to make a lot of people feel, honestly, pretty awful. The world has all of a sudden become very inhuman or there are these inhuman burdens being put on the humans who don’t have agents yet to work on their behalf. And that imbalance is going to make a lot of people pretty mad.
You wrote for The Atlantic that we are not ready for our coming AI agent future. How are we not ready for this?
If it reaches a critical mass, the argument is that we aren’t ready for it because the economy is built off of, and in a lot of ways thrives off of, inefficiency — off of the fact that people aren’t paying perfect attention to everything.
People aren’t moving their money from savings account to savings account every day because they’re getting the margins on a slightly better interest rate or something like that. This entire subscription economy is based off of inefficiency. You don’t cancel the thing that you don’t use for a long period of time or it lays dormant for a while.
But what these AI agents offer in their most idealized fashion is that they pay perfect attention to everything, all the time. They are hypervigilant and able to act on your behalf in inhuman ways. And if a large portion of the population is using these to do their banking, to do their e-commerce, and at the same time you have these large organizations like banks, healthcare companies, platforms like Amazon and Walmart, you’re going to see just incredible amounts of chaos.
The economy would, in that way, start to behave more like the stock market, where prices fluctuate on the order of milliseconds. And from watching the stock market over decades, I don’t know if we want diapers to behave like securities.
One of the more speculative but also illustrative ideas here is what people refer to as an agentic bank run. This is the idea that, say, 5 million people are using the same agent to do all of their banking and they all identify at the same time that there is a high-yield savings account that everyone should be in. So they move money en masse: millions of agents pulling money out of one account to the next, and then those banks are struggling because they’ve just lost all of these deposits at once. It’s theoretically possible that something like that could happen all of the time.
Is this a two-way street? Are the companies also adopting agents into every part of their processes and consumer relations?
Yes. It’s slower on that end, but I like to think of this as an arms race.
A lot of retailers, especially Amazon, have blocked a number of these agents from accessing their platform. Because even though Amazon can make good money off of these sales, they don’t yet want these companies to have access to their backend infrastructure.
There are a lot of corporate secrets like inventory and who’s buying what and who’s selling what. These agents can act as really good intelligence gatherers if they’re granted access to these platforms.
What you’ll see eventually is that the retailers are going to have demands: “You guys can let the agents on the platform, but you can’t undercut our prices in this way.” It will just be something that you have to trust that your AI agent company is making a deal in your best interest.
I think that that’s really interesting because you could end up having this future where everything feels really good as a consumer because it’s frictionless: “My agent’s going to do all this stuff for me while I sleep or while I’m hanging out with my family or whatnot.” And in reality, what’s going to happen is you’re just having someone do something for you, but nothing else has really changed. You’re not getting a better deal. It’s not that much more helpful to you because these companies have taken care of themselves first.
But that is the promise. That is what Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg are trying to sell us.
Do you think it’s a pipe dream or do you think there is some reality, one day, when we as a society will say, “This consumer-facing AI agent world of ours is better than the one we had a hundred years ago”?
Something that I think is really funny is Meta, with Muse, has really dominated the conversation about these AI assistants. And this is the company that wanted to connect the world, that says that us being together is this universal good, it is strengthening the bonds of humanity.
This is a tool that is fundamentally antisocial. You don’t have to interact with those people if you don’t want to. I’m not trying to romanticize running really annoying errands when you’re busy and your kids are sick and you’ve got work deadlines and things, but there’s also the experience of interacting with people on a day-to-day basis that is foundational to our humanity and these things basically want to automate that away.
That’s a real thing that we need to think about and grapple with. And the other part of this is, what are we freeing this time up for?
I’m always wondering that myself, because that’s what they keep promising. You’re going to have so much time…to do what? To then just spend more time scrolling your platforms?
To spend more time scrolling your platforms, spend more time working. There is a lack of thought about what a human is for if we fully embrace automation in all these different ways, right? It’s one thing to say, “I wish it was easier to buy paper towels on Amazon.” It’s another to say—
It’s pretty easy, though. I don’t do it that often, but I’m pretty sure it’s really easy.
It is. I think it’s good to have those interactions and it’s okay to sand down some of them, but this future suggests, what if you never had to do anything you didn’t want to do? And I don’t know if they’ve thought that through.

Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died aged 54 after recently announcing deteriorating health.
The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, led the tributes on Tuesday morning, saying his thoughts were with Russell’s loved ones.
“Vale Todd Russell,” Rockliff wrote on social media.
“Thoughts this morning are with Todd’s loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him.”
The disaster sparked global headlines and became a rallying event for the nation in 2006 after a minor earthquake sparked a collapse at the Beaconsfield goldmine.
The event killed miner Larry Knight, with fears Russell and his co-worker, Brant Webb, were also entombed by thousands of tonnes of rock and debris.
But rescuers used thermal imaging cameras and found the pair alive five days later, trapped in a safety cage almost a kilometre.
The men had survived on a shared cereal bar and water that seeped through the rock, before meals were able to be passed down to them through a pipe.
A major technical rescue effort to free the pair was launched, and they ultimately walked free after two weeks underground, throwing their hands into the air before embracing their loved ones.
In 2025, Russell announced he had started treatment in hospital for an undisclosed illness.
Earlier in November, he announced he would return home to “see out his days” with friends and family.
“After years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles, plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give,” he posted on social media.
‘Stopped a nation’
The Beaconsfield disaster was “two weeks that stopped a nation,” Rockliff wrote on social media on Tuesday. “But Todd didn’t let it define him. He continued to serve proudly at the Beaconsfield fire brigade until February this year, an exemplary 31-year career of community service.
Russell told the ABC’s I Was Actually There podcast in 2024 he had struggled with his mental health and relationships after the disaster, saying he had developed PTSD.
“I needed a reality check, which [my then wife] Carolyn gave me, to go and seek the help that I needed from the right people [about] the PTSD and the depression,” he said at the time. “There are days that are good days, there’s days that are bad days and there’s days that trigger little things.
“I’m continuously trying to rebuild that relationship [with my kids]. I’ve got a one-year-old granddaughter. She’s absolutely beautiful, so I’ve got that to focus on now.”
Rockliff praised Russell for sharing his story on Tuesday.
“He told his story, and became an advocate for mental health,” the premier wrote, “and made the community around him a better place.”

Homes and temples glow across India as Diwali celebrations begin
- Published
Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.
The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.
Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.
But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.
Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.
In the capital, Delhi, the air quality index (AQI) reached 391 on Friday morning, placing it in the "very poor" category ahead of the festival. There are fears that pollution levels could rise further after the celebrations.
India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks, with its AQI reaching 322 on 24 October. Although air quality has improved in recent days to reach "moderate" levels of 104 on Friday, there are concerns that Diwali fireworks could trigger another spike.
In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.
These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% less emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are in reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.
Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.
The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil.
In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.
The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.
Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.
The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.
The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.
The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.
The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.
The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.
Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.
For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.
With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.
The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali auspicious. Known as known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.
Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has reportedly requested a new passport and identity card ahead of her previously announced return to her home country in December. According to Reuters, Hasina, who has been living in self-imposed exile in India since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024, requested new documents on Monday.
“In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the Interim Government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card for our client,” Hasina's lawyers at London-based Matrix Chambers wrote to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at Bangladesh's embassy in Delhi, Reuters reported.

The letter asked for the applications to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with "obligations arising under international human rights instruments".
Sheikh Hasina to return to Bangladesh
In July, Hasina, who is facing a death sentence, had made her intention to return to the country she ruled for nearly two decades. While no date has been formally set, Hasina’s aides told Reuters on Monday that it will be announced once various formalities are completed.
Earlier, on Sunday, Bangladesh’s Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman reiterated his country's demand that ‘convicted criminal’ Hasina should be extradited, and added that the extradition request is already with New Delhi.
"To me, she is a criminal. A criminal convicted by our tribunal. To us, this is her identity," he said, according to a report on bdnews24.
Asked about bringing Hasina back to Bangladesh, the law minister said the government would act in accordance with the law and would not be guided by emotion.

"Although the Law Ministry is not directly involved in this matter, the Ministry of Home Affairs is concerned, as it relates to the extradition treaty with India. The matter will be dealt with in accordance with the law, leaving no room for emotions. We have requested her repatriation under the treaty and through due process," Asaduzzaman was quoted as saying by the state-run BSS news agency.
Sheikh Hasina faces death penalty
In November 2025, the International Crimes Tribunal convicted her of crimes against humanity. The charges relate to the July and August 2024 uprising. The tribunal sentenced her to death.
Her party, the Awami League, was the country's largest before it was banned following her fall. Many of her party colleagues have either been jailed or are in self-imposed exile in India or elsewhere.

A shipment of Nvidia hardware valued at $11.4 million vanished in transport between Oakland and Texas over the summer, and more than two months later, police have announced no arrests or recovery of the cargo.
As reported by The Mercury News, six pallets of unknown Nvidia equipment left Oakland on August 29 on a truck bound for Fort Worth, Texas. The hardware was reportedly picked up as scheduled by a truck bearing the logo of a food transportation company before vanishing off the grid. The theft wasn’t noticed until early September, when the buyers realized that the shipment had never been received. Police attempting to trace the truck’s route found it had made several multi-hour stops after picking up the hardware before losing the truck somewhere in San Bernardino County, California.
Oakland police confirmed that there was a grand theft report filed on September 13 and that the investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not said what Nvidia hardware was stolen or exactly how the theft was carried out.
The theft in Oakland is the latest in a wave of increasingly bold hardware heists. As Ars’ Ashley Belanger reported recently, thieves have made off with more than $100 million in similar shipments since June. According to investigators cited by NBC News, the criminals have shown planning and sophistication by employing techniques like GPS location spoofing and even arranging collisions with police escort vehicles. Stolen components can be stripped down and sold in gray-market transactions or shipped overseas where access to US tech hardware may be restricted.

Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week
Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass but conviction appears unlikely.
WASHINGTON: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war.
William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress.
US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday (Nov 9), setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power.
Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.
"They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment," he told a press conference.
Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with President Donald Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.
US President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military's performance in Iran and Venezuela: "Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him."
House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see”.
Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections, intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as “courageous and historic”.
Accused of taking huge kickbacks, Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, “burst into tears”. The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of the required two-thirds majority.
By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight.
HEGSETH SAYS HE IS NOT WORRIED
Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: "It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."
Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: "We're not worried about that." He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push "unfair," telling reporters: "I think Pete's done a good job. I really do."
Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth's performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where the US military deposed that country's president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital.
"Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, where we fought forever and nothing happened?" Trump asked.
DEFENCE SPENDING AT RISK?
Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package.
Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January.
"They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," Massie said.
Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a "hard yes" on a measure to impeach Hegseth.
US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial.
"Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting," he said.
Massie's articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanours" ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat.
Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was "punishable by DEATH!"

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."

After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.

Addressing social media debates over the scientific validity of Temple's eponymous brain-monitoring wearable, founder Deepinder Goyal issued a statement directed at “Concerned Indian Doctors”, asserting confidence in the R&D behind the wearables. Goyal pointed out that Temple had already spent $30 Mn on its development, including $20 Mn of his personal money. He also noted that the company is raising funding from its employees and customers. “Selling a few thousand devices recovers a small fraction of this investment. A scam that pays nothing is not a scam anyone would run,” the CEO wrote in his post. Goyal further said the product’s 14-day no-questions-asked return policy would validate its product in the market. On questions over Temple’s credibility and scientific validation, he argued that many wearable makers initially relied on internal studies before publishing external validation. He said the company would release pre-prints before peer-reviewed publications and it expects independent studies to emerge once the device becomes available more widely. In a follow-up post, Goyal also said, “Temple is a fitness tracker, and wellness device. We are not a medical device,” adding that the device hasn’t been clinically validated. Important to highlight that pre-orders for the wearable officially opened on November 1, with a hefty listing price of ₹85,000. Units are hand-made to order and expected to begin shipping roughly three months after purchase, starting in early 2027. What Doctors Say About Temple? For context, several medical experts had criticised Temple over its claim that a wearable sensor placed near the temple can reliably measure cerebral blood flow. Hepatologist Dr Cyriac Abby Philips, popularly known as The Liver Doc, published an Instagram carousel calling the product “the biggest health scam and wellness fraud in India,” saying the device can only detect when blood rushes to one’s face. Gurugram-based gastroenterologist Dr Zubin Sharma also noted that blood flows to the brain via arteries in the neck and back of head, not the temple. Additionally, many on social media pointed out that studies published on Temple’s website were not peer-reviewed, and were funded and conducted by the company itself. They also raised questions about the validity of Goyal’s Gravity Ageing Hypothesis, which links the long-term effects of gravity on blood circulation to ageing. In fact, Dr Philips doubled down on the criticism of Temple in a reply to Goyal's latest post, calling out Temple's claims of reading blood flow to the brain and the company's explanation of its proprietary 'Entropy' score. The Temple Journey So Far Goyal’s move into brain-monitoring wearables has been taking shape through a series of bets on longevity research. This began with his personal research initiative Continue Research, which he referred to as his personal health and wellness venture back in 2024. The initiative remained largely under wraps for over a year before unveiling its first hypothesis, Gravity Ageing, in November 2025. The hypothesis proposed that gravity's effect on cerebral blood flow (CBF) could be an overlooked contributor to human ageing. Temple emerged around the same time as a commercial extension of this research. Inc42 first reported in November 2025 that Goyal was exploring a wearable device company focused on health monitoring. The device, which he had been seen wearing near his temple, was being used experimentally to measure blood flow to the brain in real time. “I left the Eternal CEO role to chase purpose with Temple. This is not about money. I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck,” Goyal said. On the product front, Temple has been developing a wearable that sits on the forehead near the temple and tracks signals associated with cerebral blood flow. Goyal revealed a smaller version of the device in August, claiming it was less than half the size of its earlier iteration. It has worked with contract manufacturers Zetwerk and Ethereal Machines to scale production, while retaining some manufacturing capabilities in-house. The startup began taking shape as a standalone venture earlier this year. In February, Temple raised $54 Mn (around ₹493 Cr) in a seed funding round at a post-money valuation of approximately $190 Mn. The round was led by Goyal, who invested a little over ₹100 Cr, with participation from Steadview Capital, Peak XV Partners, Vy Capital, Info Edge Ventures, among others. More than 30 employees also participated in the round. Temple subsequently expanded its ambitions beyond hardware. In July 2026, it acquired London-based longevity medicine practice Longevous for an undisclosed amount, bringing clinical and scientific expertise into the business.

The next time someone tells you that artificial intelligence, or any other new technology, is going to cure every disease, point them to the effort to fight heart attacks and strokes, which together are the largest killer in the developed world.
Because again and again, pharmaceutical researchers have learned the same hard lesson: technologies that were supposed to speed new medicines to patients have fallen short. Two studies presented Saturday at the annual meeting of the American Heart Association are a perfect example. A new understanding of genetics was supposed to increase the odds of success – and did anything but.
One study showed that a Novartis drug, pelacarsen, had no effect on the rate of heart attacks and strokes despite lowering a substance in the blood called lp(a), which genetics said should reduce cardiovascular risk. Another large study, from Novo Nordisk, of an anti-inflammatory targeting a protein called IL-6 also showed no benefit.

4 of family, including 2 children, killed in Odisha fire; short circuit suspected: Cops
The cause of the fire is yet to be ascertained, though a short circuit is suspected, the police said.
Four members of a family, including two children aged 11 years and eight months, were burnt alive in a fire that broke out in their house in Odisha’s Jajpur district, police said on Sunday.
The incident occurred around 8pm on Saturday, at Sk Nizam Uddin’s residence in Nalipur village under Badachana block of Jajpur district. The cause of the fire is yet to be ascertained, though a short circuit is suspected, the police said.
According to local resident Ajay Kumar Samal, Nizamuddin arrived from Gopalpur on Saturday with his daughter and grandchildren. "The fire broke out when his elder daughter-in-law was cooking. His daughter, daughter-in-law and the two children died in the incident," Samal said.
On being informed, fire services personnel from Chandikhol and Balichandrapur police rushed to the spot and launched firefighting and rescue operations.
The deceased were identified as Nizamuddin's daughter Gul Afsa Parveen (26), daughter-in-law Tabassum Parveen (40), granddaughter Roshni Parveen (11) and an eight-month-old grandson, Jajpur Superintendent of Police (SP) Yashpratap Shrimal said.
A youth sustained serious burn injuries in the incident. He was initially admitted to the Badachana Community Health Centre but later shifted to Cuttack after his condition deteriorated.

The countertop kitchen composter is a lovely thought. Instead of a smelly bucket of vegetable scraps and coffee grounds breeding fruit flies on your counter or attracting rats to your backyard, you could just put it all into a nifty electric gadget. Then, at some undetermined point in the future, you'll have a bountiful supply of nutrient-rich compost to use in your garden.
Unfortunately, none of the more popular electric kitchen composters do exactly this. Though some of these devices are marketed as “composters” and include instruction booklets and companion apps detailing the many ways to use compost, most will only grind up and dry your food scraps. You will greatly reduce your food waste output, and it will no longer smell, but if you’re hoping to put eggshells and banana peels into a machine and magically scoop out the kind of compost you’d buy at the garden center, that’s just not going to happen.
That said, you can mix small amounts of these grounds into potting soil in tiny ratios or use them as a feeder for a “real” compost pile. But again, most of these machines are meant for reducing the volume of household food waste. This is, itself, a legitimate goal, as cast-off food makes up an estimated 24 percent of municipal solid waste, resulting in the release of methane, a destructive greenhouse gas, as it breaks down in the landfill.
Or maybe you'd just like your food grounds to be odor-free and shelf-stable before adding them to your green waste bin for municipal composting or your backyard compost. In any case, despite critics’ cries of greenwashing and corporate astroturfing, there is indeed value to these devices. They make people more aware of their food waste. They don't use a huge amount of power (around 1 kilowatt-hour was typical in my testing). And my top pick, the Reencle Essential (8/10, WIRED Recommends), even produces something close to compost.

Best Overall
As I mentioned above, none of these machines makes truly ready-to-use, biologically stable, fully decomposed compost, but Reencle comes closest to creating what you'd scoop out of a traditional compost bin or pile. Popular in South Korea years before it appeared in the US, Reencle machines arrive with a starter bag of Reencle Compost Starter (which you can purchase separately for $52) containing activated carbon, wood pellets, glucose, and a trio of patented thermophilic microbes ready to chow down. There's also a prefilled charcoal filter that slots into the back.
The Essential is Reencle’s newest—and least expensive—model, with a refreshed, contemporary exterior; controls on the front instead of the top; and a lid that opens and closes manually. It's too large for a kitchen counter, but it conveniently operates much like a heated trash can. The lid opens via a manual button on the top of the unit, and in goes your organic matter. That's it. There are no cycles, tablets, or auxiliary buckets to worry about, and the cycle is barely louder than a refrigerator fan—about 28 decibels. Within hours to days, depending on the item, the scraps break down into a material resembling a cross between dirt and sawdust.
The smell isn't always pleasant, but you can usually mitigate this with the control panel's Dry and Purify buttons or by adding what, in composting lexicon, is called “browns”—dry, carbon-rich materials, like bread or shredded paper. The Reencle also tends not to stink when you feed it its preferred diet of 1.5 to 2.2 pounds of scraps per day. Unlike other machines, it can also accept meat and dairy.
When the volume reaches the fill line, it’s time to scoop out the grounds. At this point, you can mix the grounds with potting soil at a 1:4 ratio and leave it to cure for three weeks. (I used a large tub in my garage for this step.) Afterward, you can use it for both outdoor and indoor plants. I’ve used the resultant mix to positive effect both indoors and outdoors.

The Prime is Reencle’s original flagship model. It's pretty much identical to the new Essential, but with the controls on the top instead of on the front, plus a convenient sensor-activated auto-open and -close lid. The entire top also hinges open, making it easier to scoop out the grounds for curing. It's only about an inch taller than the Essential but accepts the same 2.2 pounds of kitchen scraps per day.
I found its fan noise to be slightly less intrusive than the Essential above, despite both units measuring at 28 decibels. It’s ultimately up to you if this, plus the auto-close lid, feels worthy of spending an extra $100. (I did like the latter feature very much.)
Also worth noting is that one of the stirring paddles broke off my Prime after a year and a half of daily use. I contacted Reencle to ask what customers should do in this situation. I learned that if the Reencle is within the warranty period (two years for units purchased on or after May 13, 2026; one year for units purchased previously), they can contact customer service to receive a paddle repair kit at no charge. If you need a larger capacity: For larger households, there's also the Reencle Gravity ($649), which is Reencle's largest unit by both dimensions and capacity. It can accept 3.3 pounds of waste a day and sports the same convenient sensor-activated lid as the Prime. When I tested it last year, I found it to be significantly quieter than both the Prime and the Essential—not that either is noticeably loud, but the Gravity is nearly silent. I did, however, find that over time, the Gravity contents went anaerobic (read: smelly) much faster than with the Prime. The increased volume seemed to retain more moisture. If you go with a Gravity, I recommend keeping plenty of browns (old bread, shredded paper) on hand to maintain microbial balance or adding in a few more sessions of manual stirring per day with the included shovel.

Best Grind-and-Dry Food Recycler
Most kitchen “composters" simply grind and dry your food scraps, but the Lomi 3 countertop composter does the best job of this of the bunch. I'm always impressed when companies listen to feedback and adapt, and Lomi's most updated model solves a couple of the quirks found on the now-discontinued Lomi 2: Gone are the multiple modes, the annoying twist-off lid, and the need to put scraps right into the machine. Now there's a convenient 3-liter, 7.5-inch-tall countertop bucket, just like the FoodCycler below; an easy push-button lid; and Grow and Express modes. The Lomi 3 is also smaller and supposedly quieter than the Lomi 2, but my decibel meter found the difference to be negligible. One feature I did like on Lomi 2 that's missing from the 3, however, is Lomi mode, which could break down a list of approved bioplastics, including Lomi's own packaging. Lomi confirms the new model cannot accept bioplastics.
Like with the Lomi 2, there's a companion app for basic management, but I enjoyed not having to use it; simply press an on-device button, and the Lomi starts. When it's done (cycle lengths vary from three to 16 hours, depending on the amount and moisture level of its contents), it will play a little chime, and you can either put the processed grounds—which are very fine and look like Folgers—in your outdoor compost pile, top-dress your lawn with them, or add them to soil at a 1:10 ratio (1:15 if using meat or dairy). I also like that the Lomi 3 has a clear lid, so you can see exactly where it is in its cycle.
It's a lot to pay for what's essentially a grinder-and-dryer, which is why I generally recommend the Reencle above, especially if you want to generate something close to compost. However, for those simply looking to reduce their waste output, or who live in an area that's subject to composting fines, the Lomi 3 is a thoughtfully engineered, easy-to-use option.
Note that my test unit originally came with a lid that warped after several months, allowing odors to escape and attracting fruit flies. Lomi said the initial batch of lids was made with faulty plastic and sent a new lid, but the new version is starting to warp as well after a couple of months.

First off, I appreciate that FoodCycler doesn’t even pretend it's making compost. “The FoodCycler is a food-waste recycler,” the company explained firmly before agreeing to ship a test unit. “Our primary goal is to provide a modern food-waste solution for users who may lack access to traditional composting or other disposal options that divert from the landfill. Therefore, the resulting byproduct cannot be labeled as ‘compost.’” And indeed, the FoodCycler breaks down food so quickly, and with no microbial involvement, that there’s no way anyone could think this was actual finished compost. But if you are opting for a grinder/dryer, know that the Eco 3 makes more groaning and creaking noises while in operation than the Lomi 3 above, but it is still a great pick.
Launched in 2024, the Eco 3 is a smaller version of the Vitamix FoodCycler FC-50 (7/10 WIRED Recommends), sporting a larger 3.5-liter capacity and, according to FoodCycler, better grinding capability. At 11 by 9 by 13 inches, it is small enough to sit on a counter or tabletop, though the real convenience with this machine is its auxiliary pail. Fill the sleek, 8-inch-tall lidded container with scraps (in my household of three people, this took about three days). Once it's full, swap out the lids, seat it in the machine, and press a button.
A few hours later, you'll have a handful of “Foodilizer,” a "homemade soil amendment” that looks like finely ground dirt, per FoodCycler. The output is among the most finely ground of any of these machines. There's no assembly (other than filling a filter with carbon granules), no app, no making an account, no pods or tablets or choosing various cycles—you don't even have to plug it in until you're ready to use it.
The cycle runs from four to nine hours, depending on the water content of the scraps. Though its base sound is an audible but unobtrusive whir (about 36 dB on my decibel meter), it has started making loud groaning and creaking sounds after six months of regular use, so I only run it at night or when I won't be home. I also occasionally had trouble getting the bucket to seat correctly, but the manual addresses this, and I figured it out after a couple of tries.
Note: If you know you like the FoodCycler, but you need a larger capacity, FoodCycler's XL Eco 5 model (see Also Tried, below) can accommodate 5 liters of kitchen waste with slightly larger dimensions (14 by 14 by 10 inches). A Decent Budget Grind-and-Dry Option
Like many of these devices, the R800 is called a “composter,” but it does not compost, and this detail irks me. There's a “Bio Compost” mode where you can add Airthereal Revive Magic Compost Starter. This is not included, costs $30 on Airthereal's website, and simply adds thermophilic bacteria, akin to the Reencle above. This will get the process started, but the result will not yield anything close to fully decomposed compost. To even achieve pre-compost, you will still need to mix small amounts with large amounts of soil and then let it cure for weeks.
However, amid the landscape of grind-and-dry kitchen-scrap processors, the Airthereal isn't half bad for the price. It's not as seamless or slick as the Lomi or FoodCycler, but it will effectively reduce the volume of your kitchen scraps. There's also a digital screen on the front that tells you what's happening. I also like that you can see into the machine thanks to its clear lid.
The biggest detractor was the lack of a lid for the bucket. The bucket is intended to sit in the machine (where there’s no need for a lid), but after using these kinds of devices for more than two years, I've found it is much more convenient to have a bucket handy for scraps while you're working, instead of having to periodically go over to the machine and press a button with dirty hands. Airthereal does make a bucket-and-lid option for an extra $60.
The R800 isn’t obnoxiously loud during its grind cycle, at about 40 decibels, and while there is an app, it's not required to use the machine. The device requires a fairly large footprint, so don't expect to put it on your kitchen counter. Another note: Remember that the carbon filter is on the back and its location is not immediately obvious—you will need to remove it and its stickers before using the device, lest you run the risk of going on an errand and coming back to the house smelling like a dumpster in the hot sun. (Don't ask me how I know.) Some Amazon reviews mention issues with overheating and jamming, but I've been using the Airthereal off and on for a year and have never experienced any mechanical issues.

Largest Capacity
All of these machines do a great job breaking down food scraps in some way or another, but none fully address what to do with them, absent a yard or compost pile. Adding them at a 1:10 (or even 1:15!) ratio to potting soil is kind of a pain, and many people don't have the space to store all this dirt. The Mill is the only device that solves this issue by allowing users to ship their grounds in a box via USPS to a farm in Washington state that repurposes the broken-down scraps for chicken feed (for an extra fee).
When I first tested the Mill in 2024 (6/10 WIRED Recommends), I didn't care for this idea, which seemed inefficient at best and canceled out the benefit of recycling the food waste at worst. I also didn't love the coarse texture of the grounds, having tried to use them in my garden and finding them too easily rehydrated. The price also seemed over the top for what's essentially an oversized Lomi. But if you're looking to reduce the amount of food waste leaving your house, the Mill has the best ease of use, requiring the least amount of work on a user's part.
Like the Reencle, it acts as a big trash can—you can throw in whatever you'd like at any time, and you can program a cycle any time you'd like via the app, which is exceedingly complete and user-friendly. There's an almost encyclopedic directory of what can and can't go in the machine, as well as a tracker that shows how many pounds of waste you've diverted over time. The Mill also has a massive capacity that only needs emptying about once a month—a claim I found to be accurate during my testing period. It's on the louder side at around 60 dB, so I highly recommend scheduling its processing cycle to run at night.
There are now two versions of the Mill: the Plus, which is the 27-inch version with a stylish wood-veneer top and lid-opening foot pedal that I tested, and the Essential, which is $200 cheaper, 4 inches shorter, and lacks the convenient foot pedal and wood-veneer finish. Both models have the same capacity.

The Analog OG
In order to understand the intended purpose of electric composters, one first needs to know about the original indoor home composting method: the bokashi bin. Unlike traditional outdoor composting, which is straightforward anaerobic decomposition, the bokashi method, invented in Japan in the 1980s, is anaerobic fermentation. This method is a bit like quick-pickling your food waste to prep it for the decomposition process. The food scraps still need to decompose, but this gets it part of the way there with the least amount of hassle and time. In fact, some gardeners even prefer bokashi to compost, as the output retains nitrogen, a critical plant nutrient.
To start, put your food scraps in the included bucket, and once you have about a 1-inch layer of waste, add a sprinkling of microbe-infused bran (a 2-pound bag of bran with a little spouted measuring cup is included with the Bokashi Living kit). The instruction booklet for my Bokashi Bin also recommended putting a plate inside the bucket to push down the contents. Compost “tea,” or liquid byproduct of the fermentation process, can drain through a spigot on the bottom every couple of days and then be added to your outdoor plants. The smell is reminiscent of kombucha brewed in a hot dumpster with diapers and stale beer, so be sure to rinse out the cup each time.
Once your bin is full, let it sit for two weeks, and your food waste will have broken down enough to bury in your garden or add to your backyard compost. I admit I struggled with this part—after two weeks, my scraps looked much the same, only stinkier and slimier. Bokashi Living says on its website that this is normal: If it has a pickle-like smell and produces bokashi tea, it's a success.
I’ll admit it was refreshing at first to have a device that didn’t make noise, need maintenance, or use electricity, but a few weeks into testing the Bokashi Bin, I found myself sorely missing my Reencle. I didn’t keep a separate scrap bin on the countertop, so every time I needed to add refuse to the bucket, I had to peel the lid off with my dirty hands and remove the plate, which then made my hands even dirtier. The smell of fermenting food waste would then immediately—and as time went on, almost violently—permeate the kitchen and its vicinity. I certainly prefer any of the electric options listed above, but bokashi has its devoted adherents. If what I've detailed above doesn't sound bothersome to you, it may be worth a try.

Other Kitchen Composters I Tried
Clear Drop Organics Collector (OC) for $399: From the makers of the innovative Soft Plastic Compactor, this simple white box does not claim to grind, process, or compost your food scraps; it simply stores up to 3.5 gallons' worth of them in an enclosed container with a fan and carbon filter for odor control. For its part, the OC did this well. I also appreciated the included paper-bag liners, which made it easy to drop off the scraps at a nearby collection bin, as my town does not have municipal compost. I also loved the sensor-activated lid that slides back and forth. Clear Drop posits that municipal composting is the best option overall for reducing waste via compost, because the process can be standardized for quality and is easy for everyone to comply. I agree, but let's be real: You can get a carbon-filter compost canister for less than $30. If taking the compost out every couple of days instead of every seven days is a chore you're willing to pay $400 to avoid, then knock yourself out. But you should know that the OC makes a loud fan noise—40 decibels on my decibel meter—which annoyed everyone in my household so much that I didn't even make it through the full test period.
Vego Countertop Kitchen Composter for $360: This grind-and-dry processor is roughly the same size as the Lomi, with many of the same operational features, but it is significantly less expensive. However, there are definitely some inconveniences that come with the lower price point. For one, you need to add scraps into the bucket while it’s seated in the machine. You can remove the bucket, but unlike with the FoodCycler, there's no separate lid for the bucket, and the metal mechanism underneath is exposed. Further, the machine’s lid is a bona fide pain to get on and off, requiring precise alignment of notches and two hands to wrench it open or closed. Needless to say, this is no easy feat with fists full of scraps. Vego claims its Vego mode does create a biologically active soil amendment when processed with one of the included VegoTabs (packet of 30, $30 if purchased separately). In all modes, but Vego mode especially, the barrel turns every couple of minutes, emitting a loud whirring. Because the sound isn't constant, it's more noticeable. Even from 10 feet away, I found it obtrusive enough to want to turn up the TV volume.
GEME Terra II for $700: Billed as the first “AI-powered kitchen appliance that uses industrial-grade microbes to turn waste into living soil,” this machine was the largest and bulkiest one I've tested (12 inches long, 22 inches high) and operates much like the Reencle, with a heated, enclosed container and a bag of proprietary starter microbes. Instead of a replaceable carbon filter, it uses a metal-ion purification system. Also similar to the Reencle, the GEME does not make ready-to-use compost but, rather, pre-compost that can be mixed with dirt. The role AI plays in this process is unclear: I couldn’t find an explanation on the website, on the machine itself, or in the instruction booklet. (GEME says it is working on an improved description.) The Terra II's signature feature is that its industrial-grade microbes can withstand the supposed high heat of the breakdown process. However, when I put a temperature probe into the Terra II's pre-compost after I'd had it running for about a week, it was 97 degrees Fahrenheit—nowhere near hot enough to kill pathogens. Further, during my testing period, this machine emitted a constant fan noise, like a range hood on medium speed—46 decibels on my decibel meter, which was loud enough to be disruptive.
FoodCycler Eco 5 for $500: Like the Eco 3 above, this is a food recycler and doesn’t claim to create true compost. It’s a large, quiet machine; my 3-year-old likes to turn it on when I’m not looking, and I don’t notice until I see that the blue light is on. The result doesn’t look like compost, but it does get ground down to some bare-bones food bits after several extra cycles my son initiates with his sneaky button-pushing. Each cycle runs between four and nine hours. It hasn’t been stinky, and I’ve found it handy to have nearby in the kitchen for food waste. It is quite large, though—nearly as bulky as my robot vacuum station due to its 5-liter capacity. The cheaper Eco 3 is likely a more efficient use of space in the kitchen, unless you have a ton of food scraps on a regular basis and really need the larger-capacity bin. —Nena Farrell
How I Tested
I cook daily for my family of three, and I've been processing our kitchen scraps in these composters in my home kitchen since the summer of 2024. I tested each machine under typical household use for a minimum of four weeks each, and in several cases, six weeks or longer. I tested all cycles offered, with all manner of foods allowed, according to each manual. I even attempted to use the finished product in my yard and potted plants (to varying effect). I acquired the units either by purchasing them myself or receiving them as samples from companies (with no expectation of coverage). When I completed testing, I donated or returned some units and kept others in office storage.

Your iPhone Duo can do more than multitask! These 10 quirky apps turn the foldable into a retro computer, cassette player, Nintendo DS, accordion, instant camera, virtual fridge, and even a grilled cheese toaster. Some are free, others paid, but all make clever, fun use of its folding design.
The iPhone Duo is perhaps the most radically different iPhone since the original iPhone. While its arrival was rumored for over a year, Apple finally launched it this September. The phone can fold in half to become nearly passport-sized and can be unfolded to shape-shift into a bigger, tablet-ish smartphone. Ever since its launch, we have been constantly hearing about its multitasking prowess, its computer-like processing abilities, how well it handles productivity apps, yada yada yada…
But all this is pretty basic, something we expect with all new iPhones, or rather flagship smartphones at this point. With the kind of price and specs these high-end smartphones come with, it hardly is a surprise that they can handle power-hungry tasks with ease. The foldable form-factor and the added display real estate make it a different experience, surely. But surely there is way more to the device than the same old tasks and apps? So, we are on a mission to make your iPhone Duo fun, using all that processing and multitasking magic that it possesses.
The result is these ten apps.
They are not at all useful. But they make the Duo a-not-just-another-serious (read: boring) device out there. They add an element to it that we all so need to survive – they make it fun. Got an iPhone Duo? Download! (Note: relax, all of these are optimized for the iPhone Duo)
