For years, GTA 5 has been one of the clearest examples of how far a game can stretch beyond what its developer originally built. Rockstar created Los Santos as a huge playground, then gave players years to find new ways to use it through GTA Online, mods, and roleplay. However, watching NoPixel V footage made me realise just how much further that idea can go in terms of GTA 6 UGC when creators are given the tools to reshape the world itself.
NoPixel V looks close enough to GTA 5 to feel familiar, while being different enough to resemble the kind of evolution I would expect from a GTA 5.5. That is where my mind went straight to the possibilities of UGC in GTA 6.
Roblox Taught Me That One Game Can Become Hundreds
Roblox has already shown how powerful creator content can become when players are allowed to build experiences of their own. Give players enough tools, and they will stop treating your game like a single game.
Blox Fruits can feel like a full action RPG, with its own progression, combat, and exploration, while Brookhaven turns the same platform into a social roleplaying space. Dress to Impress goes somewhere else entirely, focusing on fashion competitions and player expression.
The impressive part is how little these experiences need to resemble one another. Roblox gives creators enough freedom to establish their own rules, systems, and identities. The platform has become so large that players can spend their time inside experiences that feel completely removed from the original Roblox concept.
Some of these experiences have also reached enormous audiences, with Blox Fruits surpassing 64 billion visits and games like Grow a Garden and Steal a Brainrot reaching more than 20 million concurrent players during their peaks.
That tells us something important about UGC. Players are perfectly willing to follow the experience rather than the game it was built inside. That is the part Rockstar should be paying attention to.
GTA Online Had the Ingredients, Then Kept Players Inside the Box
GTA V always felt like it had the raw ingredients for something much bigger. The world was detailed enough to support almost any fantasy, while the character creator, vehicles, properties, and businesses gave players plenty of ways to make Los Santos feel personal.
GTA Online eventually added an enormous amount of content, but Rockstar still controlled the boundaries. For most of its lifespan, players could customize characters and properties or build basic races and jobs, while deeper structural changes remained out of reach.
Even with Rockstar introducing the in-depth Rockstar Mission Creator for branching custom missions in late 2025, true world-building on the scale of a custom server stayed locked behind PC modding. You could play inside Rockstar’s world, yet you could rarely fantasize about the world itself.
That is why FiveM and NoPixel became so important and popular. They showed what happened when the community received access to systems that Rockstar itself had kept separate from the standard experience.
Rockstar eventually brought Cfx re, the team behind FiveM and RedM, into the company. These creator communities then expanded the possibilities of GTA 5 Online. NoPixel took that idea even further.
NoPixel V Feels like GTA 5.5 for a Reason
Playing NoPixel V feels less like loading another GTA 5 server and more like opening a strange alternate version of the game. The team has spent nearly three years rebuilding parts of the map, adding new districts, creating interiors, and introducing more than 1,000 ownable properties.
The character system alone shows how far the idea can go. NoPixel V rebuilt character customization around greater flexibility, added more than 150 hairstyles, and launched with 270 custom clothing items. The team also rebuilt major interfaces, including the map, minimap, and inventory, instead of simply reskinning GTA V’s existing systems.
Rockstar has officially backed the project, with invited players accessing the closed beta through the Rockstar Games Launcher. This is still GTA V underneath. Yet the experience can feel like GTA 5 v2 because creators have been allowed to push so much further.
That makes the imagination of GTA 6 UGC far more interesting to me than another collection of custom races or missions. NoPixel V is showing Rockstar what happens when a community gets enough freedom to treat GTA as a platform rather than just a AAA game.
GTA 6 UGC Could Take the NoPixel Idea Much Further
I do not expect Rockstar to hand players the entire RAGE engine and say, “Go wild.” That would create obvious problems with moderation, quality control, and the consistency of Rockstar’s world. The more realistic possibility is a controlled creation system that gives players access to powerful tools without giving them unlimited control.
That could mean custom missions, businesses, roleplay systems, interiors, vehicles, cosmetics, and entire activities. Some reports and speculation have already pointed toward creator tools and custom experiences similar to Roblox and Fortnite UGC for GTA 6.
Rockstar has already moved from watching communities build around GTA to officially supporting one of the biggest examples of that creativity. A former Rockstar developer has also said he believes Rockstar could eventually allow players to create and monetize their own stories, provided the company can build safeguards around the tools.
That does not confirm anything about GTA 6 UGC. However, it does show that the conversation inside Rockstar is very different from what it was a decade ago.
Rockstar Has Seen What Happens When Players Build the Game
Epic has already paid more than $1 billion to third-party Fortnite developers. Their creator ecosystem now offers publishing, analytics, discovery, and several ways for creators to earn from their work.
Rockstar does not need to copy that model exactly. It only needs to recognize the larger lesson. Give talented players strong tools, put their creations in front of a huge audience, and the community will produce ideas that a traditional development team could never build at the same pace.
NoPixel V is probably not a secret preview of GTA 6 Online. Rockstar has not said that it is. Online roleplay features have not been confirmed for the next GTA either. Still, it is difficult to ignore the timing.
Rockstar now knows how much players can do when they are given room to experiment. It also knows that the world can support far more than the GTA 6 activities Rockstar originally designed.
If the company combines that knowledge with the technology behind GTA 6, UGC could become something much larger than a creator mode. Honestly, I don’t think Rockstar needs to make GTA 6 a Roblox-like platform. Roblox succeeds because it can become almost anything, while GTA succeeds because its world has a very specific identity.
We already know from Rockstar’s 26-minute GTA 6 Extended Look showcase that the foundational simulation of Leonida is built like a roleplayer’s dream. Native systems where diet, sleep, and stress physically alter your character’s body, police AI that tracks clothing and compromised vehicles, customizable properties, and persistent criminal profiles are all baked directly into the base game ahead of its November 19 launch.
Features that NoPixel spent years scripting from scratch for GTA V will exist out of the box in GTA 6. This means creators won’t have to spend their time building basic life-sim mechanics, and can instead focus on transforming the world itself. Rockstar Games already shared what GTA 6 roleplay mechanics we are getting.
The exciting possibility is combining those strengths. Imagine opening GTA 6 Online and finding a sci-fi roleplay city. That with a completely original story-driven experience, a social space, a racing league. A strange game in a familiar world that feels nothing like traditional GTA.
Or what if it is a zombie apocalypse with the same fidelity? That is built within the GTA 6 map but with entirely different mechanics built from scratch. The world would remain Rockstar’s, but the reasons to keep returning would come from everyone else.
That is what NoPixel V has made me think about. It takes a game I have known for years and makes it feel unfamiliar again.
If Rockstar gives players even a fraction of that freedom in its next online game, I think GTA 6 UGC could become one of the biggest parts of the entire experience.

This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?
At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.
This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.
Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.
Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.
And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.
NPR spoke to Jain through a video call about the experiences that inspired him, the challenge of persuading boys and men to join the conversation on periods and what he has learned about changing deeply entrenched attitudes.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You were just 14 when you became concerned about menstrual health. What happened to make you realize that something needed to change?
It started with something that happened to a very close friend of mine in 2023, when we were in the tenth grade. We had been friends since the fifth grade. She used to call me her brother and would tie a rakhi every year [a sacred thread that girls tie around the wrist of a brother or brother-like figure, as a symbol of their bond, during the Indian festival of Raksha Bandhan].
During our midterm examinations, I noticed that she was struggling. She was in so much pain. I could not put a finger on it. What's happening? Does she have a fever? What's going on? So I checked in on her, and she said "I'm on my period, and I'm having really bad cramps." And then she just started crying. We took her to the medical room, where she was given a painkiller, and her parents were called to take her home. In India, menstruation is something that is very concealed. It's a very hush-hush topic. Not a lot of people talk about it openly in their families.
She had been experiencing severe cramps for six to eight months, and before that, her periods had been very irregular. But the next day, she was back in school, with the same pain. Her parents thought she was trying to get out of her examinations.
She is such a bright person, but for one or two weeks every month, she would become like a wilted rose. She couldn't concentrate in class or do well in her tests.
I went home and asked my mother what we could do. My mother spoke to our teacher, who contacted my friend's parents and encouraged them to take her to a doctor.
She was subsequently diagnosed with PCOS [now referred to as PMOS, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome], and doctors were also investigating the possibility of endometriosis. She received treatment, made changes to her lifestyle and gradually improved. She's so much better now, because of her own efforts, and because she got the help she needed at the right time.
That experience really stayed with me.
Why did her experience affect you so deeply?
I remember once breaking my little toe against the edge of my bed. My father left his office, which was two hours away, came home and took me to the emergency room. I had an X-ray, and my foot was bandaged.
I thought, what if we responded to menstrual pain with the same concern?
What if a girl could simply tell her father, "Dad, I'm having really bad cramps, and I can't go to school today," and he would say, "Okay, let me get you a heating pad"?
But because menstruation is such a hush-hush topic, especially around the men in a family, that kind of conversation often doesn't happen.
And sometimes, even the women in a family aren't able to support other women in the way they deserve.
I realized that this was something that needed attention.
How did that concern and empathy develop into Team Period?
I studied at Amity International School, and our school runs a program called Youth Power through its student newspaper, The Global Times. [the only registered school newspaper in India].
Schools form teams of four students, choose a social cause and spend several months working to create change in their communities. Then the schools compete with each other [to see who has the best ideas]. Our team consisted of me, Shivansh Arora, Aaratrika Jha Anand and Navya Manglik — so we're two boys and two girls.
Initially, Team Period began like any other school competition. We spent about six months working on the issue. But when the competition ended, I didn't want the work to end.
There is a certain feeling you get when you're talking to people, knowing that what you are saying matters, and maybe one day it could even change someone's life. But it wasn't just about that feeling. It was about the change we were creating at the grassroots level.
I have always been interested in public health, and I hope to work with an organization like the WHO or the United Nations one day. But as a 16- or 17-year-old, you can't just show up at the WHO and say you want to change things.
You have to start somewhere.
As a teenage boy, did you encounter resistance when you began talking about menstruation? Did girls ever accuse you of mansplaining?
Of course, people were surprised that a 15-year-old boy wanted to tackle menstrual shame.
But our friends were very supportive because we never approached the issue as experts. We approached it as learners. I never thought that I could explain what happens to a woman's body better than a woman herself.
At times, I was the face of the campaign. I was the spokesperson delivering speeches and talking to young women about menstruation. But it never came from a place of thinking that I knew more than they did. It came from a place of wanting to help solve a problem.
Everything we did was approached with empathy, sensitivity and respect. One girl might be completely comfortable talking about her periods in front of a classroom, while another might be deeply embarrassed.
Our goal is to end that shame, but we don't want to do it by shaming the person herself.
Were there moments when you realized that it might be harder than you thought to include boys in this conversation?
Yes. There was a workshop we organized at a school where the boys were asked to leave the room, so the girls could discuss these issues freely.
Initially, I was very upset because the whole point of our project was that boys should learn about menstruation, too.
But once the boys left, I saw girls who had been completely silent suddenly asking questions, laughing and speaking openly.
That was a learning experience for me.
Sometimes, girls need their own space to talk about these things. You can't force everyone to be comfortable immediately. We later held a separate session for the boys and eventually brought everyone together for a discussion. So at the end of the day, boys and girls were able to talk about it openly. I learned that creating an open environment is a process.
Can you describe an experience that convinced you your work was making a difference? Anything that really surprised you?
We once held an activity with middle-school students where we taught them to make simple heating pads using socks filled with lentils or chickpeas.
There was a boy, about 12 years old, who was very disruptive. He kept interrupting us and asking why he needed to learn about periods. His attitude was essentially that this had nothing to do with him. The teacher wanted to send him to another classroom, but we said no. We wanted him to stay and participate. About a year later, after I had finished school, I returned to visit my teachers and met that boy again.
He told me that his younger sister, who was barely 9 years old, had got her first period when they were alone at home. She was terrified. She had gone to the bathroom, seen the blood and started crying and screaming for help. But because of our workshop, he knew what was happening. He called his mother and asked where she kept the sanitary pads. He reassured his sister, helped her get cleaned up, made her a heating pad and even ordered chocolates for her.
By the time his mother returned, his sister was feeling much better.
He came up to me and thanked me. He said that when we first held the workshop, he couldn't understand why he needed to know any of this.
But when his sister needed help, he knew what to do. The fulfillment I felt in that moment was incomparable. To know that you've touched even one life is such a big honor.
You have used some unusual ways to get people talking about menstruation, including dance performances and flash mobs. How did those work?
We wanted to tackle menstrual shame from different directions, including through culture and performance.
One of our productions was a dance drama set during Durga Puja [a major Hindu festival honoring Goddess Durga's victory over a demon].
In the story, a young girl is performing the aarti [a Hindu ritual where a lamp is lit and prayers are offered] when her grandmother notices a menstrual stain on her clothes. The grandmother immediately excludes her from the prayers.
But Durga [the goddess] sees what has happened. She appears, comforts the girl and brings her back. I came up with the story, but the whole school helped put it together — the dance teachers, art teachers, costume designers, students and everyone involved in the production.
We performed it before an audience of more than 500 people in April 2025, and we've since performed or screened it at other events.
We also organized a flash mob at a mall and held activities at our school's winter carnival, where students, parents and grandparents participated in games about menstrual health.
One game involved picking colored chits containing questions about menstruation. People had only a short time to respond, which encouraged spontaneous answers instead of rehearsed ones. Sometimes a young boy would play, pick up a question and ask, all confused, "What is PCOS?"
We would stop the game and spend 10 minutes explaining it.
Our goal was to spark conversations.
You conducted surveys. Did this give you an insight into the way people think about menstruation?
We have been conducting surveys among students, parents and the wider community. At this point, we have collected around 4,000 responses.
One response that really struck us came from an eighth-grade girl.
She was angry that nobody cared if someone got a vegetable stain or ketchup on their clothes, but if a girl had a red menstrual stain on the back of her uniform, it became a huge issue.
Until then, our approach had been to teach boys to be sensitive — if a girl had a stain, you could quietly tell her or offer her your jacket.
But her response made us question that approach. Why should a menstrual stain be so embarrassing in the first place?
So we decided to normalize it.
We began wearing red stains on our uniforms. Some were stitched from red cloth, while others were stickers. At first, everyone laughed at us. Even the school objected because we were ruining the look of our uniforms with these big red patches.
But over the course of a week, more and more students joined in.
By the end, there was a sea of students wearing red stains. Some wore them on their backs, others on their shirts or identification cards.
When we conducted another survey months later, many students said they no longer felt that it was such a shame to spot or have a red stain.
We can't change attitudes across all of India immediately, but we were able to change something in our school.
In addition to changing attitudes and addressing stigma, what other aspects of menstrual care are you looking into?
There are several aspects to our work.
One is cultural — breaking down taboos and stigma. Another is logistical. How do you ensure that girls and women have access to menstrual products without feeling ashamed to ask for them? We installed a sanitary pad dispenser at our school.
Now we're talking to companies about how we could make dispensers available to other schools at a nominal cost. We are also exploring the possibility of developing our own design.
Disposal is another major issue. Used sanitary pads are often wrapped in newspaper and thrown into the garbage. But think about the people who sort that waste. How are they supposed to know what is inside the newspaper?
We're exploring a disposal system in which used pads can be sealed in specially designed bags, with clear warnings and illustrations in different languages. We want to think not just about the people using menstrual products but also those who handle the waste.
Your work has largely been concentrated in Delhi. Any plans to expand?
Until now, we've worked in government schools, orphanages, underserved neighborhoods and our own school in Delhi. We've also organized health camps.
But we were students, and our budgets were limited. We couldn't simply fly to Chennai or another city to replicate everything.
Now we want to decentralize Team Period and create local chapters.
Our team members are already spreading out to different cities and countries for their studies.
We'd like to bring in volunteers who speak different regional languages so that we can communicate more effectively with communities.
What does winning the Diana Award mean to you? Does it provide funding to help expand Team Period?
The Diana Award doesn't come with prize money.
But I think what it gives us is something equally valuable: recognition that our work matters.
When you're young and approaching potential sponsors or partners, people naturally have questions. They want to know whether you're legitimate and whether your work is making a difference. An international recognition like the Diana Award helps establish that credibility.
It gives us a platform to take our work to a larger audience.
For me, personally, it's deeply meaningful because we've faced moments when people questioned why boys were talking about menstruation. We've received strange looks from older people and even people of our own generation.
But this recognition tells us to keep showing up, even when things are difficult.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times , The British Medical Journal , the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

What to know about upcoming peace talks involving Russian, Ukrainian and US officials
For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark

For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda.
The two-day session starting Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, follows previous rounds of negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.
The negotiations follow last month's localized truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.
But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the weeklong ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line. Both sides also have escalated their long-range attacks on each other with drones and missiles.
A look at the talks and what's on the agenda:
Russia and Ukraine have sharply divergent demands
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal.
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed early in the war but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that such a pause would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede Ukrainian territory Russia has not been able to take on the battlefield and agree to limits on the military and arrangements with Western partners, which it sees as essential security guarantees to stop Russia invading again in the future.
Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.
Security guarantees top the agenda
Russia and Ukraine said the Abu Dhabi talks will focus on security guarantees.
Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine and its allies have discussed security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5, which states the alliance sees an attack on one of its members as an attack against all.
In an interview broadcast Nov. 5, he said Ukraine's security guarantees boil down to what Western allies would do if Russia launches a new invasion of his country.
“If Russia starts again, what will happen,” Zelenskyy asked. “Who will do what, with what means, and when?”
Some European nations have mulled a possible deployment of their troops to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal. Russia rejects that as a nonstarter, warning it would view any European troops on Ukrainian soil as legitimate targets.
The Kremlin insists that any prospective deal should offer security guarantees for Russia as well. Just before Moscow launched the all-out invasion in 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments of troops and weapons from the alliance's members in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal put forth by Russia.
U.S. President Donald Trump said after meeting Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House on Nov. 4 that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, although he did not elaborate.
“It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that it might include all of Europe.
Ukraine wants Europe at the table but Russia says no
Ukraine insists its European allies must have a seat at the negotiating table, while Russia opposes any such involvement at this stage.
“No one is going to invite them to the negotiating table,” Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov snapped when asked if European envoys could join the Abu Dhabi talks. He added that if they fly there, they won't be allowed into the room.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Europeans would need to be involved in broader negotiations, but only later.
“Since the discussion will touch upon the future security architecture in Europe while addressing the mutual security of Russia and Ukraine, at some stage it would be impossible to do it without the Europeans,” he said.
On Oct. 27, Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Putin in their first known direct conversation since shortly after the 2022 invasion. They said they spoke in their capacity as the heads of Russia's Nordic neighbors and not on behalf of the European Union, which has struggled to pick a negotiator with Moscow.
Peskov sarcastically noted that EU members “can’t even decide yet who is authorized to speak on their behalf,” calling it “a protracted indecisiveness and a lack of readiness on its part.”
On Nov. 4, Zelenskyy said in a post on X that he had held a 90-minute conversation with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, saying the talks “must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible.”
Kushner said on X that “our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment.”
For over 30 years, “Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework,” Kushner wrote. “Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace.”
He noted the main goals of the talks were “permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”
Russia’s envoy took a hard line at earlier talks
Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia’s delegation in the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022 and in subsequent sessions, remains Moscow’s chief negotiator.
A former culture minister who wrote books about purported Western plots against Russia over the centuries, Medinsky is known for his hard-line views and blustery statements. At the 2025 talks, also in Istanbul, he reportedly said it took Peter the Great 21 years to defeat Sweden in the 18th century and Moscow also is ready now to fight as long as it takes.
Russia ramps up strikes on Ukraine’s power grid
Putin has said repeatedly that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Ukraine fails to accept its conditions for peace.
Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukraine’s power system, seeking to undermine the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy said last week that “every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by attacks” and urged Kyiv's allies to provide generators and other equipment to keep the electricity flowing.
He also pleaded with allies to tap their own air defense stockpiles to help Ukraine fend off Russia's attacks and replenish them later.

Your Mac's hard drive is full ... again. What's taking up all that space? Endless applications promise to answer this question and help you free up space, most with a subscription. I've tested many over the years, and few are easier to recommend than Purge.
This totally free, open source app gives you a quick breakdown of what's taking up space on your hard drive and offers a few specific ways to free it up. Even better: There are no ads or upsells. Purge can even delete Apple Intelligence's offline models from macOS 27, which could free up over 10 GB.
But even if you want to keep Apple's AI features, you can still clear up plenty of space. Your Mac, like any computer, tends to build up clutter over time. Sure, you might have forgotten about the games, images, and videos you downloaded, but caches also take up space. These are files downloaded and saved to speed things up, which can be useful. The problem is they can stick around longer than necessary and take up space. And then there are caches and settings left behind by apps you uninstalled ages ago—they're still there, eating up precious bytes.
Purge is designed to help you clean all that out, but it can do more. It's built around lists of files known to be safe to purge. There's also a list of things it will never touch, including crucial system files and your own documents. Finally, Purge sends files to the Trash instead of deleting them outright, so you can always recover them if something breaks.
To get started, download Purge and install it. Open the application, and it will show you what's taking up space on your Mac.
If you want, click the Clean Safe Items button, and the app will handle it, assuming you trust it. I recommend paying a bit more attention, though. First, delete some caches. You'll see a list of caches, all of which are safe to purge periodically.
You'll also see Apple's Aerial screen savers here. These videos are very cool, but take up a lot of space—delete them if you, like most 21st-century people, don't use a screen saver.
There's also a Dev Tools section, which isn't relevant for most people. If you use Homebrew, though, don't skip this—it's an easy way to delete cached installation files you don't need anymore.
The next tool shows you only the largest files on your computer, likely videos or other large media. I ended up moving a few things I'd forgotten about off my laptop—I bet you'll find something, too.
Up next is a tool for uninstalling apps. Note that this doesn't just remove the application—it also removes every file associated with it, including your settings, caches, and anything the application downloaded. Deleting applications in Finder doesn't do this, meaning you might leave all kinds of files behind.
Speaking of that, there's also a tool that shows leftover data from applications you've already deleted. In my case, it was several gigabytes, all basically wasted. I highly recommend checking this section and deleting anything large that you're confident you won't use again.
Finally, so long as we're talking about things you're not using, there's Apple Intelligence. Apple's most recent operating systems come preloaded with offline AI models, which power things like notification summaries, writing suggestions, and the new AI-powered Siri. You might like and use these features, but if not, Apple removed the toggle in macOS 27 that lets you disable them altogether.
That's why Purge has one final tool that can completely remove the Apple Intelligence models. Click it, and you'll see a list of installed models above a delete button. Click the button, and Purge will delete the models and prevent macOS from reinstalling them.
These features are why I plan on keeping Purge around. It's a great way to see what's taking up space on your drive and then do something about it.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Israel’s president has chosen Gadi Eisenkot, the prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s strongest rival, to try to form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.
Netanyahu is fighting to hold on to office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc in parliament.
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, 66-year-old Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.
Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.
Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of Eisenkot’s partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.
Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.
Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.
Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.
Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.
Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement; these types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse.
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
But he opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.
Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.
After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.
If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.

U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth
Secretary of War says he is happy to litigate military actions of the administration 'all day long'
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
The impeachment resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran. It also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie said the secretary's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanours" and his leadership at the Pentagon "thus warrants impeachment."
A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.
House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.
"Impeaching a cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that," Johnson, a Republican, said as he opened the chamber.
"We don't impeach cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that's what this is and I think everybody knows it."
Hegseth defends actions
Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Massie said Hegseth has violated international norms and the U.S.'s own conventions of war in Iran.
"It's to the disadvantage and the dishonour of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflict," he said.
Hegseth said earlier Monday he's eager to litigate the military actions that he and U.S. President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela's previous leaders.
"If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you're taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic," Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis' attacks on shipping in the Middle East.
Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May, and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other U.S. military actions since then.
The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress. Massie pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the conflict.
Hegseth gave a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Sept. 30, but has not held a media availablity since May. (Alex Wong/Pool/The Associated Press)
Hegseth waves off impeachment push as 'noise'
Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the possible impeachment push.
"There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long."
"My team, we're not worried about the noise — it's what I told the troops, too — don't worry about the noise," he said.
Asked about U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive Republican losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and "I agree."
He largely repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters a day earlier: "It doesn't have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary."
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because "someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon" and said "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move."
Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms of uranium that is enriched up to 60 per cent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent.
Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night.
"He's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," Trump said. "I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it's awfully hard to say let's impeach somebody who did that."
Hegseth insists 'Iran is devastated'
Hegseth reiterated that "Iran is devastated," even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters' pocketbooks.
He said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including telling Iran: "Hey, we're done, and we're going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it."
With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be "all about the politics of personal destruction" and insisted that "won't work with me. You can rest assured of that."
Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections
- Published
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
- ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline 
  - Published4 days ago
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 years
NEW DELHI: Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday's AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025's post-Diwali air quality.Diwali AQI in 2025 (Oct 20) was 345, 328 in 2024 (Oct 31), 218 in 2023 (Nov 12), 312 in 2022 (Oct 24) and 382 in 2021 (Nov 4). Post-Diwali AQI in 2025 was 351, 339 in 2024, 358 in 2023, 303 in 2022 and 462 in 2021. Diwali-eve this year, Nov 7, was the most polluted since 2016, with AQI of 369.Meanwhile, several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data. Initially, hourly data went missing for 35 air quality monitoring stations. Although DPCC later updated data at some of its stations, several went blank at peak pollution hours, and only 47 contributed to average AQI on Diwali day. Delhi has 60 monitoring stations managed by DPCC, CPCB, IITM and IMD, of which one had been defunct for a few months.Firecrackers emerged as the biggest contributor a day before Diwali (Chhoti Diwali), accounting for 41.1% of the total load, according to IITM data till 9am Nov 8.
On a wind and prayer, capital braces for uncertain times as winter sets inWhile traces of lead, potassium and sulphur in the air were confirmed, officials said they can confirm the presence of mercury only in a long-term study.At midnight on Nov 8, IITM recorded its highest average PM2.5 concentration, at 671.1 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³). Among individual stations, Jahangirpuri in northwest Delhi recorded a peak of 4,985 µg/m³ Sunday night and Monday morning. However, DPCC later updated to park PM2.5 level of 776µg/m³ at 11am Sunday. Mundka in west Delhi recorded PM2.5 level at 3,744 µg/m³ at 2am, which remained unchanged, followed by 3,023.2µg/m³ at JNU. The prescribed 24-hour average national limit for PM2.5 is 60 µg/m³.The average PM2.5 concentration on Diwali 2026 stood at 257 µg/m³, against 228 µg/m³ last year, 201 µg/m³ in 2024, 134 µg/m³ in 2023, 176 µg/m³ in 2022 and 318 µg/m³ in 2021.On Monday, Delhi saw the season’s first dense fog, with visibility dropping to 50m at Safdarjung at 6.30am, which kept the AQI in the upper range of very poor levels. However, a sudden, unusual shift in winds from northwesterly to strong easterly, aided by faster dispersion, kept stubble smoke from Punjab and Haryana at bay, preventing a sharper spike, especially when Punjab on Nov 8 saw the highest farm fire incidents of the season, at 1,152.The post-Diwali reprieve, said experts, was more meteorological than the result of pollution-control measures. With winter conditions setting in, the wind reversal could bring back the familiar pollution cocktail, they added.Gufran Beig, founder of System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research (SAFAR) and chair professor at the National Institute of Advanced Studies (NIAS), said Delhi was “very lucky” this year, not cleaner.“An unusual weather development associated with an approaching cyclone and a western disturbance caused winds to turn easterly from their persistent northwesterly direction. These winds, travelling at around 6.7 metres per second from the surface to nearly 400 metres, against the usual 3-4 m/s, helped disperse pollutants rapidly and prevented stubble-burning smoke from reaching Delhi,” he said. The easterlies were expected to persist until Tuesday morning, before winds potentially reverted to northwesterly.Calling the situation a reflection of the region’s worsening pollution-control battle, Anumita Roychowdhury of Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) said, “This post-Diwali pollution crisis is the direct result of a toxic convergence of adverse winter meteorology, escalating pre-Diwali traffic gridlocks and a rise in contribution of farm fires. Firecrackers were an uncontrolled tipping point.”
Delhi and the wider region, she added, were losing the battle to curb emissions from both continuous local sources and episodic spikes, at a very high health cost.The scale of the firecracker contribution was even more stark in an analysis by Sunil Dahiya, founder and lead analyst at Envirocatalysts. He estimated that crackers added roughly 450 µg/m³ to peak-hour PM2.5 concentrations and contributed around 270-400 µg/m³, or more than half the PM2.5 Delhi residents breathed, during the 9pm-2am period.Dahiya said pollution began building from around 8pm, peaked between 1am and 3am, and remained above 500 µg/m³ for four hours.

- Microsoft could soon consider selling Xbox following the Democrats' victory in the 2026 US midterm elections.
- Analyst Joost van Dreunen believes growing opposition to data centers could threaten Microsoft's AI expansion plans.
- He believes Microsoft's declining Xbox revenue could push the company to sell the division to fund its AI ambitions.
The Democrats have won control of both the House and Senate in the 2026 US midterm elections, marking a major political shift that could also affect Xbox. Gaming industry analyst Joost van Dreunen believes the US election results could push Microsoft to sell its gaming division, despite Xbox CEO Asha Sharma recently stating that Xbox is not for sale.
In the analyst’s November 5 Substack post, Van Dreunen points to growing voter opposition to data centers, with a recent Wall Street Journal report saying that more than 40 towns and counties discussed measures to limit data center construction, with at least 10 voting to restrict or ban new projects. For Microsoft, which is heavily invested in AI, this isn’t good news.
Microsoft’s growing focus on AI and data center expansion also played a part in the “XBOX Reset” in July 2026, which saw the company cut more than 3,000 jobs and make major changes across its gaming division. Furthermore, while PlayStation continues to grow its gaming revenue, Xbox is lagging behind Microsoft’s other business divisions.
Xbox generated $5.4 billion in revenue in the previous quarter of 2026, which includes Xbox Game Pass and other services, down 2% from the same period last year. Meanwhile, Microsoft’s Search and Advertising division grew from $5.9 billion to $6.6 billion, highlighting the gap between Xbox and the company’s other businesses.
Van Dreunen believes Microsoft could sell Xbox to free up resources and, mainly, revenue for its AI ambitions. He also argues that CEO Asha Sharma’s announcement of Xbox XP, a division focused on turning gaming IPs into films and TV shows, could make the brand more appealing to potential buyers, since it showcases Xbox as a more traditional entertainment company.
Asha Sharma also recently announced Xbox Labs, an experimental R&D unit exploring AI-powered game development. So, with Democrats now controlling both chambers of Congress, Van Dreunen believes Microsoft’s AI ambitions could make an Xbox sale a more serious possibility. That said, do you think Microsoft will sell Xbox after the US election results? Let us know.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

Packers & Bengals win in style - NFL week nine
- Published
The potential Super Bowl contenders are starting to emerge in the NFL with the regular season having reached its halfway point this weekend.
The San Francisco 49ers have the league's best record after winning on Sunday and will be joined on 7-1 by either the Buffalo Bills or Minnesota Vikings - provided they do not have a tie in Monday's game.
The Chicago Bears and Denver Broncos both ground out hard-fought wins to improve to 7-2 heading into their bye weeks.
The Cincinnati Bengals put on a show as the NFL's international series continued while the Green Bay Packers outclassed one of last season's Super Bowl teams.
Here are the top stories from week nine in the NFL.
Broncos claim NFL record
After winning at defending champions Seattle last week, Chicago looked set for another impressive victory as they charged into a 14-0 lead against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Sunday's primetime game.
Bears quarterback Caleb Williams then threw a career-high four interceptions before the Bucs drew level with three minutes remaining.
But Williams managed to lead the hosts into field-goal range, with Cairo Santos making a 38-yard kick as time expired to beat the Bucs 27-24 for Chicago's fourth straight win.
The Bears are now second in the NFC North, the only division in which all four teams have a winning record, but will go top if the Vikings lose to the Bills on Monday.
Denver are top of the AFC West after they scored two touchdowns in the final quarter and sacked Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young with just over a minute left to clinch a 26-21 road win.
Not only did it extend the Broncos' winning run to five but was their 16th straight win in one-score games in the regular season - a new NFL record.
Bengals put on a show in Spain
Joe Burrow attended Milan fashion week this summer and modelled in Paris in 2024, but this week he visited Madrid to play his first international game.
The Cincinnati Bengals quarterback vowed to put on a show at the Bernabeu Stadium in the seventh of a record nine international games this season, and the Bengals did just that as they beat the Atlanta Falcons 34-17 to go 6-2.
After being involved in six touchdowns last week, Burrow played a part in another four in Spain. The 29-year-old completed 24 of his 29 passes for 271 yards to cement himself as a contender for his first Most Valuable Player award.
Ja'Marr Chase had a season-high 155 receiving yards as the Bengals scored more than 30 points for a fourth straight game – tying a team record.
The Bengals are now 6-2 and joint-top of the AFC North with the Pittsburgh Steelers, who they face in next Sunday's primetime game.
Their divisional rivals the Cleveland Browns lost 23-22 at the New Orleans Saints in overtime.
Packers ruin return of Patriots legends
Four-time Super Bowl winner Rob Gronkowski was inducted into the New England Patriots' hall of fame while his former team-mate Tom Brady returned to Gillette Stadium for the first time in his broadcasting career.
Yet they had to watch Green Bay quarterback Jordan Love put on a masterclass as the Packers romped to a 45-27 win against a New England team that reached last season's Super Bowl. It was the most points the Patriots had allowed at home since 1970.
Love went deep time and again, racking up 372 passing yards, three touchdown passes and a touchdown run. Wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden became the first Green Bay players to each claim more than 150 receiving yards and a touchdown in the same game since 1942.
Brady and Gronkowski are third all-time for passing yards from a quarterback-tight end duo (9,186) and Kansas City Chiefs pair Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce went top of that list on Sunday.
Mahomes brushed off an injury scare against the New York Jets to ensure he and Kelce surpassed Philip Rivers and Antonio Gates (9,352) to reach 9,360 during a 35-12 win for the Chiefs.
Garrett stars on Rams return
Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald finally played together for the first time as the Los Angeles Rams won 20-13 at the Washington Commanders.
After making his Rams debut in Australia in week one, Garrett needed knee surgery and Donald didn't make his return from retirement until week two.
While Donald, 35, is still waiting for his first sack of the season, Garrett claimed three and forced a fumble to help the former Super Bowl favourites clinch a third straight win.
Puka Nacua racked up 150 receiving yards and a touchdown but could join fellow wide receiver Davante Adams (hamstring) on the sidelines as he injured a knee. Nacua will have an MRI on Monday.
Although the Rams are now 5-4, their NFC West rivals the San Francisco 49ers and Seattle Seahawks both got back to winning ways.
The 49ers (7-1) won 38-17 against the Las Vegas Raiders while defending champions Seattle (5-4) beat the Arizona Cardinals 17-3.
More Colts trades before deadline?
The Indianapolis Colts have already begun a rebuild, trading away two key players during the season, and they could have more big-name departures before the trade deadline on Tuesday.
The Colts slipped to 2-7 with a 27-23 loss to the Dallas Cowboys but had already been in talks over running back Jonathan Taylor, their prized asset.
They have reportedly taken calls about quarterback Daniel Jones too, while wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade.
The New York Giants withdrew an offer for Taylor but head coach John Harbaugh said that "things do change" after Sunday's 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles – a seventh straight loss for Philly and the Giants' first win at their divisional rivals in 13 years.
Down to their third-choice quarterback, the Baltimore Ravens have completed a trade for Jacoby Brissett from Arizona but despite speculation over Derrick Henry, the Ravens reportedly have no intention of trading the veteran running back.
Arizona pair Budda Baker and Josh Sweat have been linked with a trade while there has been interest in wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr, who has slipped down the pecking order at the 6-2 Jacksonville Jaguars.
